areas.title: SEC bulk backfill performance deep dive
areas.summary: I traced the full sec-backfill path end to end: ZIP member, then JSON, then metadata, then one sequential HTTP fetch per filing, then a cache write with fsync, then XML parsed twice, then trade mapping, then one SQLite transaction per filing, then a full checkpoint rewrite. The main reason the run never gets halfway is the checkpoint. After every filing it sorts the whole completed set, pretty-prints it as JSON and fsyncs it. Measured on this machine (benchmark at C:\Users\lukas\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\ca06d48fbcec0067\e24a750a-1bcd-4398-9d3f-359558b4187e\scratchpad\BULK\bench.py), one save takes 20 ms at 10k completed, 169 ms at 100k, 1.17 s at 500k and 2.5 s at 1M. That makes the run quadratic: about 1.25e-6·N² seconds, so about 3.5 h of checkpointing alone to reach 100k filings and about 87 h to reach 500k. Other measured fixed costs per filing: DB upsert 38 ms (one BEGIN IMMEDIATE per filing, NullPool reconnect, rollback journal with synchronous=FULL); cache write with fsync 11.8 ms plus 3.5 ms of repeated Path.resolve checks; parsing 0.8 ms. The network uses requests.get with no Session (TLS handshake to www.sec.gov measured at 30–100 ms per new connection) and no parallelism, which I estimate at about 0.15–0.3 s per filing. Current throughput is roughly 10–14k filings/h at the start, about 7k/h at 100k completed and about 2.5k/h at 500k. The archive has an estimated 5–7M unique XML-era Form 3/4/5 accessions, and each appears once per related CIK, so roughly 2x as many metadata rows. Even with every local fix in place, fetching each filing is capped by SEC fair access (8 req/s by default, about 28.8k filings/h), so about 6M filings would take about 9 days. The structural fix is the SEC DERA Insider Transactions Data Sets. I confirmed by web search (sec.gov/dera/data/form-345 and the readme PDF) that they are built from the XML part of Forms 3/4/5, are updated quarterly, and include SUBMISSION, REPORTINGOWNER and NONDERIV_TRANS/DERIV_TRANS tables keyed by ACCESSION_NUMBER. History would then take about 80 downloads plus bulk inserts, measured at about 150 µs per filing with executemany, so minutes to about an hour in total. The per-filing pipeline would only be needed for the current quarter. Secondary issues: errors that will always fail (pre-2003 non-XML Form 4s, xs:date values with a timezone) are fetched again on every run; the checkpoint is deleted after a 'complete' run even when there were failures; the parser keeps only the first reportingOwner; and after a backfill, query_latest and the feed scan or sort the whole multi-million-row table.

kept.title: Checkpoint rewrites, sorts and fsyncs the entire completed set after every filing (O(N^2))
kept.evidence:
if ok and reached_sink[0]:
                    completed.add(meta.accession_number)
                    self._save_completed(zip_path, completed)
...
                    "completed_accessions": sorted(completed),
kept.description: After each successful filing, _save_completed calls sorted(completed), then json.dumps(indent=2) (json_state.py:29), writes a temp file, fsyncs it (json_state.py:39) and calls os.replace. The cost grows with the number of completed filings. Measured on this machine: 6 ms/save at 1k, 20 ms at 10k, 169 ms at 100k (2.9 MB file), 1,175 ms at 500k (14.5 MB) and 2,528 ms at 1M (29 MB). Total time is about 1.25e-6·N² s: about 3.5 h to reach 100k filings, about 87 h to reach 500k and about 14 days to reach 1M, before any network time. This alone explains 'takes hours and does not even get to half'. The module docstring (lines 8-10) admits the set 'can grow large' but misses that it is rewritten for every filing.
kept.suggestion: Replace the JSON snapshot with an append-only log: one accession per line, opened once, flushed every K filings, fsynced every M filings or T seconds, and loaded into a set on start. Better still, make the database the checkpoint: add a sec_ingested_filings(accession PRIMARY KEY, status, attempts, last_error, ingested_at) table and write its rows in the same transaction as the trades. Persisting trades and progress atomically also removes the crash window between the upsert and the checkpoint. If a snapshot is kept, throttle it to every few thousand filings or 30 s and drop indent=2 and sorted().
kept.verifier_note: sec_backfill.py:158-160 calls _save_completed after every successful filing, and that rebuilds sorted(completed) (line 208) and calls atomic_write_json, which uses json.dumps(indent=2) plus fsync plus os.replace (json_state.py:29-40). Cost per save grows linearly with the completed set, so the total is quadratic. The quoted timings are the right order of magnitude (a fit at 1.7e-6 s per entry gives about 2.3 h to reach 100k, against the reviewer's 3.5 h).

kept.title: Fetching every filing over the network cannot finish a full history; use the DERA Insider Transactions Data Sets
kept.evidence:
ok = process_filing_row(
                    row,
                    client=self._client,
                    cache_root=self._cache_root,
                    counters=counters,
kept.description: Every ownership accession in submissions.zip turns into one HTTP GET for the full .txt submission. XML-era Forms 3/4/5 (mid-2003 to now) number roughly 5–7M unique accessions (estimate). At the client's own cap (DEFAULT_REQUESTS_PER_SECOND = 8.0, sec_fair_access.py:23) the theoretical floor is 6M/8 = 750k s, about 8.7 days of nonstop fetching. The realistic sequential rate today is 3–5 req/s, which means 2–4 weeks even with BULK-01 fixed. I confirmed by web search that SEC publishes the 'Insider Transactions Data Sets' (sec.gov/dera/data/form-345, readme at sec.gov/files/insider_transactions_readme.pdf). They are extracted from the XML part of Forms 3/4/5, updated quarterly, and have SUBMISSION, REPORTINGOWNER, NONDERIV_TRANS, DERIV_TRANS, footnote and related tables keyed by ACCESSION_NUMBER. Those tables map almost one-to-one onto InsiderTrade/sec_detail_json.
kept.suggestion: Add a 'sec-backfill-dataset' path. Download each quarterly ZIP (about 80 requests for the whole history), stream the TSVs with the csv module, join SUBMISSION, REPORTINGOWNER and the transaction tables on ACCESSION_NUMBER, and build InsiderTrade rows with the same sec_row_id scheme. Use NONDERIV_TRANS_SK/DERIV_TRANS_SK, or a per-accession ordinal that matches the parser's ':nonDerivative:{idx}' so keys line up with daily ingestion. Bulk-insert with executemany, which measured about 150 µs per filing. Keep the per-filing XML pipeline only for the current, not-yet-published quarter, through the daily index catch-up. Keep submissions.zip only for targeted --cik repairs.
kept.verifier_note: Confirmed: every metadata row becomes one rate-limited fetch of the full .txt submission (sec_backfill.py:150 -> fetch_filing), and 8 req/s caps throughput at about 28.8k filings/h, so a full XML-era history takes days to weeks. The DERA Insider Transactions Data Sets are the right structural fix, with one caveat: they start at 2006 Q1, not mid-2003, so the 2003-2005 filings would still need the per-filing path (or have to be accepted as a gap).

kept.title: Each request opens a new TCP+TLS connection (requests.get with no Session or keep-alive)
kept.evidence:
return requests.get(
            url,
            headers=headers,
            timeout=timeout,
            allow_redirects=allow_redirects,
            stream=stream,
kept.description: requests.get builds and discards a Session and its connection pool on every call, so each filing pays a TCP and TLS handshake plus Session setup. Measured from this machine to www.sec.gov:443: TCP 6–31 ms, TCP+TLS 30–102 ms per new connection. Across millions of sequential requests that is about 8–28 h of handshakes per 1M filings. It also limits per-filing latency, so in practice the 8 req/s limiter is rarely reached.
kept.suggestion: Have RequestsSecTransport own a requests.Session, using one per worker thread if BULK-06 is adopted, with an HTTPAdapter(pool_connections, pool_maxsize) and urllib3 Retry for connect errors. Close it in a context manager. The frozen dataclass can hold the session through field(default_factory=requests.Session).
kept.verifier_note: RequestsSecTransport.get calls module-level requests.get (sec_client.py:84), which builds and tears down a Session and connection pool on every call. So every filing pays a new TCP and TLS handshake. SecClient holds a single transport, so making it own a Session is a small change.

kept.title: One BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction per filing over a new NullPool connection, with a SELECT before each row (38 ms/filing)
kept.evidence:
with immediate_transaction(self._engine) as connection:
                for trade in trades:
                    key = us_canonical_key(trade)
                    existing_row = (
                        connection.execute(
                            select(us_trades).where(us_trades.c.canonical_key == key)
kept.description: The backfill sink calls self._persistence.us_trades.upsert(trades) once per filing (sec_backfill.py:148). Each call opens a fresh SQLite connection, because engine.py:46 uses poolclass=NullPool and every connect re-runs the PRAGMAs. It then issues BEGIN IMMEDIATE, runs a SELECT before each trade, then an INSERT, and commits with a rollback-journal fsync. Measured on a temp DB file: 38.5 ms per filing for 3 trades with current settings; 2.7 ms per filing with WAL and 500 filings per transaction; 0.15 ms per filing with raw executemany INSERT OR IGNORE. At 1M filings the current path spends about 10.7 h in SQLite commits alone.
kept.suggestion: Gather trades from N filings (e.g. 500–2,000, or about 5 s of work) and upsert each batch in one transaction. For source='sec_edgar' rows with a deterministic SEC canonical key, use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(canonical_key) DO NOTHING/UPDATE through executemany instead of SELECT+merge for each row. Keep the merge path only when a non-SEC row already holds the key. Use a pooled engine (SingletonThreadPool/QueuePool) for long CLI runs, or keep one connection open for the whole backfill.
kept.verifier_note: The sink calls us_trades.upsert once per filing (sec_backfill.py:148). That runs immediate_transaction on an engine created with poolclass=NullPool (engine.py:46), so each call opens a new sqlite3 connection, re-runs the PRAGMAs, issues BEGIN IMMEDIATE, and does a SELECT then INSERT per trade (repositories.py:75-89), followed by a journaled commit. The measured per-filing cost is plausible.

kept.title: No SQLite journal_mode=WAL or synchronous pragmas: each commit pays full fsyncs, and readers block the backfill writer
kept.evidence:
cursor.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON")
            cursor.execute(f"PRAGMA busy_timeout={busy_timeout_ms}")
kept.description: The database runs with SQLite defaults: journal_mode=DELETE, synchronous=FULL and a small page cache. Each per-filing commit creates, fsyncs and deletes a -journal file. Switching only to WAL with synchronous=NORMAL cut per-filing upserts from 38.5 ms to 23.6 ms in my benchmark. Without WAL, a GUI that reads the same DB during a long backfill (feed queries scanning millions of rows) holds a SHARED lock. The writer then waits up to busy_timeout=5 s, after which SQLAlchemy raises OperationalError → PersistenceError → process_filing_row returns False. That filing is counted as failed and refetched on the next run.
kept.suggestion: In configure_sqlite_connection, set PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL once (it persists in the file), PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, a larger cache_size (e.g. -65536) and temp_store=MEMORY. For bulk loads, optionally run PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint with a larger value and a final wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE).
kept.verifier_note: configure_sqlite_connection sets only foreign_keys and busy_timeout (engine.py:61-62), and journal_mode or synchronous is not set anywhere in persistence/. In rollback-journal mode a long GUI read holds SHARED and blocks the writer from getting EXCLUSIVE at commit. After 5 s that raises OperationalError -> PersistenceError (repositories.py:106-107), and process_filing_row returns False (sec_downloads.py:294-299), so the filing is not completed.

kept.title: Fetching is strictly sequential, so latency rather than the 8–10 req/s fair-access cap limits throughput
kept.description: Each filing completes fetch, parse, cache fsync, DB commit and checkpoint before the next request starts. The RateLimiter (sec_fair_access.py:53-59) already supports threads through its lock, but only one thread calls it. With realistic per-filing wall time of 0.25–0.4 s before BULK-01's growth, the run reaches about 3–4 req/s, which is 40–50% of the allowed rate.
kept.suggestion: Use a bounded producer/consumer pipeline. The ZIP iterator feeds a queue, and 4–8 fetch workers (each with its own requests.Session) share the existing RateLimiter set at about 8–9 req/s. Workers parse and map, then send trades to one writer thread that batches DB upserts and checkpoint appends (BULK-01, BULK-04). Keep the queues bounded so memory stays flat. This approaches the fair-access ceiling of about 28.8k filings/h.
kept.verifier_note: The loop at sec_backfill.py:124-160 handles one filing at a time from fetch to checkpoint. The RateLimiter is already lock-protected (sec_fair_access.py:53-59) but only one thread ever calls it, so per-filing latency, not the limiter, sets throughput.

kept.title: Every fetched filing is written to a cache with fsync that the backfill never reuses (24 h freshness, deleted on read)
kept.evidence: promote_validated_filing(pending, cache_root=cache_root)
kept.description: For each downloaded filing, promote_validated_filing runs mkstemp, write, flush, os.fsync and replace (sec_downloader.py:298-308). I measured 11.8 ms per 8 KB file on this machine, against 1.2 ms for a plain write. The cache has no value for the backfill. Completed accessions are skipped through the checkpoint before fetch_filing is called. cache_freshness_seconds is 24*60*60 (sec_security.py:213), and _read_fresh_cache unlinks anything older (sec_downloader.py:275-277), so a resume after more than a day refetches anyway. All entries go into one flat validated-v1 directory, so a multi-million-file directory builds up during the run (Defender scans each new file), and purge_stale_cache later walks all of it. Cost: about 3.3 h of I/O per 1M filings, plus tens of GB of disk.
kept.suggestion: Add a cache=False (or write_cache policy) option to process_filing_row and use it for the backfill: parse straight from the bytes in memory and skip promote. If caching stays for diagnostics, drop the per-file fsync (atomic replace is enough for a cache), shard the namespace into subdirectories (e.g. the first 2 hex characters of the digest), and use a longer freshness for immutable archive documents.
kept.verifier_note: promote_validated_filing (sec_downloads.py:282) writes through _write_atomically with fsync (sec_downloader.py:298-308) into one flat validated-v1 directory, keyed by sha256 of an archive_path that includes the CIK. Completed accessions are skipped before fetch, and _read_fresh_cache unlinks entries older than 24 h (sec_downloader.py:275-277). The only case where the cache helps the backfill is retrying a persist failure within 24 h. The Defender remark is speculation, but the main claim holds.

kept.title: Redundant Path.resolve and symlink checks run twice per filing (3.5 ms/filing on Windows)
kept.evidence:
content_path = _content_path(row, cache_root)
    _validate_content_path(content_path, cache_root)
kept.description: fetch_filing runs _validate_inputs (cache_root is_symlink/exists/is_dir) and _validate_content_path (two Path.resolve calls plus two is_symlink calls). promote_validated_filing (lines 118-121) repeats all of it, then _prepare_cache_directory runs two mkdir calls plus is_symlink/is_dir. bulk_metadata_to_index_row has already validated the archive path, and cache_root is constant for the whole run. Measured at 3.49 ms per filing, about 1 h per 1M filings.
kept.suggestion: Validate and resolve cache_root and the namespace directory once per run, for example in a small CacheLocation object created when the service starts. Per filing, check only the leaf: a lexical join of a hex digest, which cannot escape the root.
kept.verifier_note: fetch_filing runs _validate_inputs and _validate_content_path (two resolve() calls via resolves_within plus two is_symlink calls) at sec_downloader.py:84-87. promote_validated_filing repeats them at lines 118-121, and _prepare_cache_directory adds two mkdir calls and more stat calls (lines 290-295). Each filing therefore makes redundant filesystem syscalls. This is low impact next to the network cost.

kept.title: Checkpoint is deleted after a 'complete' run even when filings failed, so the next run restarts from zero
kept.description: fully_done only means the ZIP iterator was exhausted. It ignores counters['failed'] and mapping failures. Failed accessions are never added to completed (the documented retry design), but deleting the checkpoint also discards the millions of successful accessions. Re-running the documented 'resume' command to retry failures then re-iterates and refetches the entire archive, because the cache expired after 24 h (BULK-07). Upserts would skip the rows, but every network request is repeated: days of wasted fetching.
kept.suggestion: Delete the checkpoint only when failures == 0. Otherwise keep it and record the failed accessions. Better, use the DB-backed ingest table from BULK-01, so a re-run retries only status='failed' rows (with an attempts cap) and successes never need fetching again, whatever happens to the checkpoint file.
kept.verifier_note: fully_done = not interrupted (sec_backfill.py:164-166) ignores counters['failed'] and mapping_failures and unconditionally deletes the checkpoint, which holds every successful accession. Some failures can never succeed (pre-XML filings), so a completed full run always has failures and always wipes the success set. A re-run then refetches everything, and the cache does not help because it expires after 24 h.

kept.title: Filings that will always fail (pre-XML Form 4s, permanently malformed XML) are refetched on every run and never converge
kept.evidence: filing_date = _parse_date_lenient(raw_date)
kept.description: The metadata filter accepts any OWNERSHIP_FORMS row whatever its date. Ownership XML became mandatory only from mid-2003. Earlier electronic Form 3/4/5 submissions in the submissions JSON contain no <ownershipDocument>, so extract_ownership_document raises NonOwnershipDocumentError → counted failed → not completed (sec_backfill.py:12-18 documents this non-convergence). Each such accession costs a full rate-limited fetch on every run. The cost doubles because the same accession is also listed under each reporting owner's CIK (BULK-11).
kept.suggestion: Skip rows with filing_date before about 2003-06-30 cheaply in _filter_ownership_rows or the service, and count them as skipped_metadata. Record permanent failure classes (NonOwnershipDocumentError, SecOwnershipParseError, SecXmlSecurityError, 404) as status='failed_permanent' in the ingest table or checkpoint, so they are not refetched. Retry only transient classes (SecTransportError, 429/503, PersistenceError).
kept.verifier_note: Confirmed that _filter_ownership_rows filters only on form type (line 358), with no date cutoff, and that failed filings are retried on every run (the docstring at lines 12-18 says so). One detail is wrong: a pre-2003 text Form 4 has a <TYPE>4 block, so _extract_from_full_submission returns its plain text, and _validate_ownership_xml then raises SecOwnershipDocumentError ('not well-formed'), not NonOwnershipDocumentError. The outcome is the same: a permanent failure that is refetched on every run.

kept.title: The same accession is yielded once per related CIK (issuer and each reporting owner); dedup happens only after success and counters double-count
kept.evidence:
cik_no_zeros = str(int(meta.cik))  # meta.cik is 10-digit zero-padded
    archive_path = f"edgar/data/{cik_no_zeros}/{meta.accession_number}.txt"
kept.description: In submissions.zip a Form 4 appears in the issuer's CIK JSON and in every reporting owner's CIK JSON, so the same accession is yielded roughly twice or more. The service dedupes only through the completed set (sec_backfill.py:129), which holds successes only. Any failed or never-completing accession is therefore fetched again for each CIK. Because archive_path embeds meta.cik, each copy also gets a different cache key (sha256 of the path), so even a fresh cache entry is not reused. filings_discovered counts every copy, which makes the CLI summary and any progress percentage misleading.
kept.suggestion: Keep a set of attempted accessions for the run (not only successes) and skip repeats. Better, collect unique accessions first (one pass over the ZIP, a few minutes at the measured 50 MB/s JSON throughput), then process each once. Key the cache by accession, not by path. Report discovered_unique separately from discovered_rows.
kept.verifier_note: iter_ownership_filings yields rows for each CIK JSON separately, and the only dedup is the success-only completed set (sec_backfill.py:129). archive_path embeds meta.cik (sec_bulk.py:97-98) and the cache key is sha256(archive_path) (sec_downloader.py:251), so copies of the same accession under other CIKs never share a cache entry. discovered += 1 counts every copy.

kept.title: Transport failures (timeouts, connection resets) are never retried, so they turn into per-filing failures
kept.evidence:
except Exception as exc:
            raise SecTransportError(url) from exc
kept.description: _request_with_retry retries only HTTP statuses in retry_policy.retry_statuses (429/503). Any requests exception (ReadTimeout with the 15 s timeouts, ConnectionError, ChunkedEncodingError while reading the body, which _read_bounded maps to SecTransportError) fails the filing at once. Over millions of requests, transient network errors run to thousands. Each one is left out of completed and costs another fetch on the next run, and with BULK-09 it is lost entirely once the checkpoint is deleted.
kept.suggestion: Treat SecTransportError (connect/read timeout, connection reset) as retryable inside _request_with_retry, using the same bounded backoff and attempt cap. Also retry 500/502/504. Keep security errors non-retryable.
kept.verifier_note: _send wraps every transport exception as SecTransportError (sec_client.py:245-246). _request_with_retry retries only on retry_statuses {429, 503} (sec_fair_access.py:75), and its docstring says plainly that 'Transport failures are not retried'. 500/502/504 also go straight to SecHttpError. The behavior is deliberate but costly over millions of requests.

kept.title: No progress reporting or graceful cancellation during a multi-day run; summary counters reset on resume
kept.description: on_progress is called once, after the loop finishes. cmd_sec_backfill (cli.py:521) passes neither on_progress nor cancelled, so the CLI prints only 'Starting full bulk backfill ...' and then nothing for hours or days. The user cannot see the rate, how many are done, or the ETA, which is why the slowdown from BULK-01 went unnoticed. Ctrl+C raises KeyboardInterrupt through the loop, so no summary is printed. The counters are not stored in the checkpoint, so after a resume the final summary covers only the last session.
kept.suggestion: Emit progress every N filings or T seconds with discovered/completed/failed, filings per second and an ETA, and wire it to stderr in the CLI as cmd_sec_catchup does. Install a SIGINT handler that sets a cancelled flag so the loop exits cleanly, flushes the batch and checkpoint, and prints the summary. Store cumulative counters in the checkpoint or ingest table.
kept.verifier_note: on_progress is called only once, after the loop (sec_backfill.py:180-181). cmd_sec_backfill passes neither on_progress nor cancelled (cli.py:521). Ctrl+C raises KeyboardInterrupt, which passes through process_filing_row (not in _RECOVERABLE) and out of run(), so no summary is printed (the per-filing checkpoint does survive). The counters are not persisted across resumes.

kept.title: query_latest loads the entire us_trades table into Python and slices it, which breaks down after a backfill
kept.evidence:
result = [
                    us_from_row(row)
                    for row in rows
                    if not requested_sources
                    or requested_sources.intersection(us_provenance(row))
                ]
                return result[:count]
kept.description: UsScanService's latest scans (services/us.py:167 and :245) call query_latest(count, sources=selected). The statement has no LIMIT. Every row is fetched, turned into an InsiderTrade dataclass and filtered on provenance JSON in Python, then sliced to count. After even a partial backfill (millions to tens of millions of SEC rows), each 'latest' scan uses gigabytes of memory and takes minutes, on whatever thread runs the scan.
kept.suggestion: Push the filter and LIMIT into SQL. Filter by source = ANY(selected), or use EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(source_provenance_json) WHERE value IN (...)), or normalize provenance into a us_trade_sources(trade_id, source) table with an index. Then apply .limit(count) on top of the existing ORDER BY filing_date DESC, which can use an index on (filing_date, trade_date).
kept.verifier_note: query_latest builds the ORDER BY with no LIMIT (repositories.py:172-181), turns every row into an InsiderTrade, filters provenance in Python, and slices result[:count] (line 191). UsScanService calls it with only count and sources (us.py:167, 245), so there is no date bound either. After a backfill, every latest scan materializes the whole table.

kept.title: Each feed page runs a full COUNT, a full sort and a MAX(created_at) over a UNION ALL subquery that cannot use indexes
kept.evidence:
total_count = int(connection.execute(count_statement).scalar_one())
                rows = connection.execute(statement).mappings().all()
                freshness = _aware_utc(
                    connection.execute(
                        select(func.max(feed.c.created_at))
kept.description: _projection() is a union_all of us/congress/european projections with computed keys. Each FeedRepository.query runs (1) COUNT(*) over the whole union, (2) ORDER BY sort_expression IS NULL, sort, filing_date IS NULL, filing_date DESC, key LIMIT/OFFSET, which forces a full materialize and sort because no index can serve expressions over a UNION subquery, and (3) MAX(created_at), and created_at has no index. With tens of millions of backfilled us_trades rows, every page load or filter change in the GUI costs several full-table scans. The rollback-journal locking also slows the concurrent backfill (BULK-05).
kept.suggestion: Add indexes on us_trades(created_at) and (filing_date, id). Push the WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT into each branch of the union (top-K per branch, then merge). Cache or approximate total_count, or compute it only when filters change. Use keyset pagination instead of OFFSET.
kept.verifier_note: FeedRepository.query runs COUNT(*), an ORDER BY over computed expressions with LIMIT/OFFSET, and MAX(created_at) over the union_all projection, all at feed.py:479-484. us_trades has no index on created_at (schema.py:88-97, 383-384). SQLite may push some WHERE predicates into the union branches, but the sort, the count and the MAX still scan everything.

kept.title: Parser keeps only the first <reportingOwner>, so joint filings lose their other insiders
kept.evidence: el = root.find("reportingOwner")
kept.description: Form 3/4/5 XML allows several reportingOwner elements, as in joint filings by fund entities, their general partners and individual managers, which are common among 10% owners. Only the first is parsed, so insider_name, cik_insider and insider_title in every mapped trade show only that owner. The others are silently dropped. Because the same accession is also listed under the other owners' CIKs in submissions.zip, those owners' entity pages never show the trade, and the deterministic canonical key prevents a second row.
kept.suggestion: Parse all reportingOwner elements into a tuple. Either store the primary owner in the existing columns plus the full list in sec_detail_json, or emit one row per (owner, transaction) with the owner CIK in sec_row_id. Document whichever you choose.
kept.verifier_note: _parse_reporting_owner uses root.find('reportingOwner') (sec_ownership_parser.py:268), which returns only the first element. The mapper takes cik_insider from filing.reporting_owner (sec_trade_mapping.py:395), and the canonical key is (accession, sec_row_id) with no owner component, so other owners in a joint filing are dropped.

kept.title: Dates with an xs:date timezone suffix reject the whole filing, permanently
kept.evidence: return date.fromisoformat(raw)
kept.description: The ownership schema types transactionDate, periodOfReport and related fields as xs:date, which allows a timezone suffix. I verified that on Python 3.13 date.fromisoformat('2004-05-12-05:00') and date.fromisoformat('2004-05-12Z') raise ValueError. The parser turns that into SecOwnershipParseError, which fails the whole filing. Under the backfill's retry design such a filing is refetched on every run and never ingested (BULK-10).
kept.suggestion: Normalize the value before parsing, e.g. take raw[:10] when it matches r'^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}(Z|[+-]\d{2}:\d{2})?$'. Apply this in _value_date and _parse_date_elem, and add a fixture with a timezone-suffixed date.
kept.verifier_note: _value_date calls date.fromisoformat(raw) (sec_ownership_parser.py:601) and turns the ValueError into SecOwnershipParseError. I checked on the local Python (3.15.2): '2004-05-12-05:00' and '2004-05-12Z' are both rejected. How often real filings carry these suffixes is not verified, so low is right.

kept.title: Each ownership XML is parsed twice with a new hardened parser each time
kept.evidence: root = etree.fromstring(xml_bytes, hardened_xml_parser())
kept.description: extract_ownership_document already encodes, guards, parses and tree-walks the XML (sec_ownership_document.py:231-242) and then throws the tree away. parse_ownership_document repeats all of it and also builds a second XMLParser. Measured extract+parse+map at about 0.8 ms per small filing, of which the duplicate parse is roughly half. That is minor next to the network but amounts to about 7 CPU-minutes per 1M filings, plus extra complexity.
kept.suggestion: Have extract_ownership_document return the validated root element (or carry it in OwnershipDocument as a private field) and let parse_ownership_document accept it, re-validating only when given raw text from an untrusted caller. Reuse one hardened parser per thread through threading.local.
kept.verifier_note: _validate_ownership_xml parses and guards the tree (sec_ownership_document.py:231-242) and discards it. parse_ownership_document then re-encodes, re-guards and re-parses (sec_ownership_parser.py:201-210). Its docstring says this is intentional (a 'self-contained untrusted boundary'), so a fix must keep that contract, for example by passing a trusted root through an internal API. The CPU saving is minor.

kept.title: ZIP location check is a no-op because the trusted root is set to the ZIP's own parent
kept.evidence: zip_path, cache_root=zip_path.parent, policy=self._policy, ciks=ciks
kept.description: iter_ownership_filings documents cache_root as an 'injected trusted root the archive must live under'. The backfill passes zip_path.parent, so resolves_within(zip_path, cache_root) is always true and _validate_zip_location only checks for symlinks. The containment check adds code and test surface without protecting anything, and it can mislead readers into thinking the ZIP location is constrained.
kept.suggestion: Either pass a real configured root (for example a dedicated bulk-download directory) or drop the containment parameter from this call path and keep only the symlink check, with a comment explaining why.
kept.verifier_note: The backfill passes cache_root=zip_path.parent (sec_backfill.py:120), so resolves_within(zip_path, cache_root) in _validate_zip_location (sec_bulk.py:222) holds by construction. Only the symlink checks do anything.

kept.title: ZIP preflight limits are close to the real submissions.zip size; when it grows, the run aborts with a generic error
kept.evidence:
zip_max_entries=2_000_000,
    zip_max_member_bytes=64 * _MIB,
    zip_max_total_bytes=16 * 1024 * _MIB,
kept.description: _preflight_members rejects the whole archive if it has more than 2M entries or more than 16 GiB uncompressed in total, raising SecBulkSecurityError with only the reason 'zip'. submissions.zip holds about 900k+ CIK JSONs plus continuation files and grows every night. I did not verify current headroom, but once it crosses either limit the backfill stops immediately with a message that does not say which limit was hit. The limits are module constants and the CLI cannot override them.
kept.suggestion: Report which limit was exceeded and the observed value in the error, without member names. Read the current entry count and total size of the real archive (e.g. len(infolist()), sum(file_size)), set the limits with a documented margin, and allow a CLI override for trusted local archives.
kept.verifier_note: The limits are at sec_security.py:222-224, and _preflight_members raises a bare SecBulkSecurityError() with reason 'zip' (sec_bulk.py:232-239) that does not say which limit was hit, so the diagnostics gap is real. The claim that the real archive is close to the limits is unverified. The user's runs get past preflight today, so this is not a current failure.

kept.title: A targeted --cik backfill deletes the full-archive checkpoint because both share one file keyed only by ZIP name
kept.description: cmd_sec_backfill always uses the same checkpoint path, EDGAR_CACHE_DIR/sec_backfill_checkpoint.json (cli.py:340-344, 518), whether or not --cik is given. _load_completed matches only on zip_path.name, and the ciks filter is not stored in the checkpoint. Suppose a user is partway through a multi-day full run and runs a quick `sec-backfill --cik X` repair against the same submissions.zip. That run loads the full completed set, iterates only CIK X, finishes without interruption, and calls _delete_checkpoint(). All progress from the full run is lost, and the next full run refetches from zero.
kept.suggestion: Store the ciks filter (or a hash of it) in the checkpoint and either use a separate checkpoint per scope or never delete the checkpoint after a filtered run. Better, use the DB-backed ingest table proposed in BULK-01, so progress is not tied to one file that any run can delete.

kept.title: One malformed archive member aborts the whole backfill with an uncaught exception, deterministically on every resume
kept.evidence:
except (json.JSONDecodeError, UnicodeDecodeError) as exc:
        raise SecBulkError("Malformed JSON in bulk archive member") from exc
kept.description: _read_member_json raises SecBulkError (or SecBulkSecurityError on an oversized read) from inside the generator, in the middle of iteration. In SecBackfillService.run only bulk_metadata_to_index_row is wrapped in try/except SecBulkError (sec_backfill.py:132-136). The `for meta in gen` loop is not, so the exception ends the run. cmd_sec_backfill (cli.py:521) does not catch it either, so the user gets a traceback and no summary. The same member fails on every resume, so a single truncated or corrupt member (common in a partial multi-GB download) blocks every later CIK for good.
kept.suggestion: Catch per-member read and parse errors in iter_ownership_filings, or yield an error marker. Log the member index without its content, count it as skipped_members, and continue. Keep only archive-level preflight violations fatal. In the CLI, catch SecBulkError and print a clear message plus the partial summary.

kept.title: Mapping failures are swallowed without logging and marked completed, so they are never retried or diagnosed
kept.description: When ownership_filing_to_trades raises (for example the period_of_report > filing_date check at sec_trade_mapping.py:158), the sink increments a counter and returns normally with no log line and no accession recorded. reached_sink[0] is already True and process_filing_row returns True, so line 159 adds the accession to completed. Its trades are dropped for good: after a mapper fix, resuming will never re-ingest those filings, and nothing records which accessions were affected. The fetch failures this is meant to mirror are logged with the CIK and reason.
kept.suggestion: Log at WARNING with the accession and the exception type. Record these accessions as status='mapping_failed' (in the ingest table or a failed set in the checkpoint) rather than 'completed', so a later run with a fixed mapper can retry just them.

kept.title: The whole .txt submission must be valid UTF-8; one non-UTF-8 byte in any attachment rejects the filing permanently
kept.description: The backfill fetches the full submission (edgar/data/{cik}/{accession}.txt, sec_bulk.py:98), which bundles every document in the filing, including EX-24 power-of-attorney exhibits and HTML attachments. extract_ownership_document decodes the whole payload strictly before it looks for the ownership block. Legacy EDGAR text can contain Latin-1 or cp1252 bytes, so one such byte in an exhibit fails a filing whose ownership XML is valid. Under the backfill retry design it is then refetched on every run. I have not checked how often this happens on the real archive. The code path is certain.
kept.suggestion: Find the ownership <DOCUMENT> block at the byte level, or decode with latin-1 for envelope scanning, and strictly decode only the extracted XML (honoring its XML encoding declaration). Alternatively, fetch the primary XML document itself using the primary_document already captured in BulkFilingMetadata but never used. That also cuts bandwidth.

kept.title: _write_atomically may close an already-closed, possibly reused file descriptor when replace fails
kept.description: When temp_path.replace fails, the with-block has already closed descriptor, yet the except block calls os.close(descriptor) on the same number. This can happen on Windows with a PermissionError while the destination is held open by antivirus, the indexer or a concurrent reader. If another thread has opened a file in the meantime (GUI worker threads, a new SQLite connection on every NullPool checkout), the OS may have reused that descriptor number, and the call closes the wrong file. The usual result is EBADF, which is swallowed, so the bug is silent until it hits a live descriptor.
kept.suggestion: Set a flag (or descriptor = -1) once os.fdopen succeeds, and call os.close only if fdopen itself failed. Or share one atomic-write helper; json_state.atomic_write_json does not have this double-close.

areas.title: SEC fetch / download / IO correctness
areas.summary: The SEC fetch layer (SecClient, RateLimiter, bounded reads, path-safe cache) is defensively written and mostly correct, but the orchestration around it has serious throughput and data-integrity problems. The slow full backfill you already know about has a clear main cause: SecBackfillService rewrites a sorted, indented JSON file of every completed accession (with fsync) after each filing. That makes the run O(N^2). A local benchmark measured about 140 ms per save at 100k accessions and about 500 ms at 500k, which is already slower than the 125 ms network budget per filing. Even with that fixed, the design still sends one sequential HTTP request per filing for all of history, with no keep-alive Session and no concurrency. Filings listed under several CIKs are fetched more than once. So a full-history backfill takes days at best. On correctness: daily/catch-up ingestion marks a date as covered even when some of its filings failed to download. Network errors and SEC's 403 throttling response are not retried. A 404 index for today or a future date is recorded as permanent coverage. The backfill deletes its checkpoint after one pass even if some filings failed, and it gets stuck forever on one malformed archive member. Smaller issues: raw OSErrors escape the recoverable-error handling, an fd is closed twice in the atomic write, the cache grows without limit, the legacy http.py rate limiter is separate from the SecClient one and not thread-safe, and the per-range checkpoint in sec_downloads repeats what DB coverage already tracks.

kept.title: Backfill rewrites the full completed-accession checkpoint after every filing (O(N^2))
kept.evidence:
if ok and reached_sink[0]:
    completed.add(meta.accession_number)
    self._save_completed(zip_path, completed)
...
"completed_accessions": sorted(completed),
kept.description: After every successful filing, _save_completed sorts the whole completed set, serializes it with json.dumps(indent=2) (persistence/json_state.py:29), writes it to a temp file, fsyncs it and os.replace()s it. Each save grows linearly, so the total cost is quadratic. Measured on this machine: 18 ms per save at 10k accessions, 138 ms at 100k (2.8 MB), 500 ms at 500k (14 MB). A full submissions backfill has millions of ownership accessions. Past about 100k completed filings, checkpoint I/O costs more per filing than the rate-limited network request (125 ms at 8 rps), and it keeps getting worse. This is the main reason the backfill 'takes hours and does not even get to half'. The run spends most of its time rewriting the checkpoint.
kept.suggestion: Replace the snapshot rewrite with an append-only journal: open the checkpoint once and append one accession per line, flushing each line (fsync every N lines or every few seconds). Load it into a set on start and compact it occasionally. Alternatively, store completed accessions in a SQLite table (INSERT OR IGNORE, committed in batches), or record (member index, row index) as a compact cursor, because the ZIP iteration order is deterministic. At minimum, save every N filings or T seconds and on exit/cancel, and drop indent=2.
kept.verifier_note: Lines 158-160 call _save_completed after every sinked filing, and it rewrites sorted(completed) through atomic_write_json (indent=2 plus fsync). My own benchmark on this machine: 6 ms per save at 10k accessions, 69 ms at 100k, 193 ms at 300k. That is linear per save and so quadratic over the run. For about 1M filings the total comes to roughly 90 hours of checkpoint I/O. The reviewer's absolute numbers are about 2x higher than mine, but the conclusion holds.

kept.title: Each request opens a new TCP/TLS connection and filings are fetched one at a time
kept.evidence:
return requests.get(
            url,
            headers=headers,
            timeout=timeout,
            allow_redirects=allow_redirects,
            stream=stream,
        )
kept.description: RequestsSecTransport calls the module-level requests.get, which builds and discards a Session on every call. So every index and filing fetch pays a full TCP and TLS handshake, with no connection reuse. Backfill and catch-up call process_filing_row strictly one after another (sec_backfill.py:150, sec_downloads.py:215). The real request rate is therefore 1/(handshake + latency + parse + fsync), well below the 8 rps the RateLimiter allows. The limiter is thread-safe (Lock plus monotonic clock), but the pipeline never uses more than one thread, so that headroom goes unused.
kept.suggestion: Give RequestsSecTransport a long-lived requests.Session with an HTTPAdapter (pool_maxsize of about 8, keep-alive), and close it with the client. Then run fetch and parse in a small bounded worker pool (for example 4-6 threads) that shares the single SecClient and RateLimiter. Keep persistence and checkpointing on one consumer thread. Together these should get close to the 8 rps ceiling.
kept.verifier_note: RequestsSecTransport.get calls the module-level requests.get (line 84), which opens and closes a new Session each time, so there is no connection reuse. Both backfill (sec_backfill.py:150) and daily (sec_downloads.py:218) call process_filing_row strictly one after another. The thread-safe limiter's headroom is never used.

kept.title: Full backfill makes one HTTP request per historical filing and has no date filter
kept.evidence:
for meta in gen:
    ...
    row = bulk_metadata_to_index_row(meta)
    ...
    ok = process_filing_row(
        row,
        client=self._client,
kept.description: The backfill turns every Form 3/4/5 accession in submissions.zip (all CIKs, all years) into a separate fetch of the full .txt submission. At the SEC fair-access ceiling (about 8 rps, roughly 29k filings per hour) the network alone puts a lower bound of days to weeks on a multi-million-filing archive, even after SECIO-01 and SECIO-02 are fixed. run() takes a CIK filter but no since/until filter, although BulkFilingMetadata.filing_date is available. A user cannot limit the run to, say, the last 5 years.
kept.suggestion: Add since/until filtering on meta.filing_date before any network work. For deep history, ingest SEC's quarterly 'Insider Transactions Data Sets' (Form 3/4/5 flattened TSV ZIPs from DERA). About 80 quarterly downloads replace millions of per-filing requests. Keep per-filing fetching for recent gaps only.
kept.verifier_note: run() has only a ciks filter. Every ownership accession in the archive becomes one .txt fetch through process_filing_row, even though BulkFilingMetadata.filing_date is available for filtering. At an 8 rps ceiling, a multi-million-filing history needs days even with no other overhead.

kept.title: Per-filing fetch failures still complete the date, so coverage is recorded and the filings are permanently lost
kept.description: process_filing_row returns True (meaning 'date can complete') for fetch failures, including transient SecTransportError, a 503 that exhausted its retries, and SecHttpError 403 from throttling. _process_date then returns True, download_filings_in_range adds the date to the checkpoint and calls on_progress. SecDailyIngestionService records that day as covered (sec_daily.py:258-264). Later ingest_range calls skip covered dates via coverage.gaps(), so any filing that hit a temporary network or throttling error is never retried. Nothing records which accessions failed.
kept.suggestion: Treat transient fetch failures (transport errors, 5xx, 429/403 after retries) as date-level failures: return False so the date stays uncovered and a resume retries it. Or record failed accessions in a persisted retry list (DB table) that later runs work through. Only deterministic failures (404 filing, security rejections, parse errors) should let the date complete.
kept.verifier_note: At lines 253-258, any _RECOVERABLE fetch error (SecTransportError, SecHttpError 403/5xx after retries) increments failed and returns True. _process_date then completes the date and sec_daily records coverage, so coverage.gaps never revisits it. The docstring says this is deliberate ('keep the existing behavior'), but it silently loses filings after transient errors.

kept.title: Network errors (connection reset, read timeout) are never retried
kept.evidence:
except Exception as exc:
            raise SecTransportError(url) from exc
kept.description: _request_with_retry retries only statuses in retry_policy.retry_statuses. _send turns any transport exception (ConnectionError, ReadTimeout, ChunkedEncodingError, SSL errors) into SecTransportError, and that escapes on the first attempt; the docstring states 'Transport failures are not retried'. Exceptions raised while streaming the body in _read_bounded (line 306) are not retried either. On multi-hour runs these blips are routine, and each one becomes a lost filing, or a lost daily index which fails that date (see SECIO-04).
kept.suggestion: Retry idempotent GETs on connect errors, timeouts and mid-body read errors, using the same bounded backoff (for example the same max_attempts). Inside fetch_bytes, wrap the whole request plus _read_bounded in the retry loop so a truncated stream is also retried. Keep security rejections non-retryable.
kept.verifier_note: This is true: _send (line 246) wraps every transport exception as SecTransportError, and the retry loop only retries statuses, as the docstring says. Mid-body errors in _read_bounded (line 306) are not retried either. On its own, though, the damage is limited. A failed daily index returns False, so that date is retried on the next run. Backfill retries pre-sink failures on resume. The data loss only happens through SECIO-04, so medium rather than high.

kept.title: SEC's 403 'Request Rate Threshold Exceeded' is not treated as throttling, and there is no circuit breaker
kept.evidence: retry_statuses: frozenset[int] = frozenset({429, 503})
kept.description: When a client goes over its fair-access allowance, SEC EDGAR usually answers 403 (with an 'Undeclared Automated Tool' or 'Request Rate Threshold Exceeded' page) and blocks the IP for about 10 minutes. It does not usually send 429. Here 403 raises SecHttpError at once. Each filing then fails quickly and is counted as failed. A daily catch-up keeps going through the block window and marks every date in it covered with all filings failed (SECIO-04). A backfill burns through thousands of accessions as failures. The 30 s cap on Retry-After and the 4-attempt limit (1+2+4 s) are also far shorter than a 10-minute block.
kept.suggestion: Detect sustained 403/429 from www.sec.gov as a throttle signal. Open a circuit breaker that pauses all requests for a long cooldown (for example 10 minutes, honoring Retry-After without the 30 s cap when it comes from SEC), then probe again. Abort the run with a clear message if blocking continues, rather than counting every filing as failed.
kept.verifier_note: This is true: retry_statuses is {429, 503} (line 75), so a 403 raises SecHttpError immediately, there is no circuit breaker, and backoff_delay caps Retry-After at 30 s. However, the single-threaded client runs at 8 rps, below SEC's 10 rps ceiling. Sustained 403 blocks are realistic mainly when combined with the separate legacy limiter (SECIO-15) or several processes. The exact 403 behaviour of SEC cannot be verified from this code. It is a hardening gap rather than a common-path failure.

kept.title: A 404 daily index marks the date complete, so today and future dates become permanently covered
kept.description: Treating 404 as 'no filings that day' is right for weekends and holidays. It is wrong for dates whose index has not been published yet. cmd_sec_daily defaults to date.today() (cli.py:442), and validate_range (services/common.py:54) accepts future end dates. The master.YYYYMMDD.idx file only appears after SEC builds the nightly index. A daytime run of `sec-daily`, or `sec-catchup --until <future>`, gets 404 for those dates, returns True, and sec_daily records coverage. Later runs skip those dates and never ingest their filings.
kept.suggestion: Accept 404 as 'empty day' only for dates strictly before the most recent published index (for example date < today in US/Eastern, or after checking the quarter's daily-index listing). For today or later, leave the date uncovered (return False). Also reject or clamp end dates after today in validate_range or in the CLI.
kept.verifier_note: _process_date returns True on SecFilingNotFoundError (lines 201-203). cmd_sec_daily defaults to date.today() (cli.py:442), and validate_range (common.py:54-64) does not check against today. sec_daily then records coverage, and future ingest_date/ingest_range calls skip the date through coverage.gaps. For a user in Europe, date.today() is also ahead of US/Eastern, which makes the problem more likely.

kept.title: The same filing is fetched once per associated CIK because dedup uses archive path, not accession
kept.description: EDGAR indexes list an ownership filing once per associated entity (the issuer and each reporting owner), each under its own path edgar/data/{cik}/{accession}.txt. Dedup by archive_path keeps all of them, so daily ingestion downloads, parses and upserts the same Form 4 two or more times. The cache does not help because the cache key is sha256(archive_path) (sec_downloader.py:251). submissions.zip has the same duplication across CIK members. The backfill skips a duplicate only after the first copy succeeded, counts it as 'skipped_resume', and inflates 'discovered', so progress numbers are misleading. If the first copy failed, the duplicate is re-downloaded under a different URL.
kept.suggestion: Deduplicate on the accession number (the last path segment without .txt) in parse_master_index and in the backfill loop, keeping a run-scoped seen-accession set separate from 'completed'. Key the filing cache by accession instead of archive_path. Report duplicates in their own counter.
kept.verifier_note: parse_master_index deduplicates by the full archive_path (line 53), but EDGAR master indexes list a Form 4 under each associated CIK with different edgar/data/{cik}/ paths. The cache key is sha256(archive_path) (sec_downloader.py:251), so each copy is fetched and parsed separately. In backfill, a duplicate is only skipped when the first copy reached the sink and was marked completed (line 129), and the skip is counted as skipped_resume, so the description is accurate.

kept.title: One malformed bulk member, or any unexpected exception, aborts the backfill, and every resume fails at the same point
kept.evidence:
data = _read_member_json(zf, info, policy)
...
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, UnicodeDecodeError) as exc:
        raise SecBulkError("Malformed JSON in bulk archive member") from exc
kept.description: _read_member_json raises SecBulkError inside the generator. SecBackfillService.run only catches SecBulkError around bulk_metadata_to_index_row (sec_backfill.py:133-136), not around `for meta in gen` (line 124). So the exception ends the whole run, and since generators cannot continue after raising, the rest of the archive is never reached. On resume the generator starts again from the first member, re-reads every member up to the bad one, and fails again. The backfill never gets past that point. A dict-shaped 'form' array in _filter_ownership_rows (line 347-355, KeyError) or an OSError from the cache (SECIO-12) behaves the same way.
kept.suggestion: Catch per-member errors inside iter_ownership_filings: log the member index/name, count it as a skipped member, and continue. Optionally take an on_member_error callback. Validate that the parallel arrays are lists before indexing. In run(), also report member-level skips in the summary.
kept.verifier_note: The mechanism is real. SecBulkError raised by _read_member_json (raised at line 309, called at line 201) propagates out of the generator. run() only catches SecBulkError around bulk_metadata_to_index_row (lines 132-136), so the run aborts, and on resume it re-reads members up to the same point and fails again. A dict-valued 'form' would raise KeyError at line 355. However, a malformed member in a genuine SEC archive is an unusual edge case, so 'high' is overstated.

kept.title: Backfill deletes its checkpoint after one pass even if filings failed, so failures are never retried
kept.description: The module docstring promises that transient failures 'are intentionally retried on every resume run'. But when iteration reaches the end without cancellation, the checkpoint (all completed accessions) is deleted, whatever counters['failed'] says. Re-running to pick up the failed filings then starts from an empty completed set and redoes the whole multi-day backfill. The only alternative is accepting the losses.
kept.suggestion: Delete the checkpoint only when there were no fetch or persist failures. Otherwise keep it, and also write a failed-accessions list so a follow-up run can retry just those. Replace the 'fully_done = not interrupted' rule with an explicit (iteration complete AND failures == 0) check.
kept.verifier_note: Lines 164-166 delete the checkpoint whenever the loop finishes without cancellation, regardless of counters['failed']. This contradicts the module docstring (lines 12-18), which says pre-sink failures are 'retried on every resume run'. A follow-up run then starts with an empty completed set and repeats the whole backfill.

kept.title: Backfill reports progress only once, at the very end
kept.description: run() accepts an on_progress callback but calls it once, after the whole (multi-day) iteration. cmd_sec_backfill (cli.py:521) passes neither on_progress nor cancelled. A user watching a run that lasts hours sees no output, rate, failure count or ETA, and cannot tell a stuck run (see SECIO-09 and SECIO-06) from a slow one.
kept.suggestion: Call on_progress every N filings or T seconds with the running summary (counts, filings per second, failures). In the CLI, print a throttled status line to stderr, as _make_cli_progress already does for catch-up. Wire a SIGINT-safe cancelled flag so Ctrl-C stops cleanly.
kept.verifier_note: on_progress is called only at lines 180-181, after the loop finishes. cmd_sec_backfill (cli.py:521) calls service.run(zip_path, confirm=True, ciks=ciks) without passing on_progress or cancelled, so the run gives no output at all until it ends.

kept.title: Filing cache grows without limit: purge only runs after a fully completed run, and backfill caches files it will never read again
kept.evidence:
if self._cleanup:
                purge_stale_cache(self._cache_root, policy=self._policy)
kept.description: process_filing_row always promotes the filing bytes to cache_root/validated-v1/<sha>.filing (one flat directory, fsync per file). purge_stale_cache runs only when a run finishes uninterrupted (sec_backfill.py:164-168, sec_downloads.py:165-170). A multi-day backfill is effectively always interrupted, so millions of filings, tens of GB, pile up in one directory. For a filing that reached the sink, the cached copy is useless because the accession is now in 'completed'. The 24 h freshness rule (sec_security.py:213, sec_downloader.py:275) is also pointless for immutable EDGAR archive documents: after a pause longer than a day, a resume deletes and re-downloads cache entries it could have reused.
kept.suggestion: Skip cache promotion in backfill, or delete the file right after a successful sink. Run purge_stale_cache (or a size/age cap) at the start of each run, not only on full completion. If the cache stays, treat archive filings as immutable (no TTL) and shard the directory by digest prefix.
kept.verifier_note: process_filing_row always promotes the filing to validated-v1/<sha>.filing with an fsync for each file (sec_downloads.py:282, sec_downloader.py:304-308). purge_stale_cache runs only on uninterrupted completion (sec_backfill.py:164-168). For filings that reached the sink, the cache copy is never read again. One nuance: the TTL re-download argument is weak, because only filings whose sink failed would ever be read back from the cache.

kept.title: Raw OSError from cache read or unlink escapes the recoverable-error handling and aborts the run
kept.description: fetch_filing wraps neither _read_fresh_cache's unlink() (lines 273 and 276) nor read_bytes() (line 278) in its OSError -> SecDownloadIoError translation; only promote_validated_filing does that. On Windows, unlinking or reading a file that antivirus or the indexer has open raises PermissionError. That is not in sec_downloads._RECOVERABLE, so one locked cache file ends the whole catch-up or backfill with a traceback, rather than counting one failure. purge_stale_cache (line 179) likewise catches only FileNotFoundError around stat().
kept.suggestion: Wrap the cache read path in try/except OSError. On unlink failure, ignore it and fall through to a network fetch. On read failure, either raise SecDownloadIoError (which is recoverable) or treat it as a cache miss. In purge_stale_cache, catch OSError around stat as well.
kept.verifier_note: _read_fresh_cache catches only FileNotFoundError, on stat (line 268). unlink (lines 273 and 276) and read_bytes (line 278) can raise PermissionError, or FileNotFoundError in a race, as raw OSError. fetch_filing does not translate these, and OSError is not in _RECOVERABLE, so the exception escapes process_filing_row and aborts the run. purge_stale_cache line 180 also catches only FileNotFoundError.

kept.title: _write_atomically can close an fd that has already been closed and reused by another thread
kept.description: Once os.fdopen succeeds, the `with` block owns the descriptor and closes it. If temp_path.replace() then fails (common on Windows when the target is momentarily locked by antivirus or a reader), the except block calls os.close(descriptor) again on a closed fd number. In a process with other threads (the GUI's QThreads, or a future worker pool for SECIO-02), the OS may already have given that number to another file, which then gets silently closed. That causes data loss or EBADF in unrelated code.
kept.suggestion: Track ownership: set a flag (or descriptor = -1) once os.fdopen succeeds, and only call os.close when fdopen never took ownership. Also consider a short retry loop around replace() for PermissionError on Windows.
kept.verifier_note: This is accurate. Once os.fdopen succeeds, the with block closes the fd. If temp_path.replace (line 308) then raises, line 311 calls os.close on an already-closed fd number, which another thread could have reused. Today the SEC pipeline only runs single-threaded from the CLI, so the practical risk is low until concurrency is added.

kept.title: Legacy http.py rate limiter is separate from SecClient's, runs at the 10 rps ceiling, uses the wall clock and is not thread-safe
kept.evidence:
def _rate_limit() -> None:
    """Block until enough time has passed since the last request."""
    global _last_request_time
    now = time.time()
    elapsed = now - _last_request_time
    if elapsed < _min_interval:
        time.sleep(_min_interval - elapsed)
    _last_request_time = time.time()
kept.description: edgar.py calls fetch_url(use_sec_agent=True), which uses a module-global limiter set to SEC_MAX_REQUESTS_PER_SECOND = 10 (config.py:93), the hard ceiling with no margin. It has no lock, so several GUI QThreads (scan tab, feed, entity pages) can read the same _last_request_time and fire together. It uses time.time(), which jumps with clock adjustments. It is also completely independent of SecClient's 8 rps RateLimiter, so legacy EDGAR lookups running alongside a catch-up or backfill push total traffic from one IP above 10 rps. That triggers the 403 block in SECIO-06. fetch_url also has no retry on 429/503.
kept.suggestion: Route SEC traffic in fetch_url through one shared process-wide RateLimiter (the sec_fair_access one, with monotonic clock and lock), or move these edgar.py calls onto SecClient. Remove the duplicate limiter.
kept.verifier_note: utils/http.py:17-28 uses an unlocked global with time.time() and a 1/10 s interval (config.py:93 SEC_MAX_REQUESTS_PER_SECOND=10). It is completely independent of SecClient's 8 rps RateLimiter. edgar.py calls fetch_url(use_sec_agent=True) at lines 106, 163, 224 and 237, and fetch_url does not retry on 429/503.

kept.title: utils/caching uses non-atomic two-file writes, unguarded reads and never purges expired entries
kept.evidence:
path.write_text(content, encoding="utf-8")
    meta_path.write_text(json.dumps({"timestamp": time.time()}))
kept.description: set_cached writes the content file and then the meta file non-atomically. A crash or a concurrent writer (two QThreads fetching the same URL) can leave a truncated .txt next to a still-fresh .meta from an earlier write, and get_cached then serves the truncated body as valid. get_cached (line 30-31) catches only JSONDecodeError/KeyError: an OSError (file locked) or a non-dict meta (AttributeError on .get) propagates into the scrapers. Expired entries are never removed, so the EDGAR and scraper cache dirs grow forever. clear_cache exists but nothing calls it.
kept.suggestion: Store the timestamp in the file itself (or use the file's mtime) and write it with an atomic temp-file plus os.replace, so there is one file per key. Catch OSError/ValueError/AttributeError in get_cached and treat them as a miss. Purge expired entries opportunistically (for example on startup).
kept.verifier_note: This is true: set_cached writes the .txt and .meta files non-atomically (lines 47-48), get_cached catches only JSONDecodeError/KeyError (line 35) and so misses OSError, AttributeError and TypeError, and clear_cache is never called. However, a truncated body is served only if a crash happens mid-write while an older .meta file is still fresh, and growth is bounded by the number of distinct URLs because each key is overwritten. So this is low impact.

kept.title: sec_downloads' range checkpoint duplicates DB coverage and in practice never resumes
kept.evidence: completed, counters = _load_checkpoint(checkpoint_path, interval)
kept.description: The only production caller is SecDailyIngestionService. It calls download_filings_in_range once per coverage gap, with the same checkpoint file, and records DB coverage in on_progress at the same moment the checkpoint records a completed date (lines 157-160). After an interruption, the next run computes smaller gaps from coverage, so the saved range never equals the new interval (line 359-364) and the checkpoint is thrown away. Its only real effect is an extra fsync'd JSON write per date, plus counters restored from an old run leaking into the new summary (see SECIO-18).
kept.suggestion: Drop checkpointing from download_filings_in_range and treat DB coverage as the only source of resume truth. If standalone (non-DB) use needs resume, keep the checkpoint as an optional feature that sec_daily does not enable.
kept.verifier_note: With sec_daily as the only caller, the next run's gaps start at the first uncovered date. The saved range then almost never matches the new interval (lines 358-364), so the checkpoint is discarded and its only effect is one extra fsync'd write per date. This is accurate, but the cost is minor, so low.

kept.title: Counters double-count retried dates and carry over between runs
kept.evidence:
rows = sec_index.parse_master_index(index_text)
    counters["discovered"] += len(rows)
kept.description: Counters change while a date is being processed. When a date ends with a sink failure (returns False) and continue_on_error is True, its partial discovered/downloaded/parsed/failed counts stay in the shared dict and are saved by the next successful date's checkpoint. A later resume processes that date again and counts it twice. Counters restored from a checkpoint also go into SecDownloadReport, so sec_daily's per-run summary (sec_daily.py:180-183) includes numbers from earlier runs.
kept.suggestion: Count each date in a local dict and merge it into the run totals only when the date completes. Do not restore counters from the checkpoint into a new run's report (or report them separately as 'previous').
kept.verifier_note: Counters are shared and are restored from the checkpoint (lines 373-378). However, restoring requires an exact range match, which the sec_daily path practically never produces (see SECIO-17). The carry-over into sec_daily summaries is therefore essentially unreachable today. Double counting is only real for standalone download_filings_in_range resumes.

kept.title: atomic_write_json leaves orphan temp files when interrupted with Ctrl-C
kept.description: The cleanup handler catches Exception, not BaseException, so KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit skip deleting the temp file. Ctrl-C is the only way to stop the CLI backfill, and checkpoint writing currently takes most of the backfill's time (SECIO-01). So an interrupt usually lands inside this function and leaves a multi-MB '.sec_backfill_checkpoint.json.*.tmp' file behind each time. sec_downloader._write_atomically already uses BaseException correctly.
kept.suggestion: Catch BaseException (re-raising afterwards), as _write_atomically does. Optionally sweep stale '.<name>.*.tmp' siblings at startup.
kept.verifier_note: atomic_write_json cleans up its temp file only under 'except Exception' (line 41). KeyboardInterrupt therefore leaves a .<name>.*.tmp file behind, and the CLI backfill has no cancel hook, so Ctrl-C is the only way to stop it. _write_atomically uses BaseException.

kept.title: Backfill's ZIP containment check passes the archive's own parent as the trusted root, so it can never fail
kept.description: iter_ownership_filings checks that zip_path resolves inside cache_root (sec_bulk.py:222). Passing zip_path.parent makes that check always true, so the 'trusted root' guard and its CACHE_PATH error reason never fire. The code looks like it enforces a policy that it does not.
kept.suggestion: Either pass a real trusted root (for example a configured downloads/bulk directory) or remove the containment requirement from iter_ownership_filings for user-supplied paths and keep only the symlink and regular-file checks. Either way, document the decision.
kept.verifier_note: Passing zip_path.parent makes the containment check trivially true for a regular file, so the check gives no real policy. The claim that it 'can never fail' is overstated: it still rejects a symlinked parent directory (cache_root.is_symlink) and a symlinked zip whose target resolves elsewhere.

kept.title: Failure logs drop the accession, HTTP status and URL, and failed filings are not recorded anywhere
kept.description: Per-filing failures are logged as 'cik=<cik> reason=SecHttpError'. A CIK has many filings, and the status code (403 vs 500 vs 404) and the safe URL label, which SecHttpError already carries in a sanitized form, are dropped. After a long run you cannot tell whether failures came from throttling, outages or bad documents, and you cannot list the affected accessions to re-run them.
kept.suggestion: Log the accession number (from row.archive_path), status_code when present, and the already-sanitized exc.url. Also collect failed accessions with a reason code in the report, or persist them, so they can be retried (this also covers SECIO-04 and SECIO-10).
kept.verifier_note: _log_recoverable_level logs only type(exc).__name__ (line 311) together with the CIK. The status_code and sanitized url that SecHttpError already carries are dropped, as is the accession, and failed accessions are not collected anywhere.

kept.title: purge_stale_cache resolves the cache root again for every entry
kept.description: resolves_within calls root.resolve() and path.resolve() on every call. For a flat directory holding millions of cached filings (SECIO-12), the purge does two filesystem resolutions plus a symlink check and a stat for each entry. Measured at about 0.2 ms per entry on this machine, that is several minutes per million files, for a containment check that is redundant once the namespace directory has been confirmed not to be a symlink.
kept.suggestion: Resolve cache_root once before the loop. Use os.scandir (DirEntry.is_symlink() and stat(follow_symlinks=False) are cached and cheap). Skip the per-entry resolve, because iterdir entries of a verified non-symlink directory are direct children by construction.
kept.verifier_note: resolves_within (_sec_paths.py) resolves both root and path on every call, and purge calls it for every entry (line 176). The purge is not a hot path, because it only runs at the end of a run, so the cost matters only with a very large cache.

kept.title: OWNERSHIP_FORMS is defined twice
kept.evidence: OWNERSHIP_FORMS: frozenset[str] = frozenset({"3", "3/A", "4", "4/A", "5", "5/A"})
kept.description: sec_bulk.py and sec_index.py:11 each define the same ownership form set. If one copy changes (for example to drop Form 3/5 for speed, or to add a variant), daily ingestion and bulk backfill quietly start accepting different filing types.
kept.suggestion: Define OWNERSHIP_FORMS once (for example in sec_index or edgar) and import it in sec_bulk.
kept.verifier_note: Identical OWNERSHIP_FORMS frozensets are defined in sec_bulk.py:36 and sec_index.py:11.

kept.title: An optional cache write blocks persistence: if promotion fails, a parsed filing is dropped and its date still gets marked covered
kept.description: process_filing_row writes the validated filing to the disk cache before calling the persist sink. A failed cache write is wrapped as SecDownloadIoError, for example from disk full (made likely by unbounded cache growth, SECIO-12), a PermissionError on os.replace from Windows antivirus, or a path-policy rejection. The function then returns True without ever calling on_filing_parsed. In daily/catch-up ingestion the date completes and coverage is recorded, so a filing that downloaded and parsed correctly is permanently lost because of a cache that only serves as an optimisation. In backfill the accession is never completed and is refetched on every resume.
kept.suggestion: Call the persist sink right after a successful parse, and make cache promotion best-effort afterwards (log on failure, do not count it as a filing failure, do not skip persistence). Better still, skip cache promotion entirely in backfill, where the bytes are never reused.

kept.title: Backfill and daily persistence commit one SQLite IMMEDIATE transaction per filing, with a SELECT for every trade
kept.evidence: upserts = upserts + self._persistence.us_trades.upsert(trades)
kept.description: Each sinked filing calls UsTradeRepository.upsert. That opens BEGIN IMMEDIATE (persistence/engine.py:20-26), runs a SELECT by canonical_key for every trade, then an INSERT or UPDATE, and commits. Each commit is a journal/WAL sync, which costs milliseconds on Windows. Over millions of backfill filings this adds hours of fsync-bound commits on top of the checkpoint (SECIO-01) and cache (SECIO-12) fsyncs, so every filing costs three durable syncs. sec_daily.py:243 follows the same pattern.
kept.suggestion: Buffer trades from N filings (for example 200-1000) or T seconds and upsert them in one transaction. Mark accessions completed only after their batch commits. Inside upsert, prefetch existing canonical keys with a single IN query, or use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, instead of one SELECT per trade.

kept.title: Every backfill resume decompresses and JSON-parses the whole submissions archive again just to skip completed accessions
kept.evidence:
cik = edgar.normalize_cik(cik_str)
            if ciks is not None and cik not in ciks:
                continue
            data = _read_member_json(zf, info, policy)
kept.description: The resume state is only a set of accessions, and iter_ownership_filings has no start position. Each resume (and each run after a SECIO-09 crash) therefore reads up to 64 MiB per member, fully json.loads every CIK member (about 1M entities, most with no ownership filings), and builds BulkFilingMetadata for every ownership row before sec_backfill.py:129 discards it. Because the checkpoint is saved after every filing, the whole pre-resume prefix is parsed again on every restart.
kept.suggestion: Add a compact positional cursor (member index plus row index, valid because ZIP central-directory order is deterministic). Let iter_ownership_filings take start_member, so a resume can skip already-finished members without opening them. Keep the accession set (or a DB table) only as a safety net for the partially processed member.

kept.title: read_json_dict claims to 'never raise' but crashes on a checkpoint that is not valid UTF-8
kept.description: read_text(encoding='utf-8') raises UnicodeDecodeError, which is a ValueError and not an OSError, when a state or checkpoint file contains non-UTF-8 bytes (disk corruption, or a file edited or replaced externally). The exception escapes read_json_dict despite its 'Never raises' contract and aborts _load_completed (sec_backfill.py:189), _load_checkpoint (sec_downloads.py:355) and the UI-state stores, instead of falling back to an empty default.
kept.suggestion: Add UnicodeDecodeError, or ValueError generally, to the handled exceptions next to OSError, log a warning and return None.

kept.title: SecDailyIngestionService accepts and stores a 'clock' parameter that nothing uses
kept.evidence:
# ``clock`` is reserved for future use (e.g. defaulting ranges to "today").
        # It is stored but currently unused by the ingestion logic.
        self._clock = clock
kept.description: The constructor takes clock: Callable[[], date] | None and stores it, but no code reads it. The exact concern it was meant to address, a 'today' notion for date ranges, is where SECIO-07 occurs. cmd_sec_daily uses date.today() directly, and nothing stops coverage from being recorded for today or future dates.
kept.suggestion: Either remove the parameter, or use it for real: clamp or reject range ends at or after clock() (in US/Eastern), and treat a 404 index as an empty day only for dates before that. This fixes SECIO-07 and makes it testable.

areas.title: SEC ownership XML parsing & trade mapping
areas.summary: The SEC ownership pipeline (_sec_xml -> sec_ownership_document -> sec_ownership_parser -> sec_trade_mapping) is cleanly layered. It is typed with frozen dataclasses, has solid XXE/DTD hardening (resolve_entities=False, no_network, a pre-parse DTD/ENTITY ban, and tree size/depth/text limits), and builds idempotency keys deterministically from accession plus table index. The main correctness gaps are in what the data model keeps. Only the first reportingOwner is parsed. 4/A amendments are stored alongside the filings they amend, and the computed "amends" key is never used. Holdings rows (all of Form 3) are dropped. A single unparseable optional value (a comma in a number, a timezone-suffixed date, exercise date after expiration) throws away the whole filing. Filings that are not UTF-8, or that declare a non-UTF-8 encoding, are rejected or come out garbled. Performance: I profiled the 3.4 KB fixture with the repo's .venv packages under system Python 3.13 (the .venv interpreter is broken). Extraction takes about 0.50 ms and parsing about 0.65 ms per filing. The pure-Python guard_xml_tree walk accounts for about 40% of that CPU time, and it runs twice per filing because the XML is decoded, encoded, guarded and parsed twice. So parsing costs about 1 ms of CPU per filing. That is real but not the main reason the full-history backfill is slow. The bigger cost sits in the in-scope extractor: every filing, including Form 3s that give no rows and pre-2003 non-XML filings that can never parse, is fetched over the network at SEC's rate limit before it fails or yields nothing. edgar.py has some dead code, repeated JSON parsing in CIK lookup, and URLs that are not encoded.

kept.title: Only the first reportingOwner is parsed; joint filers are silently dropped
kept.evidence:
def _parse_reporting_owner(root: _Element, ctx: _ParseContext) -> ReportingOwner:
    el = root.find("reportingOwner")
kept.description: The ownership schema allows 1..N <reportingOwner> elements. Joint filings are common: funds with their GP/manager entities, spouses, and groups of 10% owners. root.find() returns only the first one, so every transaction is credited to that owner alone. The other owners' names, CIKs and roles are lost. The insider_title can also be wrong: if the first owner is an LLC flagged only as a 10% owner and the director is listed second, the trade reads as a 10% owner trade, not a director trade. I confirmed this with a scratch test: a document with two owners parsed to one ReportingOwner (the first).
