kept.suggestion: Parse all reportingOwner elements into tuple[ReportingOwner, ...] on OwnershipFiling. In mapping, either emit one InsiderTrade per (transaction, owner), with the owner CIK added to sec_row_id so keys stay unique, or keep one row per transaction and store the joint-filer list (and a combined relationship) in sec_detail_json. Choose the primary owner on purpose, for example the one with isDirector/isOfficer set, not by document order.
kept.verifier_note: Confirmed: root.find("reportingOwner") at line 268 returns only the first owner. A scratch test with two owners (a 10% LLC first, a director second) produced only the 10% owner, so insider_title is wrong. I lowered severity because a joint filing reports each transaction once. Totals are not inflated; what is lost is the other owners' attribution and roles.

kept.title: 4/A amendments never supersede the original; the 'amends' key is unused and not unique
kept.description: An amendment has its own accession number. Its rows get new sec_row_ids ('<acc>:nonDerivative:<idx>'), so us_canonical_key treats them as new trades. A 4/A that restates a Form 4 therefore doubles every transaction in the database, which inflates totals, cluster-buy detection and alerts. The 'amends' string goes into sec_detail_json, but grep shows no code anywhere reads it. It also cannot identify a transaction: it is only issuer|insider|period|security_title, so all 'Common Stock' rows in one amended filing share the same key.
kept.suggestion: Store amendment linkage in real columns, not JSON. On ingest of an X/A, mark rows from earlier filings for the same (issuer CIK, owner CIK, period_of_report, base form type) as superseded, or exclude superseded rows in feed/aggregation queries, for example 'latest accession per (issuer, owner, period) wins'. If per-row matching is needed, build the key from (security_title, transaction_date, transaction_code, table index), not security_title alone.
kept.verifier_note: Amendment rows get new accession-based sec_row_ids, and us_canonical_key hashes (accession, sec_row_id), so they become new rows. grep shows nothing reads the 'amends' JSON key, and nothing filters on is_amendment (it appears only in models, schema, migrations and merger column lists). One detail is overstated: some 4/A filings correct only part of the original, so 'doubles every transaction' holds only for full restatements.

kept.title: Each filing is decoded, encoded, guarded and lxml-parsed twice
kept.description: extract_ownership_document already runs _validate_ownership_xml: encode, pre-parse guard, fromstring, guard_xml_tree, root check (sec_ownership_document.py:231-246). It then throws the tree away and keeps only a str. parse_ownership_document repeats every step. Profiling 3000 iterations on tests/fixtures/sec_form4_submission.txt gave guard_xml_tree 1.21 s of 3.0 s total (6000 calls, two per filing). The combined cost is about 1.15 ms of CPU per small filing, which adds up to hours of CPU over a multi-million-filing backfill.
kept.suggestion: Parse once. Have the extraction step return the validated bytes and the parsed root, for example a private field on OwnershipDocument or a combined extract_and_parse() used by process_filing_row. Keep the standalone parse_ownership_document re-validation for external callers, but skip it when it receives a pre-validated document from the same policy.
kept.verifier_note: The double encode, guard and parse is real (sec_ownership_document.py:231-242 and sec_ownership_parser.py:201-210). My timing on the 3.4 KB fixture with Python 3.13 was about 0.21 ms to extract and 0.29 ms to parse, roughly 0.5 ms per filing. A rate-limited SEC fetch costs 100 ms or more, so parsing is under 1% of wall time. This is not a medium contributor to the slow backfill.

kept.title: guard_xml_tree is a slow pure-Python DFS that encodes every text node
kept.description: For every element (whitespace-only tails included) the walk builds a tuple, runs a generator, and creates a new UTF-8 bytes object just to measure its length. In the profile this is the largest single CPU cost in the parse path (about 0.2 ms per call on a 3.4 KB document; extend plus genexpr alone is about 570k calls per 3000 filings). The depth check largely repeats libxml2's own depth cap, which applies because huge_tree=False.
kept.suggestion: Iterate with root.iter() at C speed for the element count. Count chars with len(text) and only compute exact UTF-8 bytes when chars*4 could exceed the limit. Compute depth cheaply, for example with a single XPath max-depth check or by tracking depth only when the element count is high. Together with SECPARSE-03 this removes most of the guard overhead.
kept.verifier_note: The pure-Python DFS at _sec_xml.py:96-118 encodes every text node and tail just to measure it. This is a real but small cost, and it only matters together with SECPARSE-03. Low is the right severity.

kept.title: Non-UTF-8 filings rejected outright; a declared non-UTF-8 encoding causes mojibake
kept.description: EDGAR .txt submissions are not always UTF-8. Older filings and some filer software produce Latin-1/cp1252 bytes, for example names with accented letters. Any such byte makes the whole filing fail (scratch test 'latin1-bytes' -> SecOwnershipDocumentError). Separately, _validate_ownership_xml and parse_ownership_document re-encode the decoded str as UTF-8 and hand the bytes to lxml. lxml obeys the XML declaration, so a document declaring encoding="ISO-8859-1" is decoded a second time as Latin-1 and the names come out garbled (scratch test 'latin1-decl-str' produced 'MÃ\x9c...' in rptOwnerName).
kept.suggestion: Work on bytes end to end. Locate the <XML> block with byte regexes and pass the original bytes to lxml so it applies the declared encoding. Alternatively, decode with errors='replace' or a cp1252 fallback, then strip or rewrite the XML declaration's encoding before re-encoding. Add fixtures for Latin-1 and for a non-UTF-8 declaration.
kept.verifier_note: _decode (line 142) strict-decodes the whole submission as UTF-8. That includes attached exhibits such as EX-24 powers of attorney, so one cp1252 byte in an exhibit rejects the filing even when the ownership XML block is clean ASCII. That makes the failure more reachable than the reviewer says. I reproduced the mojibake: a document declaring encoding="ISO-8859-1" parsed rptOwnerName as 'M�\x9cLLER'.

kept.title: One malformed optional value discards every transaction in the filing
kept.description: _value_decimal, _value_date (line 600) and _parse_date_elem (line 619) raise SecOwnershipParseError for any unparseable lexeme, even in non-essential fields such as underlyingSecurityShares, exerciseDate or conversionOrExercisePrice. The whole filing is then counted as failed and quarantined. Scratch tests: '100,000' in transactionShares and an xs:date with a timezone suffix ('2026-06-12-05:00', '2026-06-12Z') both rejected the entire filing. Both are legal or common lexical variants. date.fromisoformat does not accept xs:date timezone suffixes.
kept.suggestion: Normalise lexemes before conversion: strip thousands separators and surrounding '$', and accept xs:date timezone suffixes by stripping the trailing Z or ±hh:mm. For non-essential fields, log the problem, record it in sec_detail_json and store None instead of raising. Keep hard failures for fields that define the row (transactionCode, transactionDate).
kept.verifier_note: Confirmed: date.fromisoformat rejects '2026-06-12-05:00' and '2026-06-12Z' (I tested this on 3.13), and any bad value raises for the whole filing. Timezone-suffixed dates are valid xs:date, so this is a real risk. The '100,000' example is unlikely in practice: EDGAR validates ownership XML against the XSD on submission, and a comma is not a valid xs:decimal.

kept.title: Decimal accepts NaN/Infinity/sNaN; sNaN escapes as a non-recoverable exception
kept.evidence: return Decimal(raw)
kept.description: Decimal('NaN'), Decimal('Infinity') and Decimal('1E+99999') are all under the 128-char numeric limit and are accepted (scratch test 'nan' parsed shares=Decimal('NaN')). NaN and inf then reach the shares, price and value floats in the database. Decimal('sNaN') is worse: sec_trade_mapping computes txn.shares * txn.price_per_share and float(txn.shares), which raise decimal.InvalidOperation or ValueError (verified). Neither is a SecTradeMappingError, and neither is in _RECOVERABLE in services/sec_downloads.py. One crafted or corrupt filing therefore aborts the whole backfill or daily loop instead of being counted as a failure.
kept.suggestion: After conversion, reject non-finite values (if not d.is_finite(): raise SecOwnershipParseError) and optionally cap the exponent range. As defense in depth, catch ArithmeticError/ValueError in ownership_filing_to_trades and re-raise as SecTradeMappingError.
kept.verifier_note: Mechanism verified. A price of 'sNaN' parses, then mapping raises ValueError ('cannot convert signaling NaN to float'). Neither sink catches it (sec_backfill catches only SecTradeMappingError, process_filing_row only _RECOVERABLE and PersistenceError), so the run aborts. In practice this is very unlikely: EDGAR schema validation rejects NaN, Infinity and sNaN as xs:decimal, and content comes only from sec.gov. It is a defense-in-depth fix.

kept.title: Missing issuer/reportingOwner (or a namespaced root) yields blank trades or an empty 'successful' parse
kept.description: The parser treats every structural element as optional. A document without <issuer> or <reportingOwner> still yields trades, with ticker '', cik_issuer '' and insider_name '' (mapping line 383-395), and these are persisted as real rows. In addition, _validate_ownership_xml (sec_ownership_document.py:244) accepts a namespaced root by checking only localname, while every find() here uses unqualified tags. A default-namespaced document therefore parses to a filing with no issuer, owner or transactions. Scratch test 'ns' gave Issuer(None, None, None) and []. That filing is counted as 'parsed' and checkpointed as completed, so it is never retried.
kept.suggestion: Require issuer/issuerCik and at least one reportingOwner/rptOwnerCik; raise SecOwnershipParseError otherwise. Either reject namespaced roots in _validate_ownership_xml (require root.tag == 'ownershipDocument' exactly) or strip namespaces before the find() calls, so validation and extraction agree.
kept.verifier_note: The inconsistency is real. Validation checks only the root localname (sec_ownership_document.py:244) while the finds use unqualified tags, and a namespaced document parsed to Issuer(None,None,None) with no transactions. However, the ownership schema requires issuer and reportingOwner, and real EDGAR ownership XML has no namespace, so this is very unlikely with SEC data. Requiring the issuer CIK is still cheap hardening.

kept.title: Holdings tables ignored: Form 3 (and Form 4/5 holding rows) produce nothing yet are fetched and parsed
kept.description: Only nonDerivativeTransaction and derivativeTransaction are read. nonDerivativeHolding and derivativeHolding are skipped. A Form 3 consists only of holdings, so every 3 and 3/A always maps to zero trades. Even so, OWNERSHIP_FORM_TYPES (sec_ownership_document.py:28) and the discovery filters (sec_index.py:11, sec_bulk.py:36) include them. Each one costs a rate-limited SEC download plus a full parse during the multi-hour backfill, for no output.
kept.suggestion: Decide which you want. Either parse holdings into a separate record type (useful for initial positions), or drop 3 and 3/A from the discovery form set so they are never downloaded. If holdings are dropped, remove '3' and '3/A' from the three duplicated OWNERSHIP_FORMS sets together (see SECPARSE-19).
kept.verifier_note: Only nonDerivativeTransaction and derivativeTransaction are read (lines 377 and 390). Form 3 contains only holdings, so every 3 and 3/A is fetched at the rate limit and yields zero trades. The sink is still reached, so in backfill it is checkpointed as done, but it costs one network fetch each. The three duplicated form sets are confirmed (sec_ownership_document.py:28, sec_index.py:11, sec_bulk.py:36).

kept.title: Pre-XML (pre-2003) and non-XML ownership filings pay a full lxml parse before failing, with an unclear reason
kept.description: When a <TYPE>4 block has no <XML> wrapper, which is the case for every Form 4 filed before the June 2003 XML mandate, the raw text or HTML body is handed to the XML guards and lxml. It then fails as 'not well-formed', is counted as a parse failure and is quarantined. A full-history backfill contains many such filings. Each needs a network fetch plus a wasted parse, and they are reported as errors, not as 'not machine-readable'.
kept.suggestion: If there is no <XML> wrapper and the text does not start with '<?xml' or '<ownershipDocument', raise NonOwnershipDocumentError straight away, as a distinct, non-quarantined skip category. Better, filter by filing date or by primary-document extension at discovery so these filings are never downloaded.
kept.verifier_note: Line 197 does fall back to the raw TEXT body when there is no <XML> wrapper. The result is a generic 'not well-formed' SecOwnershipDocumentError, counted as failed. Per the sec_backfill module docstring, such filings are re-fetched on every resume because they never reach the sink. The volume is smaller than implied, because most pre-mid-2003 Forms 3/4/5 were paper filings. The parse itself is cheap; the cost is the repeated fetch.

kept.title: Data-quality checks in mapping reject the whole filing and are re-run per transaction
kept.description: A typo in one derivative row's exercise or expiration date, or a periodOfReport later than the index filing date (line 156-164), raises SecTradeMappingError. ownership_filing_to_trades then returns nothing, so all valid non-derivative purchases and sales in the filing are lost too. In sec_backfill.py the sink has already set reached_sink, so the accession is checkpointed as completed and never retried. _validate_common_dates is a filing-level check, yet it runs inside the per-transaction loop. It runs N times for N rows and never runs for filings with zero transactions.
kept.suggestion: Turn these into per-row warnings: keep the row, flag it in sec_detail_json (e.g. 'warnings': [...]) and log once. If you keep the period check, run it once before the loops.
kept.verifier_note: _validate_derivative (line 139) and _validate_common_dates (line 156) raise SecTradeMappingError, and that drops every row in the filing. In sec_backfill._sink the error is caught after reached_sink is set, so the accession is checkpointed as completed, and it is counted without logging. The repeated filing-level check per transaction is real but has negligible cost. How often this happens is unknown, probably rare, but the loss is silent and permanent.

kept.title: Missing shares, price or holdings stored as 0.0, which looks the same as a real zero
kept.evidence:
shares_val = float(txn.shares) if txn.shares is not None else 0.0
    price_val = float(txn.price_per_share) if txn.price_per_share is not None else 0.0
kept.description: Prices often appear only in a footnote (weighted-average ranges, 'see footnote'). The parser correctly returns None, but mapping turns that into price=0.0 and value=0.0, the same as a genuine $0 award or gift. Value-threshold filters, alerts and analytics then treat these as zero-value trades. The footnote_ids for the price element are not kept apart from the others, so the reason cannot be recovered.
kept.suggestion: Make the InsiderTrade/us_trades numeric fields nullable, or add explicit flags (price_missing, value_missing). Record which footnotes are attached to transactionPricePerShare in sec_detail_json so a weighted-average or range note can be shown.
kept.verifier_note: Lines 252-263 map None to 0.0 for shares, price, value and owned_after, so a missing price cannot be told apart from a real $0 award or gift. Footnote IDs are collected for the whole row (_collect_footnote_ids iterates el.iter), not per field.

kept.title: Issuer and owner CIKs are stored unnormalised while the index CIK is zero-padded
kept.evidence:
cik_issuer = filing.issuer.cik or ""
    cik_insider = filing.reporting_owner.cik or ""
kept.description: sec_index normalises CIKs with edgar.normalize_cik (10-digit zero pad), but the XML values go into us_trades.cik_issuer/cik_insider exactly as written. Filers use both '0000320193' and '320193', and the parser does not check for digits. Joins or filters on cik_issuer (it is indexed: ix_us_trades_cik_issuer) and entity pages will miss or split the same company.
kept.suggestion: Apply edgar.normalize_cik in _parse_issuer and _parse_reporting_owner (or in mapping). On ValueError, either raise SecOwnershipParseError or store '' with a logged warning. Consider cross-checking the issuer CIK against index_row.cik.
kept.verifier_note: Lines 394-395 do store the XML CIK without normalising it, and the parser does not check for digits. The claim that filers use both '0000320193' and '320193' is unverified. EDGAR-generated ownership XML consistently uses the 10-digit zero-padded form, so this is defensive normalisation, not an observed split.

kept.title: Placeholder trading symbols ('NONE', 'N/A', 'NA') are stored as real tickers
kept.evidence: symbol = _text(el, "issuerTradingSymbol", ctx) or None
kept.description: Filers of non-listed issuers often write NONE, N/A or similar in issuerTradingSymbol. These pass through unchanged, are upper-cased by persistence, and become one shared ticker 'NONE'. That merges unrelated private issuers on ticker-keyed views and price lookups (repositories.py:122 filters by exact ticker).
kept.suggestion: Normalise the symbol in the parser: strip, upper-case, map known placeholders (NONE, N/A, NA, '-', 'NOT APPLICABLE') to None, and when a comma or space separated list appears, take the first token.
kept.verifier_note: Line 259 passes issuerTradingSymbol through unchanged. 'NONE' and 'N/A' are common in real filings for unlisted issuers, so unrelated issuers end up sharing one fake ticker.

kept.title: Company fallback can take the reporting owner's name from the index row
kept.evidence: company = filing.issuer.name or index_row.company_name
kept.description: The master index lists each ownership filing under both the issuer CIK and every reporting-owner CIK, each with its own archive path, so sec_index's archive_path de-duplication does not collapse them. When issuerName is empty and the row being processed is the owner's row, company becomes the insider's name, e.g. 'COOK TIMOTHY D'.
kept.suggestion: Use the fallback only when index_row.cik equals the normalised issuer CIK. Otherwise leave it empty, or resolve the name from the issuer CIK.
kept.verifier_note: The fallback at line 384 only fires when issuerName is empty. The schema requires issuerName, so this is rare. The premise is true and is a bigger problem than the reviewer says: the master index lists each filing under the issuer and every owner CIK, with distinct archive paths, so the same filing is processed once per CIK (see SECPARSE-M1).

kept.title: Transaction-code categories mislabel W and Z as gifts and leave out several codes
kept.evidence:

    "W": "gift",
    "Z": "gift",
kept.description: Under the SEC Form 4 code table, W means acquisition or disposition by will or the laws of descent, and Z means deposit into or withdrawal from a voting trust. Neither is a gift. D (disposition to the issuer), E/H (expirations), I (discretionary), J (other), K (equity swap), L (small acquisition), U (tender) and V (voluntary report) all collapse to 'other'. Today category only feeds trade_type (everything else becomes 'Other'), but the field is public API and invites misuse.
kept.suggestion: Correct the mapping (W -> inheritance, Z -> trust, D -> disposition_to_issuer, E/H -> expiration, etc.) and document the code table next to _CATEGORY_MAP.
kept.verifier_note: Lines 75-77 map W (will or laws of descent) and Z (voting trust deposit or withdrawal) to 'gift', which is wrong under the SEC code table. The impact is small today, because _trade_type turns everything except purchase, sale and exercise into 'Other'.

kept.title: Alternative value fields in the schema are ignored
kept.evidence:
underlying_shares = (
        _value_decimal(
            underlying.find("underlyingSecurityShares"),
kept.description: The schema offers a choice for several fields: transactionShares or transactionTotalValue, sharesOwnedFollowingTransaction or valueOwnedFollowingTransaction, and underlyingSecurityShares or underlyingSecurityValue. These value variants are used for notes, debt and other non-share instruments. Only the share variants are read, so those rows silently end up with shares/value 0.0 and no underlying amount.
kept.suggestion: Read the *Value alternatives as well, keep them in separate fields (or in sec_detail_json), and use transactionTotalValue as the trade value when shares are absent.
kept.verifier_note: Only transactionShares, sharesOwnedFollowingTransaction and underlyingSecurityShares are read (lines 325-349 and 454-462). The schema's choice alternatives (transactionTotalValue, valueOwnedFollowingTransaction, underlyingSecurityValue) are ignored, so value-denominated instruments map to 0.0.

kept.title: The DTD/ENTITY byte scan rejects harmless filings that only mention '<!DOCTYPE' in CDATA or comments
kept.evidence:
if _DTD_OR_ENTITY_DECL.search(xml_bytes) is not None:
        raise SecXmlSecurityError(SecSecurityReason.XML, accession)
kept.description: The regex matches anywhere in the payload, not just in the prolog. A footnote or remark containing literal '<!DOCTYPE' or '<!ENTITY' inside CDATA or a comment (for example pasted HTML) causes the whole filing to be rejected as a security violation (verified with scratch test 'doctype-in-cdata'). lxml is already set up with resolve_entities=False and load_dtd=False, so a real DTD can only appear before the root element.
kept.suggestion: Scan only the prolog, i.e. the bytes before the first '<' that is not '<?' or '<!--'. Alternatively, keep the full scan for the strict path but check root.getroottree().docinfo.internalDTD after parsing to confirm.
kept.verifier_note: Reproduced: '<![CDATA[<!DOCTYPE html>]]>' in remarks raises SecXmlSecurityError. In practice it is almost unreachable, because escaped text (<!DOCTYPE) does not match the byte regex, and CDATA or comments in EDGAR ownership XML are very rare. Narrowing the scan to the prolog also weakens a deliberate defense-in-depth check, so the trade-off is not clearly worth it.

kept.title: Duplicated builders and validators, dead row_id checks, and the ownership form set defined three times

kept.title: Remarks read only .text while footnotes use itertext()
kept.description: _parse_footnotes correctly flattens mixed content with itertext() (line 311). _remarks reads only el.text, so remarks containing any child markup are cut off at the first child element, or come back None when they start with markup.
kept.suggestion: Use the same whitespace-normalised itertext() join as footnotes, through a shared helper.
kept.verifier_note: Reproduced: 'Hello bold tail' gave 'Hello'. The ownership schema defines remarks as plain string content, so child markup does not occur in EDGAR-validated filings. It is only a consistency fix.

kept.title: resolve_cik_from_json re-reads and re-parses the ~1 MB tickers file and scans it linearly on every call
kept.description: Each lookup (secform4.py:53 per scanned ticker, the GUI, the CLI) reads the cached file from disk, parses about 10k entries with json.loads, and walks them all. Multi-ticker scans repeat this for every ticker. The broad 'except Exception' also hides programming errors.
kept.suggestion: Build a ticker->CIK dict once, memoised with functools.lru_cache keyed on the file's mtime or a 24h TTL. Narrow the exception to network and JSON errors.
kept.verifier_note: Each call goes through fetch_url's file cache and runs json.loads plus a linear scan (lines 106-123), and secform4.py:53 calls it once per scanned ticker. A memoised ticker-to-CIK dict would remove this. The broad except Exception is also real.

kept.title: build_edgar_url_for_trade does not URL-encode names or tickers
kept.evidence:
name = trade.insider_name.replace(" ", "+")
    ticker = trade.ticker
kept.description: Insider names such as 'SMITH & CO LLC', "O'NEIL", names containing '#', or non-ASCII names are inserted raw into the query string. '&' splits the q parameter, so the verification link the GUI opens (scan_tab.py:466, 557) searches for the wrong text. The fallback date range 2020-01-01..2030-12-31 is hard-coded.
kept.suggestion: Build the query with urllib.parse.urlencode({'q': f'"{name}" "{ticker}"', 'forms': '4', ...}) and derive the fallback range from today's date.

kept.title: Daily index de-duplicates by archive_path, not accession, so each filing is downloaded and parsed once per listed CIK
kept.description: The EDGAR master index lists each ownership filing once under the issuer CIK and once under every reporting-owner CIK, as edgar/data/<cik>/<accession>.txt. The paths differ, so the archive_path de-duplication keeps every copy. sec_downloader.fetch_filing caches by sha256(archive_path) (sec_downloader.py:214/251), so the cache does not help either. Every Form 4 is therefore fetched at SEC's rate limit and fully parsed at least twice, more for joint filers. Persistence collapses the duplicate rows by (accession, sec_row_id), so data is fine, but network time and the 'discovered/downloaded' counters are at least doubled. The same pattern applies in backfill: the submissions ZIP has issuer and owner JSON files, and the accession skip only covers accessions already completed.
kept.suggestion: De-duplicate rows by the accession number taken from the archive path's final segment, not by the full path. Prefer the row whose CIK matches the issuer, if one is known, for the company-name fallback. Key the downloader cache by accession as well, and in backfill skip accessions already seen in the current run, not only those checkpointed.

kept.title: Derivative rows are merged into Buy/Sell/Exercise with no consumer filtering is_derivative, so option exercises count twice
kept.evidence:
for d_txn in filing.derivative_transactions:
        _validate_derivative(d_txn, filing, index_row)
        trades.append(
            _build_derivative_trade(
kept.description: An option exercise (code M) shows up as a derivative row disposing of the options and as a non-derivative row acquiring the stock. Both map to trade_type 'Exercise' and are emitted as separate InsiderTrades. Derivative P/S rows (buying or selling options or warrants) become 'Buy'/'Sell', with shares counting derivative units and price being the premium. grep shows nothing outside models, schema and merger reads is_derivative. price_chart.py:197 and table_style.py:152 treat 'Exercise' as a buy type, so each exercise is plotted or counted twice and option trades mix into stock Buy/Sell feeds and value totals.
kept.suggestion: Either do not give derivative rows the Buy/Sell/Exercise trade types (map them to 'Other' or a separate type), or make the feed, aggregation and chart queries filter on is_derivative by default. At minimum, keep only one side of an M/C/X exercise pair when counting.

kept.title: The GUI verification link opens the EDGAR full-text-search JSON API, and the fallback window ends before the filing
kept.description: efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index is the backend JSON endpoint for EDGAR full-text search, not the human UI (www.sec.gov/edgar/search/#/q=...). The 'verify' link that scan_tab.py opens therefore shows raw JSON. Also, when filing_date is missing the window is [first of month, trade_date], but a Form 4 is filed on or after the trade date (up to 2 business days later, often more), so the window can exclude the filing.
kept.suggestion: Build the link to https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search/#/q=...&forms=4&dateRange=custom&startdt=...&enddt=..., with urlencoded parameters. When only trade_date is known, extend enddt to trade_date plus a few weeks.

kept.title: insider_title drops the role flags when officerTitle is present, and the isOther description is never parsed
kept.description: A reporting owner who is both a director and an officer (very common for CEOs and chairs) is stored only as e.g. 'CEO', so the Director role is lost for any title-based filtering or display. The parser also never reads reportingOwnerRelationship/otherText (sec_ownership_parser.py:285-289), so isOther owners only get the label 'Other', with no description.
kept.suggestion: Build the title as the officer title plus the other active flags (e.g. 'CEO, Director, 10% Owner'). Parse otherText in _parse_reporting_owner and use it in place of 'Other'. Consider storing the flags as separate columns or in sec_detail_json.

dropped.title: Without an accession, row keys fall back to the fuzzy canonical key, so distinct transactions can collide
dropped.why: No production path has a missing accession. process_filing_row always passes _accession_from_path(row.archive_path), which is non-empty because build_filing_archive_url rejects empty segments. Full submissions also carry the ACCESSION NUMBER header. Only a direct library call without an accession reaches the fuzzy key, and no in-repo caller does that.

areas.title: US services, models and merging
areas.summary: The US service layer is cleanly split into adapters, coverage-gated scan services, SEC daily ingestion and a comparison report. Its weak spot is that coverage bookkeeping trusts every adapter result without checking it. The openinsider and secform4 scrapers turn network errors, unresolved CIKs, layout changes and openinsider's 100-row cap into a normal-looking (possibly empty) list. UsScanService/CongressScanService then mark that interval as permanently covered, and it also marks today and future dates. As a result, data can go missing quietly and is never fetched again. The unbounded ticker scan (the GUI/CLI default) never scrapes the requested ticker. The Congress query uses exact name equality, so trades it just fetched are not returned. Cross-source dedup and the SEC comparison use keys that collapse distinct transactions (exercise and sale of the same quantity) while splitting real duplicates (openinsider signs sales negative, and probably stores filing timestamps that parse_date cannot read). On performance, the SEC sink does one BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction per filing, with a SELECT per row and two json.dumps calls per existing row. The bulk backfill uses the same pattern, which is a major contributor to the slow full-history import. The legacy importer has the same per-record commit problem. Smaller issues: dead parameters (clock, the ticker branch in latest), a checkpoint that duplicates coverage, hand-written serialization boilerplate, and alert evaluation that can miss new rows.

kept.title: Unbounded ticker scan (GUI/CLI default) never fetches the requested ticker
kept.evidence:
refresh_sources = tuple(
                source for source in selected if source in self._latest_adapters
            )
...
                self._refresh_latest(
                    refresh_sources,
                    count=self._latest_overlap_count,
kept.description: When start_date and end_date are both None (the GUI scan tab when 'use dates' is unchecked, and `scan TICKER` in the CLI with no --since/--until), scan() only refreshes the global openinsider 'latest 200' feed (scrape_latest takes no ticker) and then queries the DB for the ticker. secform4 passes validate_sources but is silently ignored because it is not a latest adapter. So for a ticker never scanned before, the result is empty or stale even though the user selected sources that could fetch it.
kept.suggestion: For unbounded scans, either choose a default bounded window (for example the last N months, as CongressScanService does) and go through the coverage-gated adapter path, or call the per-ticker bounded adapters. Raise an error, rather than silently accepting, for sources that cannot serve the requested mode.
kept.verifier_note: With both dates None, scan() validates against _unbounded_sources_available (bounded+latest+sec_edgar), refreshes only the global openinsider latest feed and queries the DB. secform4 is silently dropped when combined with openinsider (and raises ValueError if alone). GUI date checkbox defaults to unchecked (scan_tab.py:124) and the watchlist loop uses the same path. test_us_unbounded_scan_uses_latest_refresh_without_infinite_coverage codifies this, so it is deliberate, but the user-visible result is still that the ticker is never scraped.

kept.title: Scraper failures return [] and the interval is still marked covered for good
kept.description: openinsider.scrape_ticker/scrape_latest and secform4.scrape_ticker (lines 54-56 for an unresolved CIK, 63-65 for fetch errors) catch every exception and return an empty list. UsScanService.scan (us.py:114-115) then upserts nothing and calls coverage.add for the gap. The ScanError path in us.py:104-107 is never reached. A timeout, HTTP 429/5xx, or a CIK lookup failure therefore permanently records that ticker/source/date range as covered with no data, and later scans never retry it. In _refresh_latest the refresh marker is set in the same way.
kept.suggestion: Let fetch and CIK-resolution errors propagate from the scrapers, or return a result object that distinguishes 'fetched, zero rows' from 'failed', so that the service raises ScanError and skips coverage.add. Keep the log line, but re-raise.
kept.verifier_note: openinsider.py:63-67 and 110-114, plus secform4.py:53-56 and 61-65, catch every exception and return []. us.py:97-115 then upserts nothing and calls coverage.add, so the ScanError branch is unreachable for these errors. _refresh_latest also sets the refresh marker after an empty result.

kept.title: openinsider ticker scrape is capped at 100 rows, but the whole gap is marked covered
kept.evidence: f"&feession=&xp=1&vl=&vh=&ocl=&och=&session=&ession=&cnt=100"
kept.description: scrape_ticker hard-codes cnt=100 and never pages. For any coverage gap with more than 100 filings (common for large caps over the 6-month GUI default, or for long first-time ranges), the response is silently truncated to the 100 newest rows. us.py:115 then records the full gap as covered, so the older rows are never fetched.
kept.suggestion: Page through results (openinsider supports a page parameter), or split the gap into smaller date windows until a response returns fewer than cnt rows. At minimum, do not mark coverage when len(rows) == cnt; instead narrow the window and retry.
kept.verifier_note: scrape_ticker hard-codes cnt=100 with no paging, and us.py:115 marks the whole gap covered no matter how many rows came back. Any gap with more than 100 filings is truncated permanently.

kept.title: Coverage is recorded for today and future dates, so later filings are never fetched
kept.evidence:
self._persistence.us_trades.upsert(trades)
                self._persistence.coverage.add("us", identifier, source, gap)
kept.description: Gaps come straight from the requested interval, and nothing clamps them to the dates that are complete (persistence/coverage.py has no today logic). The GUI end date defaults to QDate.currentDate(), so every scan marks today as covered: Form 4s filed later the same day are never fetched for that ticker/source. If the user picks a future end date, those future days are marked covered permanently. CongressScanService (congress.py:163,190) defaults end_date to today and has the same problem.
kept.suggestion: Before calling coverage.add, clamp the recorded interval to end at clock().date() - 1 (or the last fully elapsed business day). The open tail should always be treated as a gap, refreshed through the TTL/refresh-state mechanism.
kept.verifier_note: coverage.add and uncovered_gaps have no notion of today, and us.py:115 records the raw gap, so today or future end dates become permanently covered. The CongressScanService references are wrong: the file has 108 lines. The default end_date=today is at congress.py:49-51 and coverage.add is at congress.py:77.

kept.title: Filing timestamps from openinsider probably parse to None, which hides rows from date-bounded queries
kept.evidence: filing_date=_parse_date(cell_text("filing_date")),
kept.description: On the live openinsider screener, the Filing Date column appears to show a timestamp ('2023-12-15 20:18:05'). The test fixture only uses a bare date, so this is not covered by tests. parse_date tries date.fromisoformat, which I confirmed raises 'Invalid isoformat string' on that value, and then splits on '-', where int('15 20:18:05') fails, so it returns None. Every repository query filters on filing_date (repositories.py:123-126, 166-169) and drops NULLs, so openinsider rows would never be returned by bounded scans or by latest-in-range queries, would sort last in the latest feed, and would disappear from the SEC comparison window.
kept.suggestion: Check one live openinsider page to confirm the format. If confirmed, cut the cell at the first space (or try datetime.fromisoformat(...).date()) before parsing, and add a test fixture that matches the live format, including the timestamp and the negative Qty/Value used for sales.

Repository queries filter on filing_date, so NULL rows drop out. The fixture uses bare dates, so tests miss it. The impact depends on the live openinsider format, which shows timestamps in the Filing Date column.

kept.title: Fuzzy dedup key ignores trade type and sign, so it merges distinct trades and misses real duplicates

    ticker = trade.ticker.upper().strip()
    td = str(trade.trade_date) if trade.trade_date else ""
    # Round shares to nearest 10 for fuzzy matching

kept.description: The same key is duplicated in persistence/mappings.py:79-87 (us_canonical_key for non-SEC rows), so it controls both GUI merging and DB identity. (a) trade_type and price are not part of the key. An option exercise (M) and the same-day sale (S) of the same quantity, which is very common, collapse into one row; merge_trade_pair keeps only one trade_type, so data is lost. The same happens to two secform4 rows of N shares at different prices. (b) openinsider reports sales with negative Qty (parse_number keeps the '-'), while secform4 reports positive quantities, so the same sale from both sources gets buckets -5000 and 5000 and is never merged. (c) round() uses banker's rounding: 104 and 105 both bucket to 100 but 106 goes to 110. The module docstring promises 'within 1%', which the code does not do.
kept.suggestion: Make one shared key function (used by both merger and mappings) that includes trade_type and abs(shares). Treat the bucketing as a separate fuzzy-matching step, or match on exact shares plus price. Delete the duplicated key logic in mappings.py, and fix the docstring. Changing the key means re-keying existing rows in a migration.
kept.verifier_note: merger._dedup_key and mappings.us_canonical_key (lines 79-87) both omit trade_type and price, so an M exercise and an S sale of the same size on the same day collapse. round() uses banker's rounding, and the 'within 1%' docstring is false. Part (b), sign mismatch, applies to in-memory merge_trades. In the DB, negative openinsider rows cannot be stored at all because of the CHECK shares>=0 constraint (see USSVC-M1).

kept.title: SEC persist sink opens one IMMEDIATE transaction per filing, which slows bulk ingest
kept.evidence:
result = self._persistence.us_trades.upsert(trades)
            state.upserts = state.upserts + result
kept.description: Each parsed filing gets its own upsert() call, which runs BEGIN IMMEDIATE, then for every row a SELECT by canonical_key, us_from_row, merge_trade_pair (two json.dumps of the full record) and an INSERT or UPDATE, then COMMIT (an fsync on Windows). sec_backfill.py:148 uses the same pattern. Across the full history of Form 4s, that means millions of commits plus per-row round trips. This is likely a major part of why processing the downloaded all-history batch runs for hours. Re-runs are no cheaper, because every row still goes through select + merge just to be skipped.
kept.suggestion: Buffer the mapped trades in the sink and flush every N filings (for example 500-5000 rows), or once per date, in a single transaction. Coverage stays per date, so the flush must happen before the date's on_progress fires. For SEC-keyed rows, which are deterministic and immutable per accession/row_id, use a bulk INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(canonical_key) DO NOTHING, or a single SELECT canonical_key IN (...) per batch, instead of fetching and merging row by row. Consider PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL with WAL for bulk runs.
kept.verifier_note: The per-filing upsert (BEGIN IMMEDIATE, one SELECT per row, merge, COMMIT, with no WAL and default synchronous) is real at sec_daily.py:243 and sec_backfill.py:148. Calling it 'a major contributor' to the slow full-history import is overstated. Each filing first needs a rate-limited HTTP fetch (8 req/s, so at least 125 ms) plus a cache promote, and the backfill rewrites its whole checkpoint after every filing (USSVC-M2), which dwarfs one SQLite commit.

kept.title: SEC comparison fingerprint reports mismatches for matching trades

        f"{row.shares:.6f}",
        f"{row.value:.2f}",
kept.description: SEC rows have positive shares and value = shares*price to the cent (sec_trade_mapping.py). openinsider rows carry negative shares/value for sales and whole-dollar values, and openinsider combines a filing's same-day rows into one line with a weighted price. SEC also emits derivative and 'Other' (F/G/A code) rows that the legacy sources do not show. With exact sign-sensitive shares and cent-exact value, nearly every openinsider sale, and every multi-row filing, lands in both SEC-only and legacy-only, so the validation report says the sources disagree when they do not.
kept.suggestion: Fingerprint on abs(shares) and drop value, or compare it within a tolerance. Optionally group SEC rows by (accession, trade_date, trade_type) before comparing with openinsider, and filter SEC rows to non-derivative P/S/M codes (or let the caller choose) so both sides cover the same transaction types.
kept.verifier_note: The cent-exact value comparison (SEC uses shares*price while secform4/openinsider show whole-dollar totals), the unaggregated SEC rows and the derivative/Other rows do cause false mismatches. The sign part is wrong: negative openinsider shares/value cannot be persisted, because us_trades has CHECK shares>=0 and value>=0 (schema.py:84-86), so no negative legacy rows exist for the comparison to read.

kept.title: Legacy import commits once per record
kept.evidence: result = persistence.us_trades.upsert((trade,))

If a chunk hits a persistence error, fall back to per-record upserts for that chunk only, to keep the per-record error reporting.

kept.title: Congress flagging on every query: false positives for empty or short names, disk read and O(N*M) scan per call

kept.title: continue_on_error=False is not honoured across coverage gaps
kept.description: With continue_on_error=False, the downloader stops the current gap at the first failed date. ingest_range does not check for that and moves straight on to the next gap, so the run keeps going past the first error, which the flag is meant to prevent. SecDownloadReport has no interrupted flag, so the service cannot tell a stopped gap from a finished one.
kept.suggestion: Add an `interrupted`/`stopped_on_error` field to SecDownloadReport. In ingest_range, break when it is set and continue_on_error is False, or when report.dates_completed < _day_count(gap).
kept.verifier_note: ingest_range ignores a gap that stopped on error and moves on to the next gap, and SecDownloadReport has no interrupted flag. However, no production caller sets continue_on_error=False (application.py and sec_daily both default it to True), so this is currently unreachable.

kept.title: merge_trade_pair serializes both records to JSON on every existing-row upsert
kept.description: UsTradeRepository.upsert calls merge_trade_pair for every row that already exists. That runs to_dict() and json.dumps(sort_keys=True) twice, including the potentially large sec_detail_json, just to pick a tie-breaker, and then compares merged == existing. On re-ingests or overlapping backfills, where almost every row is a skip, this is pure overhead in the hottest loop.
kept.suggestion: Return early when the incoming trade equals the existing one (for SEC rows, compare document_sha256 or a stored content hash) before ranking. Compute the JSON tie-breaker only when the richness scores are equal.
kept.verifier_note: _primary_rank does to_dict and json.dumps(sort_keys=True) for both records on every existing-row upsert, including sec_detail_json. This is wasted work on re-ingest skips, but it is small next to the network cost.

kept.title: Unused clock parameter and a checkpoint that duplicates coverage in SecDailyIngestionService

kept.title: Importer does not validate other boolean fields and fails on UTF-8 BOM files
kept.evidence:

        raise ValueError("is_congress must be a boolean")
kept.description: Only is_congress is type-checked. InsiderTrade.from_dict passes is_amendment and is_derivative through unchanged, so a JSON value of "false" becomes a truthy string that ends up in a Boolean column. Numeric strings are coerced by float(), but null raises TypeError, so the whole record is rejected. In addition, path.read_text(encoding='utf-8') (line 299) rejects JSON saved with a BOM, which is common for files edited on Windows, and reports the whole file as malformed_json.

A string 'false' for is_amendment/is_derivative is not stored: SQLAlchemy's strict Boolean processor raises StatementError, so the record is rejected as persistence_error instead of invalid_record. kept.title: InsiderTrade/CongressTrade to_dict/from_dict re-list every field by hand

kept.title: Bulk backfill rewrites the entire sorted checkpoint (indent=2 + fsync) after every filing, so the run is O(N^2)

kept.description: After each filing, _save_completed sorts the whole completed set and atomic_write_json serializes it with indent=2, then writes a temp file, fsyncs and renames it. kept.title: Full-history backfill fetches every filing over the network at 8 req/s with no DB skip, which sets the throughput ceiling

kept.description: The submissions ZIP holds only metadata, so each ownership filing (forms 3, 3/A, 4, 4/A, 5, 5/A per sec_bulk.OWNERSHIP_FORMS) is downloaded individually through the shared SecClient (DEFAULT_REQUESTS_PER_SECOND = 8.0). Millions of historical ownership filings divided by 8 per second is days of wall time, before any parsing or DB work. Resume skips only accessions in the JSON checkpoint, which is keyed by ZIP filename and deleted on completion. Filings already stored by daily ingest, or by an earlier backfill whose checkpoint was lost, are fetched again even though us_trades.accession_number is indexed. Form 3/3A filings (holdings only, no transactions) are fetched as well.

For true full history, ingest SEC's quarterly Insider Transactions (Form 3/4/5) bulk data sets, which already contain the transaction rows, instead of fetching each filing document.

kept.title: SEC daily ingest permanently marks today and future dates as covered when the daily index is not yet published
kept.evidence:
def _record_coverage(snapshot: SecDownloadProgress) -> None:
            self._persistence.coverage.add(
                _COVERAGE_DOMAIN,
                SEC_DAILY_IDENTIFIER,
                _COVERAGE_SOURCE,
                DateInterval(snapshot.current_date, snapshot.current_date),
kept.description: _process_date treats a 404 on the daily master index (SecFilingNotFoundError) as 'date fully handled' (sec_downloads.py:201-203), so on_progress fires and this recorder marks the date covered. `sec-daily` with no --date defaults to date.today() (cli.py:442). SEC publishes a day's index only after that day ends, so running the command during the day (or giving a future end in sec-range) records the date as covered with zero filings, and later runs never retry it. The unused self._clock (sec_daily.py:128) was meant for exactly this kind of clamp.
kept.suggestion: Clamp the requested range to dates before clock() (or to the last business day whose index can exist). Do not record coverage for a 404 index on today or later. Record it only for past dates, such as weekends and holidays, where a missing index is expected.

dropped.title: secform4 CSS trade-type hint uses substring matching on the joined class string
dropped.why: This is speculative. The hint runs only when the text classification already gave 'Other', and secform4 uses single-letter code classes (the fixture uses class="S"). No class containing a capital S that is not the code S has been shown. Exact token membership is cleaner but fixes no demonstrated misclassification.

areas.title: Persistence layer (SQLite)
areas.summary: The persistence layer is tidy and defensive: SQLAlchemy Core, typed UTC datetimes, ordered migrations that run in a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction, parameterized SQL everywhere (LIKE input is escaped, so I found no injection risk), and atomic writes for the JSON state files. It was built for small data, though, and does not scale to a full SEC backfill. I benchmarked it on a copy of the real schema with synthetic rows in the scratchpad (scratchpad/persist/bench.py, alt.py, pool.py). Saving one filing the way the backfill does costs about 30 ms. That breaks down into a new SQLite connection per call (NullPool, about 2.4 ms each), the default rollback journal with synchronous=FULL (one fsync-heavy commit per filing), and about 1 ms per row of SQLAlchemy statement building plus a SELECT-then-INSERT for every row. Batching the writes measured about 59 us per row, roughly 17x faster. Switching to WAL with synchronous=NORMAL alone cut the per-filing cost from 29.8 ms to 10.7 ms. Over millions of Form 4 filings, the persistence cost alone comes to tens of hours. The read side has the same scaling problem. Every feed page counts, sorts and takes MAX over a UNION ALL of all trade tables, with no supporting indexes and with OFFSET paging (1.5-2.7 s per page at 300k rows; it grows linearly with row count). query_latest loads the whole table to return N rows (5.6 s at 300k). Correctness problems: SEC-native trades and scraped trades get different canonical keys, so the same trade is stored twice. The fuzzy key collapses an option exercise and a same-day sale into one row. Scan coverage marks today (and any future dates) as permanently covered. Several JSON state paths can crash the app at startup or silently lose user data.

kept.title: Row-by-row upsert (SELECT, then INSERT/UPDATE per trade, built through SQLAlchemy each time) dominates the bulk backfill cost
kept.description: Each trade runs a full-row SELECT. A new trade then gets a fresh insert(...).values(dict) statement with about 31 bind parameters, so SQLAlchemy rebuilds the cache key and coerces parameters for every row (cProfile: coercions.expect, _gen_cache_key and _get_crud_kv_pairs dominate). An existing trade instead goes through us_from_row, merge_trade_pair (to_dict plus json.dumps of both records) and an UPDATE. Measured: about 1,077 us per row even inside one transaction (300k rows took 321 s), and 270-365 us per row when every row is skipped. us_canonical_key is also computed twice per insert (once here and again inside us_to_values). sec_backfill.py:148 calls upsert once per filing (about 4 rows), so the whole per-call overhead repeats millions of times. Together with PERSIST-02 and PERSIST-03 this is about 30 ms per filing, which is enough by itself to keep a full-history backfill from finishing in a reasonable time.
kept.suggestion: Add a batch path. Compute the canonical keys once. Preload the existing rows with `WHERE canonical_key IN (...)` in chunks of about 500-900. Insert the new rows with one executemany: `connection.execute(insert(us_trades), list_of_dicts)`, or `insert(...).on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=['canonical_key'])` for SEC-native keys. Merge only the rows that already exist and update them with executemany too. Give the backfill a buffering sink that flushes every N filings, for example 200-1,000 filings or 5-10k rows, in one transaction, and save the checkpoint after each flush. A prototype of this pattern measured 59 us per row, about 17x faster.
kept.verifier_note: The row-by-row SELECT then INSERT/UPDATE inside one immediate transaction per call is real (repositories.py:76-105), and sec_backfill.py:148 calls it once per filing. But with about 4 rows per filing, the per-row SQLAlchemy cost is only about 4 ms of the claimed 30 ms; the per-call commit/fsync (PERSIST-02) and the new connection (PERSIST-03) are the larger shares. The backfill is also network-bound: process_filing_row fetches each filing through SecClient's fair-access rate limiter (at least about 100 ms per uncached filing), and the per-filing checkpoint rewrite (see PERSIST-M1) grows quadratically. So this finding does not 'dominate', and 'critical' is inflated, although batching the writes is still a worthwhile fix.

kept.title: No WAL or synchronous tuning: every per-filing commit pays rollback-journal fsyncs, and GUI reads and backfill writes block each other
kept.evidence:
cursor.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON")
cursor.execute(f"PRAGMA busy_timeout={busy_timeout_ms}")
kept.description: Only foreign_keys (useless here, because the schema defines no foreign keys) and busy_timeout are set. A grep confirms journal_mode and synchronous are set nowhere, so the database runs with journal_mode=DELETE and synchronous=FULL (bench printed 'delete 2'). Each commit therefore writes and deletes a rollback journal with several fsyncs. Measured on this machine: 29.8 ms per filing now, against 10.7 ms with WAL and synchronous=NORMAL and nothing else changed. Concurrency is worse. In rollback-journal mode a committing writer needs an EXCLUSIVE lock, so it must wait for every reader's SHARED lock to clear. Feed queries are full scans (PERSIST-05) that will take more than the 5 s busy_timeout on a large database. When that happens the backfill's upsert fails with 'database is locked', which becomes a PersistenceError, and sec_downloads.py:294 counts the filing as failed. In the other direction, GUI reads stall while a writer holds PENDING or EXCLUSIVE.
kept.suggestion: Inside the 'connect' listener, run `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` (persistent; it must run outside a transaction, which the listener already is), `PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL` (safe with WAL), and optionally `PRAGMA temp_store=MEMORY`, a larger `cache_size` (for example -65536) and `mmap_size`. With WAL, readers never block the writer and the writer never blocks readers. Drop the unused foreign_keys pragma, or keep it and document that it is for future foreign keys. Also drop either connect_args timeout or the busy_timeout PRAGMA, since both set the same thing.
kept.verifier_note: engine.py:61-62 sets only foreign_keys and busy_timeout. No code under src or tests sets journal_mode or synchronous, and the schema has no ForeignKey/REFERENCES, so foreign_keys is a no-op. feed.query (feed.py:478) holds one deferred read transaction across COUNT, the page query and MAX. In rollback-journal mode, that SHARED lock blocks a writer's commit for up to the 5 s busy_timeout. connect_args timeout and the PRAGMA busy_timeout duplicate each other.

kept.title: NullPool opens a new sqlite3 connection (and re-parses the schema) for every repository call
kept.evidence:
connect_args={"timeout": busy_timeout_ms / 1_000},
poolclass=NullPool,
kept.description: Every engine.connect() or engine.begin() opens the database file, runs the connect-listener pragmas, makes SQLite re-read the schema on the first statement, and starts with a cold page cache. Measured: 2.38 ms for connect plus one indexed SELECT, against 0.09 ms on a reused connection (about 25x). Each upsert call (one per filing in the backfill), each coverage.add, and each of the up-to-1,000 recent_by_* calls in watchlist alert evaluation pays this cost.
kept.suggestion: Use a pool. SQLAlchemy's default QueuePool for file databases works here because each connection stays in its acquiring thread for the length of a with-block; add check_same_thread=False so pooled connections can move between worker threads. Alternatively use SingletonThreadPool or StaticPool for a dedicated backfill engine. If NullPool was chosen so tests can delete database files on Windows, call engine.dispose() in test teardown instead. Long-running bulk jobs should also hold one connection for the whole run.
kept.verifier_note: engine.py:46 uses NullPool, so every engine.begin()/connect() opens a new sqlite3 connection and re-runs the connect listener. The cost is real, but at about 2.4 ms per call it is a small part of the per-filing cost; it matters mostly for the per-entry alert loops. In SQLAlchemy 2.0 the pysqlite dialect already uses QueuePool with check_same_thread=False for file databases, so dropping poolclass=NullPool is enough (call engine.dispose() in tests, which context.py and the tests already do).

kept.title: SEC-native trades and scraped trades get different canonical keys, so the same trade is stored twice
kept.description: Only sec_trade_mapping.py sets sec_row_id; openinsider and secform4 trades never do. A transaction ingested by the SEC daily or backfill pipeline is keyed on ('sec', accession, row). The same transaction scraped from openinsider or secform4 is keyed on (ticker, name, date, shares bucket). The two keys never collide, so the repository stores two rows. Feed totals, value filters, investigation lists and alerts all count the trade twice. merge_trade_pair is never invoked across the two sources, so the provenance merge the schema was designed for never happens either.
kept.suggestion: Keep one identity per economic transaction. For example, store the fuzzy key in its own indexed column (fuzzy_key) on every row. On upsert, when the SEC key misses, look up by fuzzy_key; when a scraped trade arrives, try the fuzzy match against SEC rows first. Then merge into the SEC row and add the source to provenance instead of inserting. A one-off migration should collapse the duplicates that already exist.
kept.verifier_note: SEC-native rows really are keyed on (accession, sec_row_id) and scraped rows on the fuzzy key (mappings.py:77-87), so the same transaction appears twice in the feed and in alerts. This is deliberate, though: the docstring says 'so that existing third-party rows are unaffected', and services/sec_comparison.py depends on SEC and legacy rows coexisting so it can compare them. The proposed merge-on-upsert would break that report. A dedup or 'preferred source' view at feed level is a safer fix than collapsing rows.

kept.title: Every feed page does a full UNION ALL scan three times: COUNT, sort on unindexed columns, and MAX(created_at)
kept.evidence:
with self._engine.connect() as connection:
    total_count = int(connection.execute(count_statement).scalar_one())
    rows = connection.execute(statement).mappings().all()
    freshness = _aware_utc(
        connection.execute(
            select(func.max(feed.c.created_at))
        ).scalar_one_or_none()
    )
kept.description: _projection() wraps us_trades, congress_trades and european_trades in a UNION ALL subquery. Sorting is on expressions such as `transaction_date IS NULL, transaction_date DESC, ..., key` (where key is computed as 'us:' || CAST(id)). No index covers trade_date, insider_name or created_at, so each page builds the full union, sorts all of it in a temporary B-tree, counts all of it again, and scans it a third time for MAX(created_at). Measured at 300k rows: 1.55 s for page 0 and 1.07 s for a search. Time grows linearly, so at full EDGAR scale (tens of millions of rows) each page load and each criteria-based alert evaluation (services/alerts.py:78) takes tens of seconds to minutes. The search predicates (`lower(coalesce(col,'')) LIKE '%x%'` over 7 columns) can never use an index.
kept.suggestion: Add indexes that match the default sorts, at least us_trades(trade_date DESC, id) and us_trades(filing_date), plus equivalents on the other tables. When only one market is selected, query that table directly instead of the union; when several are, push ORDER BY and LIMIT into each branch (each branch returns at most offset+limit rows) and merge those small sets. Read freshness from refresh_state or from a cached `MAX(id)`, not a full scan. Cache total_count per criteria, or make it optional or approximate. For text search, add an FTS5 table (trigram tokenizer for substring search) over issuer, person, identifier and role.
kept.verifier_note: feed.py:459-485 runs COUNT, a sorted LIMIT/OFFSET and MAX(created_at) over a UNION ALL of three tables, and sorts on expressions (sort IS NULL, lower(issuer), the string key) that no index covers. The trade tables have no index on trade_date or created_at, and the search predicates are lower(coalesce()) LIKE '%x%'. Cost grows linearly with the table size, which a backfill makes very large.

kept.title: query_latest loads and converts the entire table in Python, then slices to N rows
kept.evidence:
result = [
    us_from_row(row)
    for row in rows
    if not requested_sources
    or requested_sources.intersection(us_provenance(row))
]
return result[:count]
kept.description: The SQL has no LIMIT, so every us_trades row is fetched, sorted (`filing_date DESC NULLS LAST` cannot use the existing indexes), JSON-decoded for provenance, and turned into an InsiderTrade before the list is cut to `count`. Measured: 5.65 s for query_latest(10) at 300k rows; at backfill scale it will take minutes and use gigabytes of memory. services/us.py:167 and :245 call it on the 'latest' scan path. EuropeanTradeRepository.query_latest (line 397-403) has the same pattern.
kept.suggestion: With no sources filter, add `.limit(count)`. With one, iterate the cursor and stop after `count` matches instead of building the full list, or put the source check in SQL (for example `source_provenance_json LIKE '%"edgar"%'`, or a JSON1 `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(...))`). Add an index on (filing_date DESC, trade_date DESC), and sort with `filing_date IS NULL, filing_date DESC` so the index can serve it.
kept.verifier_note: query_latest (repositories.py:171-191) has no LIMIT. It materialises and converts every row, filters provenance in Python and only then slices [:count]. It is called from services/us.py:167 and :245. No existing index leads with filing_date, since both start with ticker or source.

kept.title: Scan coverage ignores covered_at, so a range ending today (or later) is permanently 'covered' and later filings are never fetched
kept.description: services/us.py:115 and congress.py:77 call coverage.add() with the whole requested gap after one fetch. The GUI's default end date is QDate.currentDate() (scan_tab.py:140, congress_tab.py:298). A scan at 09:00 therefore marks today as covered. A rescan at 18:00 finds no gap and never fetches the Form 4s filed later that day. The same happens for any future end date and, for Congress, for the 45-day disclosure lag. The schema stores covered_at (schema.py:242), but gaps() never reads it. add() also deletes and reinserts every interval, which resets covered_at to now and destroys the information that would be needed.
kept.suggestion: In CoverageRepository.add, clamp interval.end to min(end, today - settle_days), where settle_days is defined per source (about 2 for Form 4, about 45 for Congress), or skip recording when the clamped interval is empty. Alternatively, have gaps() treat any interval whose end_date >= covered_at.date() - settle_days as uncovered. Preserve covered_at when compacting, for example the minimum of the merged intervals.
kept.verifier_note: services/us.py:115 and congress.py:77 record the whole gap after one fetch. GUI end dates default to QDate.currentDate() (scan_tab.py:140, congress_tab.py:298), and Congress defaults end_date to today when none is given. gaps() never reads covered_at, and add() deletes and reinserts the intervals, which resets covered_at. Nothing in the code clears or resets coverage, so today's later filings are never fetched again for that ticker and source.

kept.title: The fuzzy US canonical key ignores trade_type and price, so a same-day exercise and sale collapse into one row
kept.description: A very common Form 4 pattern is an option exercise (M, mapped to 'Exercise') followed by a sale (S, 'Sell') of the same share count on the same day. From scraped sources these produce the same key. merge_trade_pair keeps only the 'richer' record, so one transaction is lost and the survivor's direction can be wrong. Trades with trade_date=None and the same share bucket also collapse together. Round-half-to-even bucketing adds inconsistent edge cases (15 rounds to 20, 25 rounds to 20).
kept.suggestion: Add trade_type to the fuzzy key, and possibly a price bucket or transaction_code when available. Changing the key requires a migration that recomputes canonical_key; do it together with PERSIST-04. Use floor bucketing or a tolerance-based match instead of round().
kept.verifier_note: The fuzzy key (mappings.py:79-87) is (ticker, name, trade_date, shares bucket) with no trade_type, so a same-day M exercise and S sale of the same share count from a scraped source collapse into one row, and merge_trade_pair keeps one whole record. Python's round() uses banker's rounding (round(1.5)=2, round(2.5)=2), as the finding says. core/merger._dedup_key has the same pattern, so any fix must be made in both places.

kept.title: Re-ingesting the same SEC row picks the stored version by lexicographic JSON order, so parser corrections may be skipped
kept.description: For SEC-native keys (accession plus row id) the incoming record is the authoritative re-parse of the same document. merge_trade_pair nonetheless chooses a whole-record winner by richness score, and on a tie by `json.dumps(stable_values, sort_keys=True)` string order (core/merger.py:59-69). If a parser fix changes price from 12.5 to 12.05, or rewrites sec_detail_json or document_sha256 without changing the richness score, the old row wins whenever its JSON sorts higher. The upsert then reports 'skipped' and the stale value stays forever. For fuzzy keys the merge is all-or-nothing: fields the losing record had populated (for example insider_title) are discarded instead of coalesced. That contradicts the merger docstring.
kept.suggestion: When both the existing and incoming rows carry SEC-native identity, prefer the incoming row (or the one with the newer filing_date or document hash) and only union provenance and edgar_url. For fuzzy-key merges, coalesce field by field (fill empty fields from the other record) instead of replacing the whole record.
kept.verifier_note: The tie-break really is score first, then json.dumps string order (merger.py:60-69), so a corrected re-parse with the same richness score can lose and be reported as 'skipped'. The claim that this contradicts the merger docstring is wrong: the module docstring says the richer record wins, and merge_trade_pair's docstring explicitly says SEC fields are intentionally not coalesced (deferred). Re-ingesting the same accession is also uncommon, because the backfill checkpoint skips completed accessions.

kept.title: Upsert failures lose their cause, and one bad row rolls back the whole batch
kept.evidence:
def _wrap(operation: str, error: SQLAlchemyError) -> PersistenceError:
    return PersistenceError(f"{operation} failed")
kept.description: The `error` argument is unused. Callers log `str(exc)`; sec_downloads.py:297 logs 'stage=persist ... reason=%s'. The log therefore shows only 'US trade upsert failed'. It cannot distinguish 'database is locked' from a CHECK violation (for example ck_us_trades_price_nonnegative on a negative parsed value) or a malformed value, which makes backfill failures very hard to diagnose. Because each upsert is one transaction, one constraint-violating trade discards every other valid trade in the filing (or in the importer batch, which is why importer.py:326 upserts one record at a time).
kept.suggestion: Put the cause in the message: `PersistenceError(f"{operation} failed: {type(error).__name__}: {error.orig if hasattr(error,'orig') else error}")`. Add a structured attribute such as `is_access_denied`, or a subclass for lock contention so callers can retry. Use a SAVEPOINT per row (`connection.begin_nested()`), or validate before inserting, so bad rows are counted and skipped without aborting the batch, and return them in UpsertResult.
kept.verifier_note: _wrap (repositories.py:41-42) ignores `error`. The cause is chained via `raise ... from error`, but sec_downloads.py:294-297 logs only `reason=%s` with str(exc), which reads 'US trade upsert failed'. Each upsert call is one transaction, so a single CHECK violation rolls back every row in that call.

kept.title: detail() looks up a record by a computed key over the whole UNION, then queries the table again by id
kept.evidence:
feed = _projection()
stmt = select(feed).where(feed.c.key == key)
kept.description: The prefix and integer id have already been parsed (row_id and prefix), but the base record is fetched by filtering `'us:' || CAST(id AS VARCHAR) = :key` across all three tables, which forces a full scan of each (0.10 s at 300k rows, linear in size). The method then runs a second, indexed primary-key query on the right table. The investigation drawer calls this on every row click.
kept.suggestion: Select the projection branch for the right table directly, for example `select(<us branch>).where(us_trades.c.id == row_id)`. Better, build the FeedRecord from the single `select(us_trades).where(id == row_id)` row that is already fetched. That removes the scan and one round trip.
kept.verifier_note: detail() filters the projection by the computed key (feed.py:552-553). 'us:' || CAST(id) cannot use the primary key, so every table is scanned even though row_id and prefix are already parsed, and a second PK lookup follows. It is a real waste, but it runs once per click, at about 0.1 s at 300k rows.

kept.title: recent_by_issuer and recent_by_person wrap the columns in lower(coalesce()), which prevents index use
kept.evidence: conditions = [func.lower(func.coalesce(feed.c.identifier, "")) == normalized]
kept.description: Tickers are stored uppercase (us_to_values normalizes them) and ix_us_trades_ticker_filing_date exists. Wrapping the column in functions on top of the UNION makes SQLite scan every row; EXPLAIN shows 'SCAN us_trades'. recent_by_person (line 652) has the same problem on an unindexed insider_name. Watchlist alert evaluation (services/alerts.py:64-72) calls one of these per entry, for up to 1,000 entries, so one evaluation can mean 1,000 full scans. Entity pages call them with limit=200.
kept.suggestion: Compare the raw column with a pre-normalized parameter (`us_trades.c.ticker == identifier.upper()` and `european_trades.c.isin == ...`) per table, not across the union. Add an index on us_trades(insider_name COLLATE NOCASE, trade_date) or a normalized insider_name_key column. For alerts, run one query with `ticker IN (...)` over all watchlist entries instead of one query per entry.
kept.verifier_note: feed.py:652 and :698 compare lower(coalesce(col,'')) over the union, which rules out any index. services/alerts.py:64-73 calls these per watchlist entry, up to _MAX_ENTRIES=1000 per list, each with limit 100 and a fresh NullPool connection.

kept.title: Feed pagination uses LIMIT/OFFSET over a sorted UNION
kept.evidence:
.limit(query.limit)
.offset(query.offset)
kept.description: With OFFSET, SQLite must produce and discard all earlier rows of the fully sorted union. Measured: 2.65 s at offset 100k against 1.55 s at offset 0 (300k rows). Infinite scrolling in gui/feed_page.py:488 gets slower with every page. If rows are inserted between page loads (for example by a running backfill), rows shift and the user sees duplicates or skipped rows.
kept.suggestion: Switch to keyset (seek) pagination. Return the last row's sort tuple (sort value, filing_date, key) as a cursor and filter `WHERE (sort, filing_date, key) < (:a, :b, :c)` using SQLite row-value comparison. Use a numeric (market, id) tiebreaker instead of the string-concatenated key.
kept.verifier_note: feed.py:473-474 uses LIMIT/OFFSET, and gui/feed_page.py:486-488 sets offset to the model's rowCount for infinite scroll. Deeper pages cost more, and rows inserted concurrently shift the page boundaries.

kept.title: Unused indexes on us_trades slow every insert while the indexes the queries need are missing
kept.evidence:
Index("ix_us_trades_accession", us_trades.c.accession_number)
Index("ix_us_trades_cik_issuer", us_trades.c.cik_issuer)
kept.description: A grep of the codebase finds no query that filters on us_trades.accession_number, cik_issuer or source; source filtering happens in Python over source_provenance_json. ix_us_trades_source_filing_date (line 93-97), ix_us_trades_accession and ix_us_trades_cik_issuer therefore add write amplification to every backfill insert without serving any read. ix_refresh_state_refreshed_at (line 280) and refresh_state.metadata_json are never used either. Meanwhile there is no index for the columns actually sorted or filtered on: trade_date (the feed's default sort), insider_name (recent_by_person, entity pages) and created_at (freshness and alerts).
kept.suggestion: In a new migration, drop the unused indexes (or keep accession only if a planned 'already ingested?' check will use it). Add indexes that match the queries: us_trades(trade_date), us_trades(filing_date, trade_date), us_trades(insider_name COLLATE NOCASE), and created_at if freshness stays as a query. For very large backfills, consider dropping the secondary indexes before the bulk load and recreating them afterwards.
kept.verifier_note: A grep finds no query on us_trades.source, accession_number or cik_issuer; source filtering is done in Python over provenance JSON. So ix_us_trades_source_filing_date (created by v1 create_all) and the two indexes from migration 3 (migrations.py:70-75) only add write cost. refresh_state is tiny, so its unused index does not matter. The indexes the feed needs (trade_date, insider_name, created_at) are missing. Keep the accession index if amendment supersession (PERSIST-M2) is implemented.

kept.title: Duplicate indexes: price_history and scan_coverage each have an explicit index identical to their UNIQUE constraint
kept.evidence:
Index(
    "ix_price_history_symbol_date",
    price_history.c.symbol,
    price_history.c.price_date,
)
kept.description: UniqueConstraint('symbol','price_date') already creates sqlite_autoindex_price_history_1 on the same columns in the same order. ix_scan_coverage_lookup (line 261-268) likewise duplicates uq_scan_coverage_interval. The benchmark database lists both pairs. Each price or coverage write maintains two identical B-trees and the file is bigger for nothing.
kept.suggestion: Drop ix_price_history_symbol_date and ix_scan_coverage_lookup in a new migration (`DROP INDEX IF EXISTS`), and remove them from the runtime metadata so fresh databases do not create them.
kept.verifier_note: UniqueConstraint('symbol','price_date') and uq_scan_coverage_interval already create autoindexes with the same column order as ix_price_history_symbol_date (schema.py:322) and ix_scan_coverage_lookup (schema.py:261).

kept.title: JSON state loaders that are documented as 'never raises' crash on a non-UTF-8 file
kept.description: read_text raises UnicodeDecodeError, a ValueError subclass, when the file contains invalid UTF-8. That can happen after a partial copy, an antivirus quarantine stub or a hand edit in another encoding. Neither the OSError nor the JSONDecodeError handler catches it. feed_state.load_feed_state (feed_state.py:204-210) has the same gap. MainWindow.__init__ calls load_feed_state, load_watchlists and load_alerts (main_window.py:95-101), so a bad file prevents the GUI from starting.
kept.suggestion: Catch `(OSError, UnicodeDecodeError)`, or `ValueError` broadly, around the read in both loaders. Better, make load_feed_state reuse read_json_dict (see PERSIST-18) so the fix lives in one place.
kept.verifier_note: path.read_text(encoding='utf-8') at json_state.py:56 (line 55 is the `try:`) raises UnicodeDecodeError, a ValueError, which neither the OSError nor the JSONDecodeError handler catches. feed_state.py:205 has the same gap. main_window.py:95-101 calls the loaders in __init__ without a guard, so a bad file stops the app from starting.

kept.title: An unreadable or corrupt state file is silently replaced with defaults on the next save, losing watchlists, alerts or saved screens
kept.description: read_json_dict returns None for invalid JSON or a wrong top-level type, and load_watchlists, load_alerts and load_feed_state then return empty stores. The GUI saves those stores back: on any edit (main_window.py:375/382) and always on close for feed state (main_window.py:612). A single malformed byte therefore permanently erases every watchlist, alert rule or saved screen, with only a log warning.
kept.suggestion: When a file exists but cannot be parsed, rename it to `<name>.corrupt-<timestamp>` (or copy it to .bak) before returning the default, and tell the user. Optionally keep the previous good version as `<name>.bak` in atomic_write_json and fall back to it on load.
kept.verifier_note: read_json_dict returns None for an OSError (for example a file locked by AV or a sync tool), invalid JSON or a wrong top-level type, and the loaders then return empty stores. main_window.py:612 always saves feed state on close, and watchlists and alerts are saved on the next edit (lines 375 and 382), which overwrites the original file.

kept.title: feed_state duplicates the atomic write and read helpers already in json_state
kept.evidence:

    fd, tmp_name = tempfile.mkstemp(
kept.description: save_feed_state copies atomic_write_json line for line, and load_feed_state (lines 202-226) re-implements read_json_dict. Fixes such as PERSIST-16 and PERSIST-17 have to be made twice, and the two copies are already the kind of thing that drifts.
kept.suggestion: Implement both as `atomic_write_json(path, state_to_dict(state))` and `data = read_json_dict(path); return state_from_dict(data) if data else FeedState()`, then drop the os, tempfile and json imports.
