kept.title: Renaming a watchlist allows duplicate names and leaves alert rules pointing at the old name
kept.description: There is no collision check here or in gui/watchlist_page.py:218-227. Renaming 'A' to an existing 'B' produces two lists named 'B'. get() then returns only the first, with_entry adds the entry to both, and without_list deletes both. AlertRule.watchlist stores the name as a string, so after any rename the rule's watchlist lookup (services/alerts.py:61) returns None and the alert silently stops firing.
kept.suggestion: Reject or merge when `new` already exists (raise WatchlistError and let the GUI show it). Propagate renames to AlertStore, for example with an `AlertStore.renamed_watchlist(old, new)` called in the same GUI action, or reference watchlists by a stable id instead of their display name.
kept.verifier_note: Neither renamed() (watchlists.py:102-106) nor gui/watchlist_page.py:218-227 checks for a name collision. with_entry updates every list with the matching name and without_list removes all of them. AlertRule.watchlist is a name string that is never updated on rename, so after a rename services/alerts.py:61-63 returns () and the alert stops firing without any message.

kept.title: Adding a rule, list or entry at the cap silently drops the new item
kept.evidence:
others = tuple(r for r in self.rules if r.name != rule.name)
return replace(self, rules=(*others, rule)[:_MAX_RULES])
kept.description: With 200 rules, adding a new one appends it and then truncates to 200, so the rule just added is the one dropped. The GUI shows no error and the user believes it was saved. Updating an existing rule also moves it to the end of the list. watchlists.with_list (line 96) and with_entry (line 119) truncate the same way: with_entry on a missing list at the 200-list cap silently does nothing.
kept.suggestion: Check the cap before adding and raise AlertStoreError or WatchlistError (or return a status) so the GUI can tell the user. Replace in place to keep the order: `tuple(rule if r.name == rule.name else r for r in self.rules)`.
kept.verifier_note: alerts.py:62-63 appends the rule and then truncates to _MAX_RULES, so at the cap the new rule is the one dropped, and an updated rule moves to the end. watchlists.with_list (line 96) truncates the same way, so with_entry at the 200-list cap is a silent no-op.

kept.title: An alert rule with unparseable criteria quietly becomes a 'match everything' rule
kept.evidence:
except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - resilient: bad criteria → default
    criteria = FeedCriteria()
kept.description: If the stored criteria fail validation (for example after a FeedMarket rename, a bad date, or value_min > value_max from a hand edit), the rule loads with the default FeedCriteria, which has no filters. The next evaluation reports up to 200 'new' matches for a rule that was meant to be narrow, and the user is not told why. The broad `except Exception` also hides programming errors.
kept.suggestion: Catch FeedStateError only. Load the rule disabled (enabled=False) and mark it invalid, for example with an `error` field, so the alerts page can show it, instead of silently widening it.
kept.verifier_note: alerts.py:114-119 replaces any criteria parse failure with FeedCriteria(), which has no filters, so a narrow rule silently becomes 'match everything'. The broad except Exception is unnecessary, because criteria_from_dict already normalises its errors to FeedStateError.

kept.title: FeedQuery has no created_at filter, so criteria alerts only check the 200 newest trades by transaction date
kept.evidence:
class FeedQuery:
    """Validated immutable query for one feed page."""

    search: str = ""
    sort_field: FeedSortField = FeedSortField.TRANSACTION_DATE
kept.description: services/alerts.py:78 takes `to_query(limit=200)`, sorted by transaction_date, and filters on created_at > last_seen_at in Python. Rows inserted after the watermark but with older transaction dates never reach the top 200: a late-disclosed Congress trade, a Form 4/A, or any backfilled history. Those alerts are missed. In addition, created_at uses `server_default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (schema.py:68-72), which has one-second resolution, while the watermark is datetime.now(UTC) with microseconds. A row inserted in the same second just after 'mark all seen' is stored with an earlier timestamp and is never reported.
kept.suggestion: Add an optional `created_after: datetime | None` field to FeedQuery and _filter_conditions, and have alerts query with that filter sorted by created_at. Index created_at, or use the monotonically increasing id as the watermark, which is more robust. If timestamps stay, write created_at from Python with microseconds (or use `strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%f','now')`).
kept.verifier_note: FeedQuery (feed.py:113-127) has no created_after field. services/alerts.py:78 takes the top 200 rows by the rule's sort (transaction_date by default) and filters created_at in Python, so late-disclosed or backfilled rows with old trade dates are missed. created_at defaults to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, which truncates to whole seconds, while the watermark is datetime.now(UTC) with microseconds (alerts_page.py:223), so the same-second race is real, though narrow.

kept.title: Case-insensitive search uses Python casefold() against SQLite lower(), which only folds ASCII
kept.description: SQLite's built-in lower() leaves non-ASCII characters unchanged, while str.casefold() folds them ('MÜLLER' becomes 'müller', 'ß' becomes 'ss'). A stored 'MÜLLER' becomes 'mÜller' in SQL and never matches the search 'müller'. Names containing ß can never be found. The same mismatch affects recent_by_person and search_entities. Separately, wrapping columns in lower() is redundant, because SQLite LIKE is already case-insensitive for ASCII, and it adds per-row function calls.
kept.suggestion: Register a Python function (for example `casefold`) on each connection in the connect listener and use it on both sides, or store normalized search columns. FTS5 with `unicode61 remove_diacritics` handles this naturally. Drop the redundant lower() around LIKE.
kept.verifier_note: str.casefold() is applied to the search pattern (feed.py:356) and to the recent_by_* parameters (645, 691), while SQLite's built-in lower() only folds ASCII. Stored 'MÜLLER' therefore never matches, not even through recent_by_person's exact-equality path. LIKE is already ASCII case-insensitive, so lower() around LIKE is redundant.

kept.title: Feed 'is_stale' is based on the last inserted row, not the last refresh, and costs a full scan
kept.evidence:
is_stale = (
    freshness is not None
    and current_time is not None
    and current_time - freshness > STALE_AFTER
)
kept.description: freshness_at is MAX(created_at) across all trades. A scan that succeeds but finds no new trades (common on weekends and holidays, or for quiet watchlists) leaves the feed marked stale even though data was just refreshed. A backfill of old trades, by contrast, makes the feed look fresh. The refresh_state table, which records actual refreshes, is not consulted.
kept.suggestion: Take freshness from refresh_state (MAX(refreshed_at) for the relevant domains) or a dedicated last-successful-scan record. That is also an O(1) indexed lookup, unlike the current full scan.
kept.verifier_note: freshness_at is MAX(created_at) over all trades (feed.py:481-494), so a successful scan that adds no rows leaves the feed marked stale, while inserting old backfilled rows makes it look fresh. refresh_state is not consulted.

kept.title: FeedQuery and FeedCriteria duplicate their fields and validation
kept.description: Nine fields, the __post_init__ normalization and the to_query copy are written twice (lines 113-149 and 152-199). Every new filter (for example created_after from PERSIST-22) must be added in four places, plus criteria_to_dict and criteria_from_dict. Missing one silently drops the filter on the way from GUI to SQL.
kept.suggestion: Compose them: `FeedQuery(criteria: FeedCriteria, limit: int, offset: int)`, or have FeedQuery hold a FeedCriteria. Validate in FeedCriteria only, and have _filter_conditions take the criteria.
kept.verifier_note: FeedQuery and FeedCriteria (feed.py:113-199) duplicate nine fields and the normalisation, and to_query copies them by hand. Adding a filter means touching at least four places, plus criteria_to_dict and criteria_from_dict.

kept.title: Congress merge picks the 'larger' value by comparing JSON strings, so numbers are ordered lexicographically
kept.description: When both records have a value for a non-key field (amount_low, amount_high, party, source_url, comment, chamber), the winner is the larger JSON string. For floats, '50001.0' sorts above '250001.0', so the smaller amount wins. Choosing by string order also means a corrected re-scrape never replaces an older value unless its string happens to sort higher.
kept.suggestion: Prefer the incoming (newer) record when both values are populated, or define rules per field (numeric max for amounts, newest for URLs and comments). Keep the populated-over-empty rule as it is.
kept.verifier_note: _deterministic_value does pick the larger JSON string (mappings.py:47-55). The amount_low/amount_high example is effectively unreachable, though, because amount_range is part of congress_canonical_key, so two rows that merge have the same range and the same parsed bounds. The real impact is limited to party, source_url, comment and chamber, where a corrected re-scrape only wins if its string sorts higher.

kept.title: Backfill rewrites and fsyncs the entire completed-accession checkpoint after every filing (O(N^2) I/O)
kept.evidence:
completed.add(meta.accession_number)
self._save_completed(zip_path, completed)
...
atomic_write_json(
    self._checkpoint_path,
    {... "completed_accessions": sorted(completed),},
)
kept.description: After every filing the backfill sorts the whole completed set and serialises it with json.dumps(indent=2) (json_state.py:29). It then writes it to a temp file, fsyncs it and runs os.replace (json_state.py:36-40). At about 30 bytes per accession, the file reaches about 3 MB after 100k filings and about 15 MB after 500k, and all of it is rewritten for each new filing. Total writes grow with N^2/2: terabytes for a multi-million-filing archive. Sorting adds O(N log N) CPU per filing. Per-filing cost therefore keeps rising during the run, which fits the user's report that the batch 'does not even get to half'. The module docstring admits the set can grow large, but not that it is rewritten on every filing. The call site is outside persistence/, but it is the persistence-side cost that grows without bound.
kept.suggestion: Checkpoint every N filings or every T seconds (and on cancel), not after every filing, and save it together with a batched DB flush (PERSIST-01). Better, keep resume state in SQLite (a completed_accessions table written in the same transaction as the trades) or as an append-only log, so each filing costs O(1). Drop indent=2 for machine-only state.

kept.title: Form 4/A amendment rows are stored alongside the originals and nothing hides the superseded rows
kept.evidence:
if accession and sec_row:
    return _digest(("sec", accession, sec_row))
kept.description: The SEC-native key includes the accession number, so a Form 4/A (a new accession) never collides with the filing it amends. Its rows are inserted as new us_trades rows. sec_trade_mapping.py:198-201 records only an 'amends' hint inside sec_detail_json. No code reads that hint: the feed projection (feed.py:290-309), query_latest, and the recent_by_* and alert paths all return both the original and the amended transaction. Totals, value screens and alerts double-count every amended trade.
kept.suggestion: Add a superseded marker, for example a superseded_by column or an index on the amends key, set it on upsert of an /A filing that matches the same issuer, insider, period and security, and exclude superseded rows in _projection and the US query methods.

kept.title: A naive last_seen_at in alerts.json makes every record 'new' on every evaluation
kept.evidence: datetime.fromisoformat(raw_seen) if isinstance(raw_seen, str) else None
kept.description: rule_from_dict accepts an offset-less ISO string, for example from a hand edit or another tool, and returns a naive datetime. services/alerts.py:40-44 then compares it with aware created_at values, catches the TypeError and returns True. Every candidate is then reported as new on every evaluation, until the user happens to run 'mark seen', which writes an aware value.
kept.suggestion: In rule_from_dict, normalise naive timestamps to UTC (`dt.replace(tzinfo=UTC)` when dt.tzinfo is None), or reject them, so the comparison never sees mixed naive and aware datetimes.

kept.title: is_fresh treats any future refreshed_at as fresh until the clock catches up, contradicting its comment
kept.evidence:
# Clamp effective age at zero by treating future clock-skew values as fresh.
return current - refreshed < ttl
kept.description: The age is not clamped: a refreshed_at that is D in the future gives a negative age, so the 'latest' refresh for that source is skipped for D + ttl, not ttl. One write made under a skewed clock (a wrong system time that is later corrected) suppresses the openinsider/secform4 latest refresh in services/us.py:193-195 for as long as the skew lasts.
kept.suggestion: Treat a timestamp more than a few minutes in the future as stale (return False), so the refresh runs and overwrites it, or clamp the age with max(current - refreshed, timedelta(0)) only within a small skew tolerance.

areas.title: Congress scrapers, prices, update script
areas.summary: The Congress pipeline (House index/PDF scraper, Senate eFD scraper, CongressScanService) has a clean structure, but several bugs in the common path make its results wrong or incomplete. (1) Named scans store and query official names in incompatible formats. The House scraper stores "Hon. Nancy Pelosi" while the GUI passes official_full ("Nancy Pelosi"), and the repository filters on exact equality, so named House scans return nothing. Senate name splitting also breaks for about 180 of 538 members, those with middle names, initials or ", Jr.". (2) The service marks date ranges as covered even when the scrapers swallowed errors, hit the silent 1000-filing Senate cap, or read a House current-year index that is never refreshed. Those trades are then lost for good. (3) House "S (partial)" sales are classified as "Other". In the price subsystem, cache coverage is just min/max of the stored dates, so holes inside that span are never filled. Stored split/dividend-adjusted values go stale after corporate actions. A single null or slightly inconsistent Yahoo bar throws away a whole fetch. Empty weekend or holiday ranges are treated as errors and fetched again on every call. scripts/update_congress.py writes to a path the app never reads. Its Open States call leaves out a parameter the API requires, and a failed federal fetch overwrites the member file with an empty list. There is also duplicated helper code and some dead code across the House and Senate scrapers and the Yahoo and Tiingo clients.

kept.title: Named congress scans return no House trades: stored official_name format never equals the query identifier
kept.evidence:
official = None if identifier == "*" else identifier
...
self._persistence.congress_trades.query(official, source=source, ...)
# repositories.py:256  conditions.append(congress_trades.c.official_name == official)
# congress_house.py:588 official = f"{filing.get('prefix', '')} {filing['first']} {filing['last']} {filing.get('suffix', '')}".strip()
kept.description: The GUI passes official_name from congress_members.json (official_full, e.g. "Nancy Pelosi"). The House scraper matches filings with a substring search but stores official_name as prefix + first + last + suffix. The real 2026FD.xml has <Prefix>Hon.</Prefix> on 67 of 70 rows, so the stored value is "Hon. Nancy Pelosi". CongressTradeRepository.query then filters on official_name == "Nancy Pelosi", so a named House scan shows zero trades even though they were scraped and saved. The same mismatch breaks the GUI sector filter (member_sectors.get(t.official_name)) for House rows, and any Senate row whose eFD name differs from official_full (nicknames, middle initials).
kept.suggestion: Store a canonical member key (e.g. bioguide id, or normalized "last first") on each CongressTrade when it is scraped. Resolve the user's selection to that key, and filter by it. At minimum, drop the honorific prefix when storing, and query with a normalized case-insensitive comparison of last name plus first name rather than exact equality on the display string.
kept.verifier_note: congress_house.py:588 stores prefix+first+last+suffix, and the runtime 2026FD.xml has <Prefix>Hon.</Prefix> on 67 of 111 members. repositories.py:256 filters with exact equality against the official_full string the GUI sends (congress_tab.py:78), so a named House scan returns nothing from the DB. Senate rows are stored as the eFD first+last (congress_senate.py:631), which also differs from official_full.

kept.title: Senate _split_name sends the wrong first/last name for middle names, suffixes and the 'Last First' seed format
kept.description: The GUI passes official_full values. "Katie Boyd Britt" becomes last_name="Boyd Britt", and "Nicholas J. Begich III" becomes last_name="J. Begich III". "Gilbert Ray Cisneros, Jr." is read as a "Last, First" name, so first="Jr." and last="Gilbert Ray Cisneros". 183 of the 538 federal entries contain more than one space. The built-in DEFAULT_CONGRESS_MEMBERS seed has no official_name, so the GUI falls back to the "Pelosi Nancy" name field, which becomes first="Pelosi", last="Nancy". In all of these cases the eFD search returns nothing, the coverage window is still marked as scanned, and no error is shown. The docstring's own examples ("Pelosi Nancy" -> ("Nancy","Pelosi")) do not match what the code does.
kept.suggestion: Pass the structured first_name/last_name fields that update_congress.py already writes to congress_members.json, instead of splitting a display string. If a string must be parsed, strip suffixes (Jr., Sr., II, III), quoted nicknames and middle initials, and search eFD by last name only, then filter by first name locally.
kept.verifier_note: The core claim holds. _split_name returns (parts[0], rest), so 'Katie Boyd Britt' gives last='Boyd Britt', and 'Angus S. King, Jr.' takes the comma branch and gives first='Jr.'. 183 seed entries have more than two tokens, and the docstring examples contradict the code. The DEFAULT_CONGRESS_MEMBERS fallback is effectively unreachable, though: ensure_dirs() copies the packaged seed (which has official_name) before init_default_congress_file in both main.py and cli.py.

kept.title: House current-year index is downloaded once and never refreshed; the refresh helpers are dead code
kept.evidence:
if xml_path.exists() and not force:
        log.debug("Index already exists: %s", xml_path)
        return xml_path
...
# line 550: ensure_house_index(year)
kept.description: scrape_house_trades calls ensure_house_index(year) without force. refresh_current_year() and refresh_all_indexes() have no callers outside tests, and the adapter ignores use_cache (`_use_cache`). Once {year}FD.xml exists, every later filing for that year is invisible. The legacy copy at data/house_disclosures/2026FD.xml shows this pattern: it is dated 2026-02-17, has its latest FilingDate on 2026-02-15, and holds only 111 members, yet today is 2026-11-14.
kept.suggestion: Treat indexes for the current year and the previous year (for January filings) as expiring. Re-download when the file mtime is older than N hours, or send If-Modified-Since. Route the service's use_cache=False to force=True, and delete or wire up the unused refresh helpers.

The adapter discards use_cache, and refresh_current_year/refresh_all_indexes are referenced only in tests. The cited data/house_disclosures copy is a legacy repo copy (the runtime dir is under LOCALAPPDATA and currently empty), but the code behaviour is as described.

kept.title: Coverage is recorded even when scrapers silently skip failed filings or years, so missed trades are never retried
kept.evidence:
self._persistence.congress_trades.upsert(
                    [replace(trade, source=source) for trade in fetched]
                )
                self._persistence.coverage.add("congress", identifier, source, gap)
kept.description: Both scrapers catch per-item failures, log a warning and continue: a PDF download timeout (congress_house.py:583-585), an index download failure for a whole year (548-553), a PTR page fetch error (congress_senate.py:644-646), and a non-ok search response (547-549). They return a partial list, which the service cannot tell apart from success. The service then marks the whole gap as covered, so later scans never look at it again. Unlike the US services (common.py:16, "refresh a recent overlapping tail"), Congress coverage also has no recent-tail re-check. kept.suggestion: Have the scrapers return (trades, complete: bool) or raise a partial-failure error that lists the failed doc ids. Record coverage only for complete runs, or exclude the failed years. Always re-fetch a recent tail (e.g. the last 45 days, the PTR filing deadline) regardless of coverage.

kept.title: Senate search silently truncates at 1000 filings
kept.evidence:
if start >= total or start >= 1000:
            break
kept.description: An 'All' scan over a wide date range (the GUI and CLI allow arbitrary ranges) stops after 1000 eFD results with no warning, while recordsFiltered can be much larger. The remaining filings are dropped, and CONGRESS-04 then marks the full range covered, so they are never fetched.

kept.title: House 'S (partial)' transaction codes normalize to 'Other'
kept.description: House electronic PTRs use the codes P, S, S (partial) and E. _TX_TYPE_MAP has 'sale (partial)' but not 's (partial)', so every partial sale is stored as trade_type 'Other'. These rows drop out of Purchase/Sale filters and statistics. The test only covers the spelled-out 'sale (partial)' form.
kept.suggestion: Normalize with a regex on the leading code (e.g. r'^(P|S|E)\b' after lowercasing), or add 's (partial)' and 's (full)'. Add a test using the literal 'S (partial)' value from a real House PTR.
kept.verifier_note: _TX_TYPE_MAP has 'S', 's', 'sale (partial)' and similar keys but no 's (partial)', so the House electronic PTR code 'S (partial)' falls through to 'Other'. No test covers that literal value.

kept.title: Expired eFD session or agreement redirect yields an empty result instead of re-authenticating
kept.evidence:
table = _find_transaction_table(soup)
    if not table:
        log.debug("No transaction table found on PTR page")
        return []
kept.description: When the Django session expires during a long run (1 second between requests across hundreds of PTRs), eFD redirects to the prohibition-agreement page with HTTP 200. fetch_page returns that HTML, parse_ptr_page logs only at DEBUG level, and the filing contributes zero trades. Combined with CONGRESS-04, those filings are lost for good. search() also never checks for an HTML or agreement response before calling resp.json().
kept.suggestion: In fetch_page and search, detect a redirect to /search/home/ or the presence of the prohibition_agreement form, then call authenticate() again and retry once. Treat a PTR page with no transaction table as an error (WARNING level, counted as incomplete), not as an empty filing.
kept.verifier_note: It is true that a PTR page with no table is logged only at DEBUG and counted as an empty filing, and that there is no re-authentication path. That eFD sessions expire within one run is unverified. A non-JSON search response would raise from resp.json() and propagate to a ScanError, so no coverage is recorded in that case and there is no data loss there.

kept.title: Senate end-date filter sent as midnight, likely excluding filings submitted on date_to
kept.evidence: form_data["submitted_end_date"] = date_to.strftime("%m/%d/%Y") + " 00:00:00"
kept.description: The end bound is the start of date_to. If eFD compares submission timestamps, which this datetime format suggests, filings submitted during date_to (often today) are excluded. The service still marks date_to as covered, so they are never fetched.
kept.suggestion: Send '23:59:59' for the end bound, or (date_to + 1 day) 00:00:00, and add a test that checks the form payload.

kept.title: Congress-member flagging of SEC insiders uses loose substring matching and a name normalizer that mangles names
kept.description: _normalize_name removes these suffix strings wherever they appear: 'petrov ivan' becomes 'petrovan', and 'kumar sriram' becomes 'kumariram'. The partial-match fallback flags any SEC insider whose name contains a member's normalized name. For example, member 'sullivan dan' matches insider 'sullivan daniel j', and 'crenshaw dan' matches 'crenshaw daniel', which are false is_congress flags. An empty insider_name matches every member. The check is O(trades x members) in Python, and services/us.py runs it on every query result after reloading the JSON from disk (load_congress_members). With state legislators included (~7,500 names) it becomes slow and very noisy.
kept.suggestion: Strip suffixes only as whole tokens at the end of the name, e.g. re.sub(r'\b(jr|sr|ii|iii|iv)\.?$', ''). Match on token sets (last name equal and first name equal or a known nickname) instead of substrings, skip empty names, cache the member lookup per file mtime, and restrict it to federal members.
kept.verifier_note: str.replace removes ' iv' and ' sr' anywhere ('petrov ivan' becomes 'petrovan'). The bidirectional substring fallback flags 'sullivan daniel j' for member 'sullivan dan', and an empty insider name matches any member. flag_congress_copies calls this with members=None, so the JSON is reloaded on every call. The ~7,500 state-legislator scaling remark is speculative, since state fetching is currently broken.

kept.title: House PDF/index cache writes are non-atomic and unvalidated, with no session, User-Agent, retry or throttle
kept.evidence:
resp = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
    resp.raise_for_status()

    cache_path.write_bytes(resp.content)
    return resp.content
kept.description: If a download or write is interrupted (or the app is closed mid-scan), a truncated PDF or XML is left in the cache. Because the code only checks exists(), it is reused forever. A truncated XML makes ET.fromstring raise on every scan of that year, and a bad PDF makes parse_ptr_pdf quietly return []. Responses are not checked as being a PDF (%PDF- magic or content-type), so an HTML error page would also be cached. Each of hundreds of PDFs opens a fresh connection with the default python-requests UA, with no backoff on 429/5xx and no delay between requests. The Senate scraper does rate-limit, so the two are inconsistent.
kept.suggestion: Use one module-level requests.Session with a descriptive User-Agent and urllib3 Retry (backoff, 429/5xx), plus a small politeness delay. Write to a temp file and os.replace() it into place. Check the %PDF- header before caching. When parsing a cached file fails, delete it and download again once.
kept.verifier_note: Each download uses bare requests.get with no Session, retry, User-Agent, delay or content validation, and cache writes are not atomic. The truncated-cache risk is narrow, though: resp.content is fully read before write_bytes, and urllib3 raises on an incomplete body. Corruption needs a crash during the write or a 200 response with an HTML body.

areas.title: GUI (Qt) and threading
areas.summary:
The GUI layer is built carefully in places. The newer feed-first pages (Feed, drawer, entity pages, global search, alerts, watchlists) run their DB work off the GUI thread with request-id guards, use immutable stores, and handle errors in a way users can act on. The older tool tabs (Scan and Congress, built on the pandas-backed SortableTableModel) are much weaker:
- In ScanTab, rows are matched to the wrong trade once filters are applied.
- Numeric columns sort as text.
- The pandas model is slow per cell, and with ResizeToContents it gets slow on large result sets.
- CIK resolution makes blocking network calls on the GUI thread.

Threading is cooperative cancellation over one shared QThreadPool. The shutdown path cancels all work, blocks the GUI for up to 5 s, and then silently refuses to close if workers are still running. Lambdas that capture `self` are not tied to widget lifetime. The `Worker`/request-id boilerplate is copied about 8 times even though a `dispatch()` helper exists. MainWindow is a god object: it owns navigation, three persistence stores, alert evaluation, screens and two duplicate theme controls. The ThemeManager sets the Fusion QPalette only once, before it restores the saved mode, so QSS and QPalette can drift apart. There are also smaller cross-page problems: the feed and alerts do not refresh after a scan, the alert badge goes stale, and buy/sell classification and value formatting are duplicated and inconsistent.

kept.title: ScanTab maps the selected/double-clicked row to the wrong trade after filtering (and saves unfiltered data)
kept.evidence:
row = index.row()
        source_index = self.trades_model.mapToSource(index)
        if row < len(self._trades):
            trade = self._trades[source_index.row()]
kept.description: `_apply_filters` (line 520) calls `_display_trades(filtered)`, so the model now shows the filtered list, but `self._trades` still holds the full unfiltered list. `_on_row_double_click` (530) and `_open_edgar` (548-551) take the source-model row and index it into `self._trades`. Once any filter is applied, the detail label shows a different insider's trade and 'Open EDGAR Filing' opens the wrong filing. The bounds check at 529 also uses the proxy row instead of the source row. `_save_results` (586) writes `self._trades`, so it saves the unfiltered set even though the user sees filtered rows. CongressTab handles this correctly with `_filtered_trades`.
kept.suggestion: Keep a `_displayed_trades` list that `_display_trades` sets, and use it for detail, EDGAR and save. Better still, store the trade object in the model (for example under Qt.UserRole) and read it with `index.data(Qt.UserRole)`, so there is no parallel list to keep in sync. Add a regression test: filter, then double-click row 0, then check that the detail matches the displayed row.
kept.verifier_note: `_apply_filters` (scan_tab.py:520) puts the filtered list into the model, but `_on_row_double_click` (530) and `_open_edgar` (551) still index the unfiltered `self._trades` by source row. `trades_to_dataframe` keeps the list order, so the source row is the index into the filtered list, not the full one. The bounds check at 529 uses the proxy row, and `_save_results` (586) writes `self._trades`. CongressTab avoids this with `_filtered_trades`.

kept.title: Numeric columns in the Scan/Congress tables sort as text
kept.description: SortableTableModel is a plain QSortFilterProxyModel with no sortRole and no lessThan override, so it sorts on DisplayRole. DisplayRole returns formatted strings, which makes 'shares', 'price' and 'value' sort as text: '1,000,000.00' < '200.00' < '95.00'. NaN becomes '' and always sorts first. In the Congress tab, 'amount_range' strings such as '$1,001 - $15,000' also sort as text, and the numeric `amount_low` is not displayed. Sorting by value, the most common way to triage insider buys, gives wrong results.
kept.suggestion: Return the raw value for a custom sort role (for example Qt.UserRole) in PandasTableModel.data and call `setSortRole(Qt.UserRole)` in SortableTableModel. Alternatively, override lessThan to compare the underlying df values. For Congress, sort `amount_range` by `amount_low`.
kept.verifier_note: SortableTableModel sets no sortRole and does not override lessThan. Both tables call setSortingEnabled(True) (scan_tab.py:201, congress_tab.py:355), and DisplayRole returns strings like f"{val:,.2f}", so shares, price and value sort as text. Congress shows `amount_range` (a string) and not `amount_low`.

kept.title: PandasTableModel.data() does expensive pandas indexing and per-cell recomputation
kept.evidence:

            row = self._df.iloc[index.row()]
            val = self._df.iloc[index.row(), index.column()]
            fg = cell_foreground(col_name, val, row, self._palette)
kept.description: Each data() call does `self._df.iloc[r, c]` (tens of µs) and `str(self._df.columns[...])`. For ForegroundRole it builds a whole-row pandas Series on every cell paint. Search is routed through GlobalSearchController. `ThemeManager.apply` (manager.py:167-180) unpolishes and repolishes visible top-level widgets right after `app.setStyleSheet`, which already repolishes every widget, so the loop is extra work on each theme switch. View>Theme and the top-bar theme combo are two controls for one setting and need sync code (`_sync_theme_actions`, `_sync_theme_selector`, `_on_theme_selected`).
kept.suggestion: Delete `_apply_global_search` and the re-polish loop. Keep one theme control, or have both controls driven by `paletteChanged` through one handler.
kept.verifier_note: `_apply_global_search` has no production callers, but tests/test_application_shell.py:119 calls it, so removing it means updating that test. The re-polish loop after `app.setStyleSheet` and the two theme controls are redundant as described.

kept.title: Feed header sort indicator is hard-coded and not synced with criteria
kept.evidence:
self.table.horizontalHeader().setSortIndicator(
            6,
            Qt.SortOrder.DescendingOrder,
        )
kept.description: The indicator is always set to Trade Date descending, whatever `initial_criteria.sort_field`/`descending` say. `set_criteria` (applying a saved screen, or a reset that keeps the sort) never updates it. The arrow can point at a different column or direction from the server-side sort, and the next header click flips the wrong state.
kept.suggestion: Add `_sync_sort_indicator(criteria)` that maps `sort_field` back to its column (reverse of `_SORTABLE_COLUMNS`) and calls `setSortIndicator` with signals blocked. Call it from `__init__` and `set_criteria`.

kept.title: Watchlist scan is all-or-nothing: one failing ticker throws away every result
kept.description: `UsScanService.scan` raises ScanError for any adapter failure (services/us.py:104-107). The watchlist loop has no per-ticker try/except, so one bad or delisted ticker, or one transient HTTP error, makes the worker emit `error`. `_on_scan_error` then shows a generic 'Scan failed', and the results already gathered for the earlier tickers are never displayed (their rows were persisted but `_trades` is not updated). On a long watchlist the user loses the whole run.
kept.suggestion: Wrap each `self._service.scan(...)` call in try/except, log the failure, collect the failing tickers, and keep going. Return the merged trades together with the failure list, and show 'N tickers failed: ...' in the status label instead of aborting.

kept.title: Entity page keeps the previous entity's table and summary while loading and after an error
kept.description: `load()` (155-156) only shows a state label. It leaves `header_label`, `summary_label` and the model holding the previous entity's data. If the new load fails, the page shows 'Could not load company activity.' above the previous company's full transaction table and summary, and the new entity is named nowhere. While loading, the old rows can be read as the new entity's history.
kept.suggestion: At the start of `load()`, set the header to the requested value, clear the summary, and call `model.replace_records(())`. Do the same in `_on_error` so the table never shows a different entity than the one requested.

kept.title: Theme change during a drawer load renders the new record with the previous record's bundle
kept.description: `show_record` assigns `self._record = record` right away (line 88), but `self._bundle` is only replaced in `_render` once the async load finishes. If the palette changes while a load is in flight, `_on_palette_changed` renders the new record's header together with the previous record's ownership, footnotes, filing metadata and recent activity, and hides the 'Loading…' state. If that load then fails or is cancelled, the mixed view stays.
kept.suggestion: Clear `self._bundle = None` in `show_record` before starting the worker. Alternatively, keep the record and bundle together as one `(record, bundle)` pair that is set only in `_render`, and re-render from that pair.

kept.title: New scan results ignore the active filter controls in the Scan and Congress tabs
kept.evidence:
self._trades = trades
        self.progress.setVisible(False)
        self.btn_stop.setEnabled(True)
        self._set_scan_buttons_enabled(True)
        self.btn_save.setEnabled(True)
        self._display_trades(trades)

The type combo, min-value spin and congress-only checkbox keep the values the user set (for example 'Buy', ≥100k), so the controls say one thing and the table shows another until 'Apply Filters' is clicked again. Save is also enabled even when `trades` is empty. CongressTab does the same at congress_tab.py:504-509, where it also resets `_filtered_trades` to the full list.

areas.title: CLI, config, utils, packaging, CI
areas.summary: The CLI, config and packaging layer is generally careful. Paths come from platformdirs, seed files are copied atomically, the SEC user agent is validated before network work starts, release publishing uses OIDC Trusted Publishing with SHA-pinned actions, and the API key files are gitignored and were never committed. The most serious problems are wrong results in the common path. (1) The shared parse_date helper returns None for OpenInsider's "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" filing dates, which I confirmed against the live site. Every OpenInsider row is therefore stored without a filing date and then dropped by --since/--until filters. (2) `sec-daily` defaults to today, whose index has not been published yet, and the downloader treats a 404 index as a completed day, so today is permanently recorded as covered with zero filings. (3) `scan TICKER` without dates never queries the ticker sources; it only refreshes the market-wide OpenInsider latest feed. For the slow full SEC backfill the CLI gives no help: it shows no progress, Ctrl+C has no clean handling, and it exits 0 even when filings failed. The likely cause of the slowdown sits in services/sec_backfill.py (reported by the services area): it rewrites the whole sorted checkpoint after every filing. Other gaps: logging is stderr-only with no file, even though six messages say "see logs"; the HTTP helper's rate limiter is not thread-safe and it reuses no connections; CI ignores uv.lock, so Dependabot lockfile bumps are untested; mypy and pip-audit are installed but never run; the release workflow does not check that the tag matches the package version; and a stale duplicate data/ seed copy exists that the congress update script writes to.

kept.title: parse_date returns None for OpenInsider datetime filing dates, so OpenInsider rows lose filing_date and are dropped by date filters
kept.description: OpenInsider shows the Filing Date column as a datetime. A live check of the AAPL screener returned values like '2026-11-12 18:58:20'. date.fromisoformat rejects a string that includes a time. The fallback then splits on '-' and gets ['2026','11','12 18:58:20'], and int('12 18:58:20') raises, so parse_date returns None (verified locally: parse_date('2024-01-15 10:30:00') -> None). openinsider.py:202 sends every filing date through this helper, so every OpenInsider trade is stored with filing_date NULL. Effects: merger.filter_trades (merger.py:189-191) requires `t.filing_date and t.filing_date >= since`, so `scan --since/--until` and `latest --since/--until` drop all OpenInsider rows. Repository range queries on us_trades.c.filing_date (repositories.py:124-126, 167-169) exclude them. Dedup in merger.py:49 and sec-compare also lose the field. No test fixture contains a datetime filing date.
kept.suggestion: Strip a time part before parsing, e.g. take text.split()[0] or text[:10] when the text matches a YYYY-MM-DD prefix, or try datetime.fromisoformat(text).date() first. Add a parsing test and an OpenInsider fixture row with '2026-11-12 18:58:20'. Then backfill filing_date for rows already persisted, by re-scanning or with a migration that re-parses from source.
kept.verifier_note: I reproduced it: parse_date('2024-01-15 10:30:00') returns None. openinsider.py:202 passes the raw Filing Date cell (which contains the time) to this helper, and merger.filter_trades:189-191 requires t.filing_date, so the rows are dropped. secform4 is not affected because it splits off the time with _br_split first. The test fixture only uses bare dates, so the tests miss it.

kept.title: sec-daily defaults to today; a 404 index for today is recorded as covered, leaving a permanent gap
kept.evidence:
day = args.date or date.today()
    summary = service.ingest_date(day, on_progress=_make_cli_progress(args.quiet))
kept.description: The help text and README both say the SEC daily index lags about one business day, yet the command defaults to today. In services/sec_downloads.py:201-203 `except SecFilingNotFoundError: ... return True` treats a missing index as a fully handled empty day. download_range then adds it to `completed` and emits progress, and the coverage recorder in sec_daily.py:258-264 writes coverage for that date. When the index is published later, running `sec-daily --date <that day>` or a `sec-catchup` over the range finds no gap and skips the day, so the filings are never ingested and nothing warns about it. `sec-catchup --until <today>` has the same problem, and so does any range that includes a day whose index is not up yet.
kept.suggestion: In the CLI, default --date to the previous business day, and reject or warn on dates >= today. In the downloader, return False (not covered) for a 404 on recent dates, e.g. within 3 business days of today, and only treat 404 as an empty day for weekends, holidays or older dates. Add a regression test: a 404 for today must not create coverage.
kept.verifier_note: cli.py:442 defaults to date.today(). sec_downloads._process_date:201-203 returns True on SecFilingNotFoundError (404), and the sec_daily coverage recorder:258-264 then writes coverage for that date. No code anywhere guards against today or future dates (the sec_daily 'clock' is unused).

kept.title: `scan TICKER` without --since/--until never queries ticker sources; it returns only what is already in the local DB
kept.evidence:
selected_sources = tuple(getattr(args, "sources", None) or DEFAULT_US_SCAN_SOURCES)
    trades = services.us.scan(
        ticker,
        sources=selected_sources,
        start_date=since,
        end_date=until,
kept.description: With no dates, UsScanService.scan (services/us.py:65-84) takes the unbounded path. That path only refreshes `_latest_adapters` (OpenInsider's market-wide latest feed, LATEST_OVERLAP_COUNT=200 rows, not filtered by ticker) and then queries the local DB. 'secform4' is selected by default but has no latest adapter, so it is never fetched. On a fresh database, the first README example (`insider-scanner-cli scan AAPL`, README.md:126) and `scan AAPL --type Buy --min-value 1000000 --save` return almost nothing for AAPL even though the command says it is 'Scanning insider trades for AAPL'.
kept.suggestion: Give scan a bounded default window when no dates are given, like cmd_price does with 365 days (until=today, since=until-365d), so the per-ticker adapters run. Or add an explicit `--local-only` flag for the current behaviour and document it.
kept.verifier_note: When start/end are both None, us.py:65-84 only calls _refresh_latest for sources that have a latest adapter. That adapter takes no ticker and fetches the market-wide OpenInsider feed. secform4 has no latest adapter, so it is skipped. The service then returns local DB rows for the ticker, so on a fresh DB `scan AAPL` returns little or nothing.

kept.title: sec-backfill gives no progress during a multi-hour run and passes no on_progress/cancel hook
kept.evidence:
print(f"Starting full bulk backfill from {zip_path} (resumable).")
    summary = service.run(zip_path, confirm=True, ciks=ciks)
    _print_backfill_summary(summary)
    return 0
kept.description: The full backfill is the process the user reports as taking hours without reaching half. The CLI prints one line and then nothing until the end, so the user cannot tell whether it is progressing, stalled or slowing down. sec-daily and sec-catchup have per-date progress and --quiet; sec-backfill has neither. SecBackfillService.run accepts on_progress but only calls it once, after the loop (sec_backfill.py:180-181). The CLI also passes no `cancelled` callback, so the only way to stop is Ctrl+C (see CLI-06). Without progress output, the slowdown cannot be diagnosed from the CLI. The likely cause is in services/sec_backfill.py:159-160 and 199-210: after every filing it sorts the whole completed set and rewrites it atomically, which is O(n^2) I/O over hundreds of thousands of accessions. That defect belongs to the services area.
kept.suggestion: Make the service emit progress every N filings or every few seconds (discovered/parsed/failed/skipped_resume, plus rate and ETA). Give sec-backfill the same `_make_cli_progress`-style stderr reporter and a --quiet flag. Wire a cancellation flag set by a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C stops cleanly after the current filing and prints the partial summary.
kept.verifier_note: cmd_sec_backfill:520-521 passes neither on_progress nor cancelled. SecBackfillService.run invokes on_progress only once, after the loop (sec_backfill.py:180-181), and it calls _save_completed with sorted(completed) after every filing (lines 159-160, 208). All as described.

kept.title: SEC ingestion commands exit 0 even when dates or filings failed
kept.evidence:
summary = service.ingest_range(
        args.since, args.until, on_progress=_make_cli_progress(args.quiet)
    )
    _print_sec_summary(summary)
    return 0
kept.description: cmd_sec_daily (line 445), cmd_sec_catchup (line 470) and cmd_sec_backfill (line 523) always return 0. The exit code is the same when summary.failures > 0, when dates_completed < dates_total (for example, the daily index fetch failed on a 5xx and the date was left uncovered), and when the backfill was interrupted. A scheduled job (Task Scheduler or cron) cannot tell a clean run from a run that missed whole days. README.md:181-183 documents only codes 0, 1 and 2.
kept.suggestion: Return a distinct non-zero code (e.g. 3) when dates_completed < dates_total or the backfill did not finish. Optionally add a `--strict` flag that also fails on per-filing failures > 0. Document the codes in the README and cover them in test_cli.py.
kept.verifier_note: All three commands return 0 unconditionally, which is true. However, README.md:180-181 explicitly documents that per-filing failures do not fail the command, so that part is intended behaviour. The 'backfill interrupted' case cannot happen through the CLI: no cancelled callback is passed, and Ctrl+C raises instead. What remains valid: dates_completed < dates_total (e.g. an index 5xx) still exits 0.

kept.title: KeyboardInterrupt skips services.close() and shows a raw traceback
kept.description: `except Exception` does not catch KeyboardInterrupt. Close is done in straight-line code after the try block, not in `finally`. Ctrl+C is the only way to stop a long sec-backfill or sec-catchup run. When it is pressed, services.close() (the persistence engine) is skipped, the user sees a Python traceback instead of a summary, and the exit code is not the conventional 130. SQLite rolls back the open transaction, but close/dispose work (connection cleanup and any WAL checkpoint) is skipped every time a long run is interrupted.
kept.suggestion: Move services.close() into a `finally:` block and add `except KeyboardInterrupt: print('Interrupted', file=sys.stderr); result = 130`. Better still, combine this with a cooperative cancel flag (CLI-04) so the services can print their partial summary.
kept.verifier_note: `except Exception` at line 804 does not catch KeyboardInterrupt, and close() runs in straight-line code rather than a finally block, so close is skipped and a traceback is shown. The impact is overstated: upserts are committed per filing, the backfill checkpoint is saved per filing, and SQLite recovers the WAL on the next open, so nothing is lost. This is mainly a UX and cleanliness issue.

kept.title: Invalid user input (bad --source, --count 0, only --since) is reported as a crash with exit 1
kept.evidence:
p_latest.add_argument("--count", type=int, default=100)
    p_latest.add_argument("--since", type=_parse_date_arg, default=None)
    p_latest.add_argument("--until", type=_parse_date_arg, default=None)
kept.description: --count accepts 0 or negative numbers, --source (lines 545-554, 564-573) has no `choices`, and scan/latest/price accept a lone --since or --until. All of these are only checked deep in the services: `count must be positive` (us.py:130), `unknown source(s)` (common.py:79), `start_date and end_date must both be present` (common.py:58-61). The resulting ValueError reaches the generic handler in run(), which logs a full traceback and prints 'Command failed. See logs for details.' with exit 1. For example, `scan AAPL --since 2025-01-01` fails this way. argparse usage errors use exit 2, and sec-compare already maps ValueError to exit 2 (lines 400-402). cmd_price also never checks since <= until.
kept.suggestion: Use `type=_parse_positive_int` for --count and `choices=('secform4','openinsider','sec_edgar')` for --source. Default a missing --until to today (or reject a lone bound with parser.error). In run(), catch ValueError from commands and print the message to stderr with exit 2, without a traceback.
kept.verifier_note: --count is type=int with no positivity check, and --source has no choices. A lone --since reaches validate_range (common.py:58-61) or us.latest count<1 (us.py:129-130), and the resulting ValueError falls into run()'s generic handler: traceback plus 'See logs', exit 1. Everything described is accurate, but the impact is a UX inconsistency, not wrong results.

kept.title: classify_trade maps OpenInsider 'M - OptEx'/'X - OptEx' to Other instead of Exercise
kept.description: OpenInsider labels trade types with a code plus an abbreviation, e.g. 'M - OptEx', 'X - OptEx', 'S - Sale+OE', 'D - Sale to issuer'. 'optex' contains neither 'exercise' nor 'option', and the `t == 'm'` check only matches a bare 'm'. I verified that classify_trade('M - OptEx') and classify_trade('X - OptEx') both return 'Other', so `scan --type Exercise` never matches OpenInsider option exercises. Matching on substrings also means 'D - Sale to issuer' (a disposition back to the issuer) is labelled Sell.
kept.suggestion: Parse the leading transaction code first (the text before ' - ': P->Buy, S->Sell, M/X->Exercise, everything else Other), then fall back to keyword matching. Add test cases for the actual OpenInsider labels.
kept.verifier_note: classify_trade('M - OptEx') and classify_trade('X - OptEx') do return 'Other' (verified). The claimed impact is not reachable today, though: both OpenInsider scrapers send `xp=1` (openinsider.py:59,106), which is OpenInsider's Purchase-only filter, so OptEx and 'Sale to issuer' rows are never fetched. secform4 also has a CSS-class fallback to Exercise. The bug is latent.

kept.title: parse_date turns two-digit years into year 24 AD
kept.evidence: return date(int(parts[2]), int(parts[0]), int(parts[1]))
kept.description: For 'MM/DD/YY' input the fallback builds date(24, 1, 15). I verified that parse_date('01/15/24') -> datetime.date(24, 1, 15). The result is a valid but absurd date that passes silently into persistence and sorting. parse_ptr_date in the same module handles %m/%d/%y correctly, so the two helpers behave differently on the same input.
kept.suggestion: Use strptime with an explicit list of formats ('%Y-%m-%d', '%m/%d/%Y', '%m-%d-%Y', '%m/%d/%y'), or reject years < 1900. Share one implementation with parse_ptr_date and keep only the placeholder handling separate.
kept.verifier_note: Verified: parse_date('01/15/24') returns date(24, 1, 15). parse_ptr_date handles %m/%d/%y correctly. Current US sources mostly emit ISO dates, so low severity is appropriate.

kept.title: fetch_url rate limiter is not thread-safe, is separate from SecClient's limiter, and accepts the placeholder SEC user agent
kept.evidence:
def _rate_limit() -> None:
    """Block until enough time has passed since the last request."""
    global _last_request_time
    now = time.time()
    elapsed = now - _last_request_time
    if elapsed < _min_interval:
        time.sleep(_min_interval - elapsed)
    _last_request_time = time.time()
kept.description: The read-modify-write of a module global has no lock. GUI worker threads that call edgar.fetch_url at the same time can all read the same `_last_request_time` and send requests together. This limiter is also independent of the SecClient fair-access limiter in core/sec_fair_access.py, so legacy edgar.py calls and SEC ingestion running at once can together exceed SEC's 10 req/s. It uses wall-clock time.time(), so an NTP adjustment can produce long sleeps or none. Lines 77-79 send SEC_USER_AGENT even when it is still the 'contact@example.com' placeholder, which SecClient rejects. As a result `resolve-cik` and other edgar.py paths hit sec.gov with a placeholder identity, which SEC may throttle or block.
kept.suggestion: Route edgar.py SEC requests through the shared SecClient/fair-access limiter, or at least guard _rate_limit with a threading.Lock and use time.monotonic(). Apply the same placeholder-user-agent validation as SecClient before any request to sec.gov.
kept.verifier_note: _rate_limit does an unlocked read-modify-write of a global using time.time(). It is independent of the locked monotonic RateLimiter in sec_fair_access.py, which runs at 8 req/s by default. edgar.py calls fetch_url(use_sec_agent=True) at lines 106/163/224/237 with the import-time SEC_USER_AGENT, which may still be the placeholder that SecClient rejects.

kept.title: fetch_url opens a new connection per request and has no retry or backoff
kept.evidence:
resp = requests.get(url, headers=req_headers, timeout=timeout)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    text = resp.text
kept.description: Each call to requests.get creates a throwaway Session, which means a new TCP and TLS handshake for every page of openinsider, secform4 and EDGAR. Paged scans pay that latency on every request. A transient 429, 503 or connection reset fails the whole source scan immediately, with no retry and no honouring of Retry-After. `resp.text` also triggers charset detection on large pages that have no charset header.
kept.suggestion: Use a module-level or injected requests.Session with an HTTPAdapter and urllib3 Retry (total=3, backoff_factor, status_forcelist={429,500,502,503,504}, respect_retry_after_header=True). Decode with resp.content plus a known encoding where possible.
kept.verifier_note: There is no Session reuse and no retry/backoff, which is true. However, neither scraper pages: openinsider fetches one URL with cnt=100 and secform4 fetches one CIK page, so a scan makes only about 1-3 requests. The 'paged scans pay latency on every request' claim does not hold, and this path is not hot. The missing retry for transient 429/503 is the real part of the finding.

kept.title: Logging is stderr-only, with no file or rotation, yet errors say 'See logs for details'
kept.evidence:
logging.basicConfig(
        level=level,
        format="%(asctime)s [%(name)s] %(levelname)s: %(message)s",
        datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
        stream=sys.stderr,
    )
kept.description: No FileHandler exists anywhere in src. Six user-facing messages, including cli.py:806 and the main.py QMessageBox dialogs, tell users to 'See logs for details'. For the GUI, logs exist only in the console window and disappear when it closes. For a multi-hour backfill there is no persistent record of which filings failed. The level is fixed at INFO with no --verbose/--log-level option, third-party loggers inherit INFO, and the time format omits the date, so logs from runs that cross midnight are ambiguous.
kept.suggestion: Add a RotatingFileHandler (e.g. 5 MB x 5) under platformdirs user_log_path and put that path in the 'see logs' messages. Add `--log-level`/`-v` to the CLI parser, or an INSIDER_SCANNER_LOG_LEVEL env var. Use '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' and set noisy libraries (urllib3, charset_normalizer) to WARNING.
kept.verifier_note: setup_logging configures only basicConfig on stderr, with datefmt='%H:%M:%S' and no FileHandler in src. In-scope 'See logs for details' messages exist at cli.py:806, scan_tab.py:452, congress_tab.py:528 and main.py:96,110 (the sixth is out of scope). The GUI entry point is a console script, so logs appear only in that console.

kept.title: init-congress is always a no-op, seed updates never reach users, and data/ holds a stale duplicate seed
kept.evidence:
init_default_congress_file()
    print(f"Congress member list created at: {CONGRESS_FILE}")
kept.description: run() calls ensure_dirs() before every command, and ensure_dirs already copies the packaged congress_members.json seed into CONGRESS_FILE. init_default_congress_file (senate.py:127-129) then sees that the file exists and does nothing. The command still prints 'created', so the init-congress command in README.md:140 never does anything. _copy_seed_if_missing (config.py:101) also never replaces an existing user file, so a newer packaged seed never reaches existing installs, and there is no refresh or reset command. Meanwhile scripts/update_congress.py:57 writes `DEFAULT_OUTPUT = _project_root / "data" / "congress_members.json"`. That repo copy is tracked and currently byte-identical to src/insider_scanner/resources/seeds/congress_members.json, but the app never reads it, so running the update script changes nothing in the app or the package.
kept.suggestion: Replace init-congress with `init-congress --force` (or `reset-seeds`), which overwrites the user copy from the packaged seed after a backup, and print accurate messages. Point update_congress.py's default output at the packaged seed path, delete the tracked data/congress_members.json and data/tickers_watchlist.txt duplicates, and keep data/ only for untracked local artifacts.
kept.verifier_note: run() calls ensure_dirs() first, and that copies the congress seed. init_default_congress_file (senate.py:127-129) then sees the file and does nothing, while the command still prints 'created'. _copy_seed_if_missing returns early when the target exists. update_congress.py:57 writes to data/, which I confirmed is byte-identical to the packaged seed (tracked despite the `data/` gitignore). Because the user copy is never refreshed, a stale congress list can cause congress trades to go unflagged.

kept.title: CI installs unpinned dependencies with pip and ignores uv.lock, so Dependabot lockfile bumps are untested
kept.evidence:
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install -e ".[gui,dev]"
kept.description: The repository commits uv.lock (90 packages), and recent history consists of merged Dependabot PRs that bump only uv.lock (e.g. 1d46281 'bump msgpack'). CI resolves fresh versions from pyproject ranges with pip, so these PRs run the same tests as before and the locked versions are never exercised. Equally, an upstream release inside an allowed range (pandas <4, numpy <3, PySide6 <7) can break CI or users on any day without a code change. The editable install also means CI never tests the built wheel; packaging is only checked at release time.
kept.suggestion: Use astral-sh/setup-uv with `uv sync --locked --all-extras` (or `uv export` piped into pip install -r) in the test job. Optionally keep a separate weekly job against the latest resolved dependencies. Add a cheap `python -m build && pip install dist/*.whl && python scripts/verify_install.py` job to CI so packaging regressions show up before tagging.
kept.verifier_note: ci.yml:34-35 runs `pip install -e ".[gui,dev]"` and ignores the committed uv.lock, so uv-only Dependabot bumps exercise nothing new. CI never builds or installs the wheel; only release.yml does.

kept.title: mypy and pip-audit are dev deps but never run in CI; ruff is unpinned; workflow token permissions are unset
kept.evidence:
- run: pip install ruff
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: ruff format --check .

areas.title: Cross-cutting architecture and duplication
areas.summary: The layering is mostly sound: core scrapers and parsers, then persistence repositories, then DB-first services, then GUI/CLI, and the SEC path has a hardened, injectable client. The main cross-cutting defect is a contract mismatch between scrapers and services. Services treat "the adapter returned without raising" as "the date range is fully covered" and write that permanently to scan_coverage. But the legacy scrapers (secform4, openinsider, House, Senate) swallow network and parse errors, silently cap results at 100 or 1000 rows, and use inclusive or exclusive end dates inconsistently. The House index for the current year is also never refreshed. Each of these leaves a permanent hole in local data that later scans never refill. The slow full backfill you reported has several compounding causes. (1) The resume checkpoint is a sorted JSON of every completed accession, rewritten and fsynced after every filing, which is O(n^2). (2) Every filing is fetched over the network one at a time at about 8 requests per second, with no HTTP keep-alive. (3) Every filing also gets a 24-hour cache file with its own fsync, which is useless for backfill. (4) SQLite runs with NullPool, no WAL and one transaction per filing. (5) There is no progress output. Beyond that, the code has three independent rate limiters, two dedup-key definitions that disagree, duplicated House/Senate helpers, and two watchlist systems. Some layering is violated: core/prices opens its own DB, the GUI builds repositories directly and imports the CLI module, and the GUI thread makes a blocking network call. There is also dead code in edgar.py, config.py and congress_house.py, plus an unused dependency.

kept.title: SEC daily ingest marks today's date covered when the daily index is still 404
kept.description: A 404 on the daily master index is treated as 'no filings that day' and the date is counted as completed. SecDailyIngestionService's progress hook then calls coverage.add for that date (sec_daily.py:258-264). `insider-scanner-cli sec-daily` defaults to today (cli.py:442 `day = args.date or date.today()`), and SEC publishes the day's index only late in the evening ET. A daytime run therefore permanently marks today as covered with zero filings, and every later sec-daily or sec-catchup skips it. The same applies to any recent business day whose index is delayed.
kept.suggestion: Treat a 404 as authoritative 'absent' only for weekends, SEC holidays, or dates older than about 2 business days. For today or recent dates, return False (not completed) so coverage is not recorded. Alternatively, default `sec-daily` to the previous business day.

The coverage recorder in sec_daily (258-264) then marks that date. cmd_sec_daily defaults to date.today() (cli.py:442). validate_range does not reject future dates either, so `sec-catchup --until <future>` also marks future dates covered permanently.

Any PTR or Form 4 filed later on the end date, or a late filing whose filing_date falls in an already-covered range (common for House/Senate, which often disclose weeks late), is never fetched again for that identifier. The `latest` path has a TTL (refresh_state + is_fresh), but bounded scans do not.

So filings for the end date that are published or indexed later, for example through House or Senate index lag, are never refetched. However, coverage and queries are keyed on filing_date, not trade_date. A PTR disclosed weeks late carries its own recent filing_date, so it is not hidden by an older covered range. The 'late disclosure' argument is wrong; only the recent-tail problem is real.

kept.title: Backfill checkpoint is a sorted JSON of all completed accessions, rewritten and fsynced after every filing (O(n^2))

If JSON is kept, write an append-only line log and compact it only at the end.

That function sorts the whole set (208), and atomic_write_json writes it with indent=2 and fsyncs (json_state.py:29-40). The cost per filing grows with n, so total work is about O(n^2 log n). Past roughly 100k accessions, each checkpoint write takes as long as or longer than the network fetch.

kept.description: submissions.zip contains only metadata, so every Form 3/4/5 accession costs one serial HTTP GET of the full .txt submission. SecClient's limiter defaults to 8 req/s (sec_fair_access.py:23). Roughly 10M historical ownership filings is about 2 weeks of wall-clock time at best. Each accession also appears in both the issuer's and every reporting owner's CIK JSON, so the 1.5 GB archive is fully decoded and `discovered` is inflated. Every downloaded filing is also written into a single flat directory `validated-v1/` with fsync (sec_downloader.py:298-308, called via promote_validated_filing at sec_downloads.py:282). That cache expires after 24h (cache_freshness_seconds), so for backfill it is pure I/O cost plus potentially hundreds of GB of disk use until the run finishes.
kept.suggestion: For history, switch to SEC's quarterly 'Insider Transactions Data Sets' (Form 3/4/5 structured TSV ZIPs from DERA). That is about 80 files instead of millions of requests, and turns weeks into minutes. Keep per-filing fetch only for incremental daily ingest. If per-filing backfill stays: skip the validated cache for backfill (promote is optional), deduplicate accessions before fetching, default to issuer CIKs only (or the --cik filter), and use a pooled keep-alive session (ARCH-08).
kept.verifier_note: Each accession is fetched serially through SecClient at 8 req/s or less. Each one is then promoted into the flat validated-v1 directory with fsync (sec_downloader._write_atomically), and those files are purged only when the full run ends. Duplicate accessions across issuer and owner CIK files inflate 'discovered' and the decode work, but they are not fetched twice: once the first copy succeeds it goes into `completed`, and the later copy is skipped as skipped_resume. The suggestion to 'deduplicate before fetching' is therefore mostly already in place. The DERA data-set recommendation is sound.

kept.title: SQLite configured with NullPool, rollback journal and no synchronous tuning, with one transaction per filing
kept.evidence:
connect_args={"timeout": busy_timeout_ms / 1_000},
poolclass=NullPool,
...
cursor.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON")
cursor.execute(f"PRAGMA busy_timeout={busy_timeout_ms}")
kept.description: With NullPool, every `engine.begin()`/`connect()` opens a new sqlite3 connection and re-runs the pragmas. No `journal_mode=WAL` or `synchronous=NORMAL` is set anywhere (grep finds none). The backfill and daily sinks call us_trades.upsert once per filing, which is a new connection plus BEGIN IMMEDIATE plus a rollback-journal commit with several fsyncs. The coverage and refresh repos also do this for every call. In rollback-journal mode, a GUI feed query blocks writers (and vice versa) for up to the 5 s busy timeout, which shows up as 'database is locked' PersistenceErrors while a CLI backfill runs and the GUI is open.
kept.suggestion: Enable `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` once at bootstrap and `PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL` per connection. Use a small pool (SingletonThreadPool or QueuePool with check_same_thread=False). In bulk paths, batch upserts, e.g. commit every 500 filings in one immediate_transaction.
kept.verifier_note: NullPool (line 46), no WAL and no synchronous pragma (grep finds none), and one BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction per upsert are all true. Reader/writer contention in rollback-journal mode is plausible. Per filing, though, this costs a few to a few tens of milliseconds against network latency of 150 ms or more, so it is not a dominant backfill cost. Medium, not high.

kept.title: No HTTP connection reuse in any SEC or scraper path
kept.description: Every SEC request (daily index, each filing, backfill) does a fresh DNS lookup, TCP connect and TLS handshake to www.sec.gov, because `requests.get` creates a throwaway Session. The same is true of utils/http.fetch_url (http.py:85, used by edgar, secform4 and openinsider) and congress_house (138, 343). At 8 req/s, the handshake (about 100-300 ms) is a large share of each request's latency, so the effective rate drops well below the limiter ceiling.
kept.suggestion: Give RequestsSecTransport a long-lived `requests.Session` with an HTTPAdapter (pool_maxsize, keep-alive) owned by the SecClient or ApplicationServices and closed in close(). Do the same for a shared scraper session in utils/http.
kept.verifier_note: RequestsSecTransport.get calls module-level requests.get (line 84), and so do utils/http.fetch_url (85) and congress_house (138, 343). None of them reuse connections. The RateLimiter spaces acquisitions 0.125 s apart, so when per-request latency, including TCP and TLS setup, is above 125 ms, latency rather than the limiter sets throughput. For a client far from sec.gov, that plausibly cuts the effective rate to about 2-4 req/s.

kept.title: UsTradeRepository.query_latest loads the entire us_trades table into Python to return N rows
kept.evidence:
result = [
    us_from_row(row)
    for row in rows
    if not requested_sources
    or requested_sources.intersection(us_provenance(row))
]
return result[:count]
kept.description: The statement has no LIMIT. Every row is materialised, its JSON provenance decoded, and an InsiderTrade built, and only then is the list sliced to `count`. There is also no index on filing_date alone, so SQLite sorts the full table. After a backfill (millions of rows), `latest`, which the GUI Scan tab and CLI `latest` use, takes minutes and gigabytes of RAM. query() has the same post-filter on provenance, which is acceptable only because it is ticker-indexed.
kept.suggestion: Filter provenance in SQL, e.g. a `trade_sources(trade_id, source)` table, or `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(source_provenance_json) WHERE value IN (...))`. Apply `.limit(count)` and add an index on (filing_date DESC, trade_date DESC).
kept.verifier_note: query_latest (154-193) has no LIMIT. It filters provenance in Python and slices result[:count] at line 191. The only indexes are (ticker, filing_date), (source, filing_date), accession and cik_issuer, so the unconditioned ORDER BY over the whole table cannot use an index. Once backfill has populated the table, this materialises every row.

kept.title: House current-year index is downloaded once and never refreshed; the refresh functions are dead code

kept.title: Three independent, inconsistent rate limiters; the SEC limit is per client instance, not per process
kept.evidence:
_last_request_time: float = 0.0
_min_interval: float = 1.0 / SEC_MAX_REQUESTS_PER_SECOND

def _rate_limit() -> None:
    global _last_request_time
    now = time.time()
kept.description: utils/http._rate_limit is a module global, not thread-safe and uses wall-clock time, at 10 req/s. congress_senate._rate_limit (congress_senate.py:72-79) is a copy of it. sec_fair_access.RateLimiter is thread-safe but created per SecClient via `field(default_factory=default_rate_limiter)` (sec_client.py:161), at 8 req/s. SEC traffic from edgar.resolve_cik (legacy fetch_url) and from one or more SecClient instances, e.g. GUI workers running in parallel in a QThreadPool, is never coordinated, so the combined rate can exceed SEC's 10 req/s and get the IP throttled. SEC_MAX_REQUESTS_PER_SECOND is also defined twice (config.py:93 int and sec_fair_access.py:22 float). The legacy path also sends the placeholder 'contact@example.com' User-Agent that SecClient explicitly rejects (config.py:89-92 vs sec_client.py:386).
kept.suggestion: Create a single process-wide SEC limiter (a module-level RateLimiter in sec_fair_access) shared by SecClient and the legacy edgar path. Move edgar's company_tickers and submissions lookups onto SecClient. Remove the duplicate constant. Reuse RateLimiter for the Senate scraper instead of a hand-rolled global.
kept.verifier_note: There are three limiters, a duplicate SEC_MAX_REQUESTS_PER_SECOND constant (config.py:93 and sec_fair_access.py:22), and a placeholder User-Agent on the legacy path. All of that is real. But SecClient is constructed in exactly one place (cli.py:313, once per command) and the GUI never constructs one, so the scenario of parallel SecClient instances in GUI workers exceeding 10 req/s cannot happen. What remains is duplication and an unsafe global limiter, which is low.

kept.title: Congress flagging marks every trade with an empty insider name, and substring matching gives false positives

kept.title: SecClient retries only 429/503; timeouts, connection resets and 5xx fail the filing immediately

except Exception as exc:
    raise SecTransportError(url) from exc

kept.title: Feed page runs COUNT(*) and MAX(created_at) over a 3-table UNION ALL on every page

Push filters into each branch of the union before the UNION ALL. Consider a materialised feed table, or normalised trade_direction columns written at insert time (see ARCH-25).

kept.title: Backfill ZIP containment check is a no-op because cache_root is derived from the ZIP path itself
kept.description: _validate_zip_location (sec_bulk.py:216-225) checks that zip_path resolves within cache_root. Passing zip_path.parent makes that always true for any path, so the 'trusted cache root' check is security theatre that adds complexity and suggests a guarantee that does not exist. Only the symlink checks have any effect.
kept.suggestion: Either drop the cache_root parameter and keep only the symlink and regular-file checks, or pass a real trusted directory (e.g. EDGAR_CACHE_DIR / 'bulk') and document that the ZIP must be placed there.
kept.verifier_note: sec_backfill passes cache_root=zip_path.parent (line 120), so resolves_within(zip_path, cache_root) in _validate_zip_location is trivially true. Only the symlink checks have any effect.

kept.title: SEC daily/catch-up marks a date covered even when individual filings failed to download or parse
kept.description: process_filing_row returns True for fetch, parse and promote failures (lines 253-258, 271-279, 283-288). Only a sink exception returns False. _process_date therefore returns True for a day where, say, 30 of 400 filings failed with SecTransportError, SecHttpError 500 or 403, or a 429 after the retries ran out. download_filings_in_range then fires on_progress, and SecDailyIngestionService._record_coverage writes the date into scan_coverage. Every later sec-daily or sec-catchup skips that date, so the failed filings are never retried. The hardened SEC path has the same 'returned means covered' hole as the legacy scrapers. Combined with ARCH-23 (no retry of transport or 5xx errors), one network blip during a catch-up permanently drops filings.
kept.suggestion: Have process_filing_row return a tri-state (ok / transient_failure / permanent_failure). Treat SecTransportError, 5xx and exhausted 429/503 as transient and make _process_date return False when any transient failure happened, so the date stays uncovered and is retried. Count only deterministic parse failures as filing-level skips.

kept.title: Backfill resume re-reads and JSON-decodes the whole submissions ZIP before reaching new work
kept.description: Resume works by filtering accessions after iter_ownership_filings has already decompressed and json.loads-ed each CIK member (sec_bulk.py:201 `data = _read_member_json(zf, info, policy)`). Every restart of an interrupted backfill, which the user does often because it 'does not get to half', re-decodes all previously processed members, several GB of JSON, plus the O(n) checkpoint load before the first new fetch. Restart cost grows with progress.
kept.suggestion: Persist a cursor of the last fully processed ZIP member (index or filename; infolist order is deterministic), and have iter_ownership_filings take a `start_member` argument that skips earlier members without reading them. Keep the per-accession set only for the current member, or drop it.

kept.title: atomic_write_json leaks temp files when interrupted (cleans up only on Exception)
kept.description: KeyboardInterrupt is a BaseException, so a Ctrl+C during the write leaves a `.sec_backfill_checkpoint.json.*.tmp` file behind. Because of ARCH-05, the multi-MB checkpoint write is where the backfill spends a growing share of its time, so interrupts often land there and each one orphans a file of up to tens of MB in EDGAR_CACHE_DIR. sec_downloader._write_atomically handles the same case correctly with `except BaseException`, so the two atomic-write helpers are inconsistent.
kept.suggestion: Use `except BaseException:` (re-raise after unlinking), as _write_atomically does. Or extract one shared atomic-write helper that both modules use.

areas.title: Test suite quality and speed
areas.summary:
The suite is large (about 28k lines, 2,045 tests) and passes: 2032 passed, 5 skipped, 8 live deselected in 107s, run on Python 3.13 with QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen. The repo's own .venv is broken (it points at a missing Python313), so I built a separate venv in the scratchpad. Nothing reaches the network unmocked: a second full run with sockets, DNS and curl_cffi blocked logged zero attempts. The slowest tests are a European test that is out of scope (8.6s), two packaging tests that each build a wheel (7.0s + 4.6s), and seven congress_senate tests that sleep for real (about 16s), so roughly 30% of the runtime is avoidable. The main problems are isolation and gaps on the paths that matter:
- Tests write into the developer's real platformdirs data directory. My runs created %LOCALAPPDATA%/Insider Scanner/Insider Scanner/ (seed files, Cache/, exports/) and rewrote feed_state.json, watchlists.json and alerts.json there.
- The packaging tests rewrite build/ and src/insider_scanner.egg-info inside the repo.
- Bulk backfill is tested only with a 4-record ZIP and loose `>= 1` assertions. A measurement shows the per-filing checkpoint rewrite costs about 0.4s per filing once 500k accessions are done. That is quadratic and very likely the cause of the known "hours and not even half-way" backfill problem.
- The concurrency tests' barrier never actually synchronises (it times out every time, as instrumentation showed).
- One full run with coverage hung for more than 9 minutes on a test_application_shell test and I could not reproduce it. There is no pytest timeout and no CI timeout-minutes to catch a hang like that.
- CI never installs from uv.lock, so the Dependabot uv.lock PRs are effectively untested.
Upsert semantics and the SEC rate limiter/retry logic are well covered by deterministic tests.

kept.title: Tests write into the developer's real user data directory (feed state, watchlists, alerts, seeds)

win = MainWindow()
...

self._state_path: Path = state_path or feed_state_path(DEFAULT_PATHS.data_dir)
# cli.py:793
