The autouse conftest fixture and pytest-qt then close these windows, and MainWindow.closeEvent (main_window.py:713-719) saves feed_state.json, watchlists.json and alerts.json into the real user data directory. Separately, every cli.run() test calls ensure_dirs() on the real paths, which creates the directories and copies the seed files. Observed: after my runs, %LOCALAPPDATA%/Insider Scanner/Insider Scanner/ held congress_members.json, tickers_watchlist.txt, eu_watchlist.txt, Cache/{edgar,scrapers,eu_scrapers} and exports/scans, all created at 13:07:14. feed_state.json, watchlists.json and alerts.json were rewritten at 13:10:39 and again at 13:11:15, once per suite run. On a developer machine this round-trips, and can overwrite (for example after a schema-normalising load), the user's real watchlists and alerts. Test results can also depend on whatever state the user has locally.

The cleanest way is an env-var override (for example INSIDER_SCANNER_DATA_DIR / INSIDER_SCANNER_CACHE_DIR) read by resolve_runtime_paths. Otherwise, monkeypatch config.DEFAULT_PATHS and the derived constants. Pass state_path=tmp_path in test_gui.py as test_application_shell.py already does. Add a guard test that fails if anything under the real platformdirs paths changes during the session.
kept.verifier_note: test_gui.py builds MainWindow() with no state_path at lines 179, 188, 206 and 214. main_window.py:94 then falls back to feed_state_path(DEFAULT_PATHS.data_dir), and closeEvent (713-719) persists feed state, watchlists and alerts there. cli.run() calls the real ensure_dirs() at cli.py:793. Only test_main_entrypoint patches ensure_dirs, and no conftest fixture redirects DEFAULT_PATHS.

kept.title: Backfill rewrites the full sorted checkpoint after every filing, making cost quadratic (measured)
kept.evidence:
if ok and reached_sink[0]:
                    completed.add(meta.accession_number)
                    self._save_completed(zip_path, completed)
...
                    "completed_accessions": sorted(completed),
kept.description: After each completed filing the service sorts the entire completed set and writes it atomically as JSON. I measured atomic_write_json plus sorted() with realistic accession strings in a scratch script (scratchpad/tests/ckpt_bench.py): 4.7 ms per save at 1k completed, 81 ms at 100k (2.9 MB file), and 398 ms at 500k (14.5 MB file). The cost grows linearly with the set, so over N filings the total is O(N^2). For about 1M ownership filings, the checkpoint writes alone add roughly 0.8 µs × N²/2, which is about 4×10^5 s (more than 100 hours). That alone explains the reported 'takes hours and does not get to half'. No test can catch it because the only fixture has 4 records (see TESTS-03).
kept.suggestion: Save the checkpoint every K filings (for example 500) or every T seconds, and once more on interruption or exit. Better still, keep completed accessions in a SQLite table (INSERT per filing, indexed) or an append-only file instead of re-serialising a sorted set. Key resume by a high-water mark (member index + row index) instead of the full set. Pair this with the scale test in TESTS-03.
kept.verifier_note: sec_backfill.py:158-160 calls _save_completed after every retired filing, and that writes sorted(completed) through atomic_write_json (199-210), so each save is O(N) and a full run is O(N^2). There is also a floor the reviewer leaves out: one rate-limited SEC fetch per filing (process_filing_row -> fetch_filing) puts about 28h on 1M filings regardless. Even so, past roughly 100k completed the checkpoint cost exceeds the fetch cost and dominates the total, so 'critical' holds for the known backfill problem.

kept.title: Bulk backfill is only tested with a 4-record fixture: no scale, progress, cancellation or checkpoint-edge tests
kept.evidence: from tests.test_sec_bulk import FIXTURE_ZIP  # reuse the 4-record fixture
kept.description:
Every backfill test runs against sec_submissions_bulk_small.zip, which has 4 ownership rows. The quadratic checkpoint cost (TESTS-02) and per-filing overheads are therefore invisible. The following are also untested:
- on_progress, which run() only calls once at the very end (sec_backfill.py:180-181), so a multi-hour CLI run prints nothing until it finishes. cli.py:521 calls service.run(zip_path, confirm=True, ciks=ciks) with no progress or cancellation.
- The 'different archive -> start fresh' branch, which keys only on zip_path.name (sec_backfill.py:192).
- A version-mismatched or corrupt checkpoint.
- KeyboardInterrupt mid-run preserving the checkpoint, which is how CLI users actually stop a run.
- A SecBulkError raised mid-archive.
kept.suggestion: Add a fixture factory that synthesises a ZIP with N members (for example 5k-20k rows), using a stub transport and an in-memory or tmp DB. Assert the number of checkpoint writes (spy on atomic_write_json) is bounded, for example at most N/K + 2, rather than asserting wall time. Add tests that on_progress is called incrementally, that a checkpoint for a different or renamed archive and a wrong version are ignored, and that an exception or KeyboardInterrupt from the sink leaves a loadable checkpoint.
kept.verifier_note: Every backfill test uses FIXTURE_ZIP, which has 3 CIK JSON members and 4 ownership rows (line 13 import). on_progress is invoked only once, after the loop (180-181), and cli.py:521 passes neither progress nor cancellation. No test covers the zip-name mismatch branch, the version branch, a corrupt checkpoint, or an exception from the sink.

kept.title: Live network tests run by default; `-m "not live"` is only applied in CI
kept.evidence:
addopts = "-v --tb=short"
markers = [
    "live: marks tests that require internet (deselect with '-m \"not live\"')",
kept.description: The live marker is registered but not deselected by default. A plain `pytest` or `uv run pytest` runs the 8 live tests in test_live.py and test_live_prices.py, which hit secform4.com, openinsider.com, SEC EDGAR and Yahoo (8 were deselected in my run only because I passed -m). Local runs then depend on the network, become slow or flaky offline, and send unsolicited traffic to rate-limited third-party sites. --strict-markers is also missing, so a typo such as @pytest.mark.lvie would silently stop gating.
kept.suggestion: Change addopts to `-ra --strict-markers -m "not live"`, and run live tests explicitly with `pytest -m live` (a later -m overrides the default). Optionally, also gate them behind an env var (skip unless INSIDER_SCANNER_LIVE=1).
kept.verifier_note: pyproject.toml:85 sets addopts = "-v --tb=short" with no -m filter and no --strict-markers. test_live.py and test_live_prices.py rely only on pytestmark = pytest.mark.live, so a plain `pytest` hits real sites.

kept.title: CI installs with unpinned pip, so uv.lock (and every Dependabot uv.lock PR) is never tested
kept.evidence: pip install -e ".[gui,dev]"
kept.description: CI resolves the latest versions allowed by pyproject ranges and ignores uv.lock entirely. The recent Dependabot commits (for example 1d46281 'bump msgpack') change only uv.lock, so their CI runs exercise exactly the same environment as before, and the green check says nothing about the bumped versions. In the other direction, a breaking upstream release inside the allowed ranges can turn CI red with no repo change. Developers run from the lockfile, so CI and local environments diverge.
kept.suggestion: Use astral-sh/setup-uv and run `uv sync --frozen --extra gui --extra dev` followed by `uv run pytest ...`, so CI tests the lockfile. If you want to keep coverage of unpinned resolution, add one separate 'latest deps' job (for example weekly) instead.
kept.verifier_note: ci.yml:35 runs `pip install -e ".[gui,dev]"`, which ignores uv.lock. git show --stat confirms that 1d46281 and 6895d1b change only uv.lock, so CI on those PRs exercises nothing that changed.

kept.title: No per-test timeout and no job timeout; one full run hung for more than 9 minutes
kept.evidence:
test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
kept.description: pytest-timeout is not a dependency, pyproject sets no timeout, and the CI jobs have no timeout-minutes, so the default 6-hour GitHub limit applies to each of the 8 matrix jobs. Many tests involve threads, Qt event loops, modal QMessageBox paths and SQLite busy timeouts. Observed: my full run under --cov stopped after 55 tests, inside test_application_shell.py (collection position 56, test_buttons_feed_only_visibility), and sat idle for more than 9 minutes until I killed it. The same tests passed with and without coverage when re-run in smaller groups, so this is an intermittent, order- or timing-dependent hang that nothing would surface quickly.
kept.suggestion: Add pytest-timeout to the dev extras and set `timeout = 60` (with timeout_method = thread on Windows) under [tool.pytest.ini_options]. Add `timeout-minutes: 20` to the test job. When a GUI test hangs, check for an unpatched QMessageBox or exec() modal under offscreen, and for workers still running when persistence.close() is called.
kept.verifier_note: There is no pytest-timeout in the dev extras, no timeout in [tool.pytest.ini_options], and no timeout-minutes on either CI job. I cannot verify the reported hang itself from the code, but the missing guard is real.

kept.title: Concurrency tests' barrier never synchronises: every wait times out, adding 0.5s and testing no interleaving
kept.description: The helper is meant to force two upserts to interleave their SELECTs. Writers use BEGIN IMMEDIATE (persistence/engine.py:66-70), so the second thread blocks on the SQLite write lock before it ever issues a SELECT, and the barrier can never fill. I instrumented threading.Barrier while running test_us_concurrent_upserts_preserve_all_source_provenance, test_european_concurrent_upserts_preserve_complementary_enrichment and test_coverage_concurrent_adds_preserve_complete_union: all six waits ended BROKEN/timeout and none passed. Each test pays about 0.5s (measured 0.59-0.61s). The race the tests describe is never constructed. They only show that serialised writes are correct, which plain sequential calls would show too. The same pattern is in tests/test_coverage.py:124.
kept.suggestion: Remove the barrier and keep a simple two-thread test that asserts the final state, which is what is actually verified. Alternatively, build a real read-modify-write race test: run the barrier before the transaction begins (for example by wrapping repository internals), or assert explicitly that BEGIN IMMEDIATE is issued, which is the actual protection mechanism.
kept.verifier_note: With BEGIN IMMEDIATE (immediate_transaction, engine.py:20-26) the barrier does time out, costing about 0.5s per test. However, it is a regression trap rather than dead code. If upsert ever dropped the IMMEDIATE option, both threads would SELECT under deferred BEGIN, the barrier would force the lost-update interleaving, and the test would fail. Plain sequential calls would not catch that, so removing the barrier as suggested would weaken the test. At most, shorten the timeout or document the intent.

kept.title: Senate EFD tests sleep for real through the module-global rate limiter (about 16s per run)
kept.description: Measured durations: TestEFDSession::test_search 3.00s, test_fetch_page 3.00s, TestSearchSenateFilings::test_empty_results 3.00s, test_filters_paper_filings 3.00s, test_authenticate_retries_403_with_browser_session 2.00s, test_authenticate 1.00s, test_authenticate_no_csrf 1.00s. That is about 16s of pure time.sleep, roughly 15% of the whole suite, on every matrix job. Because _last_request_time is a module global, the amount of sleeping also depends on test order.
kept.suggestion: Add an autouse fixture in test_congress_senate.py that monkeypatches insider_scanner.core.congress_senate._MIN_REQUEST_INTERVAL to 0, or patches time.sleep there. Better, inject a RateLimiter (as SecClient does with sec_fair_access.RateLimiter) so tests pass a no-op limiter. Also move the repeated landing/home/CSRF `responses.add` setup, duplicated 4 times, into a fixture.
kept.verifier_note: congress_senate._rate_limit (72-79) calls time.sleep against a module-global _last_request_time with _MIN_REQUEST_INTERVAL = 1.0, and it is called at lines 119, 140, 241 and 262. test_congress_senate.py never patches _MIN_REQUEST_INTERVAL, _rate_limit or time.sleep, so multi-request tests sleep for real.

kept.title: Packaging tests build the wheel twice, inside the repo tree (writes build/ and egg-info)
kept.evidence:
def _build_wheel(tmp_path) -> ZipFile:
    project_root = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
    ...
                "--no-isolation",
            ...
            cwd=project_root,
kept.description: Each of the two tests runs a full `python -m build --wheel --no-isolation` (measured 6.97s and 4.64s). With --no-isolation and cwd=project_root, setuptools writes build/ and src/insider_scanner.egg-info into the working tree; after my run both had fresh mtimes. A stale build/lib can also leak removed files into later wheels. The cost repeats on all 8 CI jobs.
kept.suggestion: Use a module- or session-scoped fixture that builds the wheel once and shares the ZipFile between both assertions, or merge them into one test. Copy the project to tmp_path first, or pass `-C--build-option=--build-base=<tmp>`, so the repo stays clean. Consider running packaging tests in one CI job only (for example ubuntu / 3.12) through a marker.
kept.verifier_note: Both tests do run a full `python -m build --wheel --no-isolation` with cwd=project_root (lines 23-40), so the duplicate build cost is real. The repo-pollution part is overstated: build/ and *.egg-info/ are gitignored (.gitignore lines 15 and 28). The real harms are the roughly 11s per job and possible stale build/lib contents.

kept.title: Autouse conftest fixture imports PySide6 in every test, contradicting its docstring
kept.evidence:
yield

    from PySide6.QtWidgets import QApplication

    app = QApplication.instance()
kept.description: The docstring says the fixture 'no-ops when no QApplication exists (so non-GUI tests are unaffected and PySide6 is only imported when an app is already live)'. In fact it imports PySide6.QtWidgets unconditionally in the teardown of all ~2,000 tests. A contributor who installs only the base or dev extras (without [gui]) gets an ImportError teardown error on every test, including pure parsing and persistence tests. It also forces Qt to load for non-GUI subsets.
kept.suggestion: Guard the import with `if 'PySide6.QtWidgets' not in sys.modules: return`, or wrap it in try/except ImportError, so the fixture really is a no-op when no Qt app was ever created. Optionally register a `gui` marker and apply it to the GUI modules (see TESTS-18).
kept.verifier_note: The docstring is wrong: line 22 imports PySide6.QtWidgets unconditionally on every teardown. The claimed impact is overstated. The dev extras include pytest-qt, which needs a Qt binding to configure, and many test modules import PySide6, so a dev install without [gui] fails before this fixture matters. This is a docstring/guard mismatch with a small Qt import cost.

kept.title: GUI tests that pass regardless of behaviour (no assertion, or sort order not checked)

kept.title: openinsider tests use vacuous `>= 1` assertions; the ticker-override test cannot fail

kept.title: Live smoke tests pass even when scrapers are completely broken
kept.evidence:
trades = scrape_ticker("AAPL", use_cache=False)
        # May return 0 if site structure changed, but should not error
        assert isinstance(trades, list)
        if trades:
kept.description: The scrapers swallow HTTP and parse errors and return []. Every live test therefore passes when the site layout changes or the request is blocked, which is exactly the regression live tests exist to catch. test_resolve_cik_aapl (line 48) also passes when resolve_cik returns None.
kept.suggestion: Assert non-empty results for a ticker that always has insider activity (AAPL), and assert that cik == '0000320193' without the `if`. If you want tolerance, use pytest.xfail or skip with an explicit reason when the response status indicates blocking, rather than passing silently.
kept.verifier_note: test_live.py asserts only isinstance(list) plus `if trades:` (lines 20-23), and resolve_cik is wrapped in `if cik:` (48). secform4.scrape_ticker returns [] or catches Exception, and resolve_cik catches Exception, so broken scrapers still pass.

kept.title: Tests enshrine that one malformed archive member aborts the entire bulk iteration
kept.evidence:
def test_malformed_json_raises_sec_bulk_error(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    bad_body = b"{not json"
    ...
    with pytest.raises(SecBulkError) as exc_info:
        list(iter_ownership_filings(zip_path, cache_root=tmp_path))
kept.description: sec_bulk.py:308-309 raises SecBulkError out of the generator for one bad JSON member, and SecBackfillService.run (sec_backfill.py:124) does not catch it. A single malformed or truncated member among the roughly 900k in a real submissions.zip therefore stops the multi-hour backfill. Every resume stops at the same point again, after re-iterating all earlier members. The tests assert this abort behaviour and have no test that the backfill survives, skips and counts a bad member.
kept.suggestion: Decide on the intended policy: per-member errors should probably be counted (skipped_metadata or a new skipped_members counter) and iteration should continue, while security violations stay fatal. Update test_sec_bulk to expect a skip, and add a backfill test with a valid / malformed / valid member ZIP that asserts both valid filings are processed.
kept.verifier_note: sec_bulk._read_member_json raises SecBulkError on bad JSON (308-309) from inside the iter_ownership_filings generator (line 201). SecBackfillService.run catches SecBulkError only around bulk_metadata_to_index_row, not around the generator, so one bad member aborts the run at the same point on every resume. test_sec_bulk.py:219 enshrines that behaviour.

kept.title: Backfill resume tests use loose `>= 1` assertions that tolerate double-processing
kept.evidence:
second = resume.run(FIXTURE_ZIP, confirm=True)
    assert second.skipped_resume >= 1
    assert second.filings_parsed >= 1
kept.description: With 4 known records and a cancel-after-one callback, the exact expected values are fixed: 1 skipped, 3 parsed, and transactions_inserted equal to the remaining filings' rows. The `>= 1` checks would still pass if resume re-processed already-completed filings (for example skipped_resume=1 with filings_parsed=4), or if the checkpoint held more or fewer accessions than were really completed. test_mapping_error_is_checkpointed_and_skipped_on_resume (lines 132, 138) has the same weakness. None of the tests reads the checkpoint file to check its contents.
kept.suggestion: Assert exact counters (skipped_resume == 1, filings_parsed == 3, failures == 0). Load backfill.json after the interrupted run and assert that completed_accessions equals exactly the first processed accession. Assert that the total DB row count after both runs equals a single uninterrupted run.
kept.verifier_note: Lines 71-72 (and 132, 138) use `>= 1` even though the outcome is deterministic: 1 skipped and 3 parsed, given that cancel_after_one cancels before the second meta. These checks would pass with double-processing, and no test reads backfill.json to check its contents.

kept.title: Test modules import helpers from other test modules; fixtures and factories are duplicated across files

kept.title: CI's Windows 'skip GUI tests' ignores only test_gui.py, while about 20 other GUI modules still run; xvfb and offscreen are redundant
kept.evidence:
- name: Run tests (Windows — skip GUI widget tests)
        ...
          pytest -m "not live" --ignore=tests/test_gui.py ...
kept.description: About 20 modules use qtbot or QApplication (test_application_shell, test_feed_page, test_investigation_drawer, test_main_window_theme and others) and they all run on Windows (and passed locally on Windows). Only test_gui.py is excluded, so it is the one GUI file with no Windows coverage, and the step name is misleading. On Linux, xvfb-run is combined with QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen, which needs no X server, so the libegl1/xvfb install and the wrapper are wasted.

kept.verifier_note: 22 test modules reference qtbot or QApplication, but the Windows step ignores only tests/test_gui.py (ci.yml:47). Linux wraps the run in xvfb-run while also setting QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen (lines 40-42), which is redundant.

kept.title: CI lint job installs unpinned ruff and skips mypy, which is in the dev extras
kept.evidence:
- run: pip install ruff
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: ruff format --check .
kept.description: The lint job installs whatever ruff is newest, while developers use the version locked through `ruff>=0.15.0` in uv.lock. A new ruff release can turn CI red, or reformat code, with no repo change. mypy (and lxml-stubs) are declared as dev dependencies but never run in CI, so type regressions go unnoticed.
kept.suggestion: Install from the lock (`uv sync --frozen --extra dev` then `uv run ruff ...`), and add a `uv run mypy src/insider_scanner` step, optionally non-blocking at first.
kept.verifier_note: ci.yml:65 installs an unpinned `pip install ruff`, and mypy, although declared in the dev extras, is never run in CI.

kept.title: Duplicate sec-backfill CLI tests; SecBackfillSummary built positionally
kept.description: TestCmdSecBackfill (lines 654-735) and the module-level tests at lines 738-800 cover the same confirm, dispatch and CIK-normalisation behaviour twice, through two entry points. Both construct SecBackfillSummary with 8 positional ints (also at line 710). If the fields are reordered or a field is added, the tests still construct a valid but semantically wrong summary, and the 'discovered=10' print check may still pass by coincidence. The cli.run variants also call the real ensure_dirs() (see TESTS-01).

kept.title: try/assert False/except pattern instead of pytest.raises
kept.description: This pattern is used here and again at lines 429-433. It works only because AssertionError is not a ConnectionError. If the code raised a broader exception type, or if `assert` statements were stripped with python -O, the test would give misleading results. It is also more verbose than the idiom.

kept.title: Calendar-dependent assertions in house year tests
kept.evidence:
def test_neither(self):
        assert _determine_years(None, None) == [date.today().year]
kept.description: These tests depend on the system clock: the production function and the assertion each read date.today() separately, so a run straddling midnight on 31 December fails. The same applies at line 205, test_from_only, and line 425. They also cannot test a fixed scenario such as 'today is 2027-01-02'.
kept.suggestion: Inject `today` into _determine_years (a parameter defaulting to date.today), or freeze time with monkeypatch on the module's date, and assert fixed years.

kept.title: Backfill passes the archive's own parent as cache_root, making the ZIP containment check a no-op (and tests depend on it)
kept.description: sec_bulk._validate_zip_location is documented to 'Reject archives outside the trusted cache root' (resolves_within(zip_path, cache_root)). Because the service passes zip_path.parent, every non-symlinked path passes trivially, so the containment guard never applies to the user-supplied --zip. The backfill tests only work because of this: FIXTURE_ZIP lives in tests/fixtures/, outside any cache root. No test asserts the intended policy either way.
kept.suggestion: Decide the policy explicitly. Either pass the real trusted root (self._cache_root or a downloads dir) and copy or require the archive there, or drop the containment check for user-supplied archives and document that, keeping only the symlink check. Add a backfill test for the chosen behaviour.

kept.title: Each resume re-decompresses and JSON-parses every archive member before reaching new work
kept.evidence:
for info in members:
            ...
            data = _read_member_json(zf, info, policy)
            ...
            yield from _filter_ownership_rows(cik, rows)
kept.description: Resume is keyed only by the accession set (sec_backfill.py:129). On restart, iter_ownership_filings preflights and then fully reads and json.loads every member of the multi-GB submissions.zip (one per CIK), including members whose filings were all completed earlier. The service then discards them one by one through `if meta.accession_number in completed`. Every interrupted run therefore re-pays the decompress-and-parse cost of all earlier members, and this compounds the per-filing checkpoint cost (TESTS-02) for the known slow backfill.
kept.suggestion: Checkpoint a member-level high-water mark (index or name of the last fully completed member) and let iter_ownership_filings take a start_after/skip_members argument so completed members are skipped without being read. Keep the accession set (or a SQLite table) only for the partially done member.

kept.title: One durable SQLite commit per filing with default rollback journal (no WAL / synchronous tuning)
kept.evidence:
cursor.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON")
            cursor.execute(f"PRAGMA busy_timeout={busy_timeout_ms}")
kept.description: No journal_mode or synchronous pragma is set anywhere in src, so SQLite uses the DELETE journal with synchronous=FULL. The backfill sink calls persistence.us_trades.upsert(trades) once per filing (sec_backfill.py:148). Each call opens its own immediate_transaction and commits, which costs several fsyncs per filing (expensive on Windows), plus a SELECT per trade. Over about 1M filings this adds substantial fixed overhead on top of the network and checkpoint costs, and there are no tests or benchmarks for bulk-insert throughput.
kept.suggestion: Enable PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL (and synchronous=NORMAL) in the connect hook. In the backfill, buffer trades and upsert in batches (for example every 500 filings, in one transaction), then retire their accessions after the commit so checkpoint and DB state stay consistent.
